query: How does Airbnb prevent double bookings with overlapping dates?
text: Airbnb System Design (Case Study) Sources: Airbnb Engineering Blog (medium.com/airbnb-engineering) Core challenge: Airbnb's central hard problem isn't just "store listings and bookings" — it's preventing double-booking of the same property for overlapping dates while serving a search experience (browsing available listings by location, dates, price) that needs to be fast across millions of listings. Preventing double bookings: The booking write path needs a strong consistency guarantee: two guests must not both successfully book the same listing for overlapping dates. This is handled with a transactional check-and-reserve against the availability calendar for that listing — the specific listing's availability is the unit that needs strict consistency, even though the overall system is large and distributed. This is a good illustration of a general system design principle: you don't need every part of a large system to be strongly consistent, only the specific slice where correctness actually matters (here: one listing's calendar), while other parts (search, browsing) can be eventually consistent. Search (a different consistency requirement than booking): Search/browse needs to be fast and handle huge read volume, but a search result showing a listing that was juuust booked a few seconds ago by someone else is a minor, acceptable inconsistency — corrected when the user actually tries to book and hits the strongly-consistent availability check. This split (fast/loose for search, strict for the actual booking transaction) is why the search index can be a denormalized, eventually-consistent copy updated asynchronously from the source-of-truth booking/listing data, rather than the search path querying the strongly consistent store directly. Service-Oriented Architecture migration: Airbnb's engineering blog has documented moving from a large Ruby on Rails monolith to a service-oriented architecture as the company scaled — driven by the same forces most large monoliths eventually hit: independent teams needing to deploy independently, and different parts of the system (search vs booking vs payments) having very different scaling and consistency needs that a single monolithic app and database struggled to serve well simultaneously. Experimentation infrastructure: Because pricing, search ranking, and UI changes all materially affect booking conversion (real revenue), Airbnb built significant internal infrastructure for A/B testing at scale — a recurring theme in their engineering blog is treating experimentation itself as core infrastructure, not an afterthought bolted onto the product. Real-world takeaway for interviews: "Design Airbnb" is a common system design interview question specifically because it forces you to identify which part of the system needs strong consistency (the booking transaction against one listing's calendar) versus which parts can be eventually consistent (search results, listing browsing) — correctly drawing that line is the core of the answer, not just listing components.

text: CAP THEOREM AND DISTRIBUTED SYSTEMS CONSISTENCY Sources: Eric Brewer, "CAP Twelve Years Later: How the 'Rules' Have Changed" (IEEE Computer, 2012); Gilbert & Lynch, "Brewer's Conjecture and the Feasibility of Consistent, Available, Partition-Tolerant Web Services" (2002) Overview: The CAP theorem states that a distributed database system can only guarantee two of three properties simultaneously: Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance. Understanding CAP is fundamental to system design — every database and architectural decision involves these trade-offs. The Three Properties: C — Consistency: Every read returns the most recent write (or an error). If you write a value on node 1 and immediately read it from node 2, you get the updated value. This is "strong consistency." Example: bank account balance — you must see the current balance, not a stale one. A — Availability: Every request receives a response (not an error), though it might not be the most recent data. The system keeps responding even if some nodes are down. Example: Netflix shows you recommendations even if their recommendation engine is partially down. P — Partition Tolerance: The system continues operating even if network messages are lost or delayed between nodes. A "partition" = network split where nodes can't communicate. In reality: you cannot opt out of P. Networks fail. Partitions happen. You MUST handle partitions. The Real Choice — CP or AP: Since P is mandatory, the real choice is: when a partition occurs, do you sacrifice C or A? CP (Consistency + Partition Tolerance): - When partition happens: refuse to answer rather than return stale data - Some requests get errors during partition - But when you respond, you're always correct - Examples: ZooKeeper, HBase, Google Spanner, MongoDB (with journaling), traditional relational databases AP (Availability + Partition Tolerance): - When partition happens: respond with possibly stale data - System always responds, never returns error - Data might be outdated temporarily - Examples: Cassandra, DynamoDB, CouchDB, DNS Neither CP nor AP fully — just P: - Technically, traditional SQL in a single datacenter: gives up P (can't run across partitions) - Rarely applicable in modern distributed systems Consistency Models (Spectrum): Strong Consistency (Linearizability): - Every read sees the most recent write - As if there's only one copy of data - Slowest — requires synchronization - Example: Google Spanner uses atomic clocks to achieve this globally Sequential Consistency: - All nodes see operations in same order, but might lag - Operations appear instantaneous but may not be truly real-time Causal Consistency: - Causally related operations are seen in order - "If you see my reply, you must have seen my original post" - Used by some distributed databases Eventual Consistency: - If no new updates, all nodes will eventually have the same value - Queries may return stale data temporarily - Highest availability, used by: DynamoDB, Cassandra, S3 - Most common choice for high-scale systems Read-Your-Own-Writes: - You always see your own updates (even if others don't yet) - Instagram: after you post a photo, you see it even

text: Amazon Dynamo (Case Study) Sources: DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store" (SOSP 2007) Why it was built: Amazon's shopping cart service needed to always accept a write — even during a network partition or node failure — because a customer being unable to add to their cart is a direct lost sale. Traditional strongly-consistent databases prioritize consistency over availability during a partition; Dynamo inverted that priority for this specific use case. Core design goal: always writable. Dynamo chose availability and partition tolerance over strict consistency (the AP side of CAP) — a write should never be rejected because some replicas are temporarily unreachable. This means the system can end up with temporarily conflicting versions of the same data, which it must reconcile later rather than prevent up front. Consistent hashing for partitioning: Data is partitioned across nodes using consistent hashing (each node owns a range on a hash ring). Adding or removing a node only reshuffles the data immediately adjacent to it on the ring, not the entire dataset — critical for a system meant to scale nodes up/down without a massive rebalancing event. Sloppy quorum & hinted handoff: Normally a write requires acknowledgment from W replicas and a read from R replicas (with W + R > N giving strong-ish consistency). But if some of the "correct" replica nodes are down, Dynamo still accepts the write on a different, temporarily-substituting node ("sloppy quorum") rather than rejecting it — the substitute node holds a "hint" to hand the data back to the rightful replica once it recovers (hinted handoff). This is the core mechanism of the "always writable" guarantee. Vector clocks for conflict resolution: Because writes can be accepted by different replicas independently during a partition, the same key can end up with multiple conflicting versions. Dynamo tags each version with a vector clock (tracks which node made which update, in what order) so it can determine if one version is a strict descendant of another (safe to auto-merge) or if they're genuinely concurrent conflicting writes (must be reconciled — Dynamo pushes this reconciliation to the application, e.g. "merge the two shopping carts," since only the application knows how to correctly merge domain data). Read-repair & anti-entropy: When a read encounters divergent versions across replicas, the coordinator can push the resolved/latest version back to the stale replicas ("read repair") instead of waiting for a separate background process — keeps replicas converging toward consistency without blocking writes to do so. Legacy and influence: Dynamo's design (consistent hashing, eventual consistency, vector clocks, "AP over CP" for write availability) directly influenced Cassandra, Riak, and Amazon's own managed DynamoDB — this paper is one of the most cited references in distributed systems design precisely because it made an explicit, well-justified trade-off (availability over consistency) that became a standard pattern to reference when discussing CAP theorem trade-offs in interviews.

Sloppy quorum & hinted handoff: Normally a write requires acknowledgment from W replicas and a read from R replicas (with W + R > N giving strong-ish consistency). But if some of the "correct" replica nodes are down, Dynamo still accepts the write on a different, temporarily-substituting node ("sloppy quorum") rather than rejecting it — the substitute node holds a "hint" to hand the data back to the rightful replica once it recovers (hinted handoff). This is the core mechanism of the "always writable" guarantee. Vector clocks for conflict resolution: Because writes can be accepted by different replicas independently during a partition, the same key can end up with multiple conflicting versions. Dynamo tags each version with a vector clock (tracks which node made which update, in what order) so it can determine if one version is a strict descendant of another (safe to auto-merge) or if they're genuinely concurrent conflicting writes (must be reconciled — Dynamo pushes this reconciliation to the application, e.g. "merge the two shopping carts," since only the application knows how to correctly merge domain data). Read-repair & anti-entropy: When a read encounters divergent versions across replicas, the coordinator can push the resolved/latest version back to the stale replicas ("read repair") instead of waiting for a separate background process — keeps replicas converging toward consistency without blocking writes to do so. Legacy and influence: Dynamo's design (consistent hashing, eventual consistency, vector clocks, "AP over CP" for write availability) directly influenced Cassandra, Riak, and Amazon's own managed DynamoDB — this paper is one of the most cited references in distributed systems design precisely because it made an explicit, well-justified trade-off (availability over consistency) that became a standard pattern to reference when discussing CAP theorem trade-offs in interviews.

text: Event-Driven Architecture & CQRS Sources: Martin Fowler's blog (martinfowler.com — "CQRS", "Event Sourcing"), Microsoft Azure Architecture Center (CQRS pattern, Event-driven architecture style) What event-driven architecture is: Services communicate by emitting events ("OrderPlaced", "PaymentFailed") to a broker (Kafka, SNS, RabbitMQ) rather than calling each other's APIs directly. Interested services subscribe to the events they care about and react independently. Producer doesn't know or care who's listening. Why use it over direct service-to-service calls: Loose coupling — order-service doesn't need to know inventory-service, billing-service, and analytics-service exist; it just publishes "OrderPlaced". Adding a new consumer (e.g. a new fraud-detection service) requires zero changes to the producer. Resilience — if notification-service is down, the event waits in its queue; order-service isn't blocked waiting on a slow downstream call. CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation): Split the model used for writes (commands) from the model used for reads (queries) — instead of one model trying to serve both efficiently. Write side: optimized for validating and persisting a change (e.g. normalized relational tables, enforcing invariants). Read side: optimized for how the data is actually queried (e.g. a denormalized, pre-joined view tailored to a specific screen). The two are kept in sync via events — write side publishes an event on every change, read side subscribes and updates its own denormalized copy. Why CQRS pairs with event-driven design: The event stream that keeps read models in sync *is* the event-driven mechanism — a write triggers an event, one or more read models rebuild themselves from it, independently and asynchronously. Trade-off: eventual consistency. Because the read model updates asynchronously after the write event, there's a window where a query might return stale data (read model hasn't caught up yet). This is fine for a lot of use cases (a "likes count" being one event behind is not a problem) but wrong for anything requiring strict consistency (reading your own bank balance right after a transfer). Event Sourcing (often paired with CQRS, but a separate concept): Instead of storing current state and overwriting it, store the full sequence of events that led to the current state ("AccountOpened", "Deposited $100", "Withdrew $30"). Current state is derived by replaying events. Benefit: full audit trail for free, and you can rebuild any past state or fix a bug in projection logic by replaying history with corrected logic. Cost: replaying a long event history to get current state is slow without periodic snapshots; more operational complexity than just storing current state. Real-world example: An e-commerce order system publishes "OrderPlaced" on write. A dedicated "OrderSummaryView" read model (denormalized, stored in a fast key-value store) subscribes and updates itself — this is the exact table the "My Orders" page in the app queries, pre-shaped for that screen, entirely separate from the normalized orders/line_items tables used to validate and place the order in the first place.

text: Bloom Filters Sources: Burton H. Bloom, "Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding with Allowable Errors" (1970), Redis documentation (Bloom Filter / probabilistic data structures) What it is: A probabilistic data structure that answers "have I possibly seen this item before?" using a fixed, tiny amount of memory — regardless of how many items have been added. Trades perfect accuracy for massive space savings. The guarantee (this is the important part): No false negatives: if the filter says "definitely not present," the item is genuinely not present. Possible false positives: if the filter says "possibly present," it might actually not be — the false positive rate is tunable (smaller filter / more items = higher false positive rate). It never says "definitely present" for something that was never added incorrectly in the wrong direction — the asymmetry only goes one way, which is what makes it usable: you only need a secondary, slower check for the "possibly present" case. How it works: A bit array of m bits, all initially 0, plus k independent hash functions. To add an item: hash it k times, set the k resulting bit positions to 1. To check an item: hash it the same k times, if ALL k bit positions are 1, report "possibly present"; if ANY bit is 0, report "definitely not present" (since adding that item would have set that bit). False positives happen because bits get shared/overwritten by other items' hashes — you can't tell whether a set bit was set by the item you're checking or by pure coincidence from other insertions. Why not just use a hash set: A hash set storing millions of actual keys uses far more memory (must store each key or at least its full hash) than a Bloom filter, which only needs a handful of bits per item regardless of key size. The trade is: a hash set has zero false positives, a Bloom filter accepts a small false-positive rate in exchange for a fraction of the memory. Cannot remove items (in the basic version): Because bits are shared across multiple items' hashes, clearing a bit to "remove" one item could break the correctness for other items that also set that bit. A Counting Bloom Filter (using small counters instead of single bits) supports removal at the cost of more memory — used when deletions are actually needed. Real-world example: A CDN or database wants to avoid an expensive disk/network lookup for keys that definitely don't exist (e.g. checking if a URL is on a known-malicious list, or if a cache key might exist before hitting disk). Check the Bloom filter first: if "definitely not present," skip the expensive lookup entirely. If "possibly present," do the real (slower, authoritative) lookup to confirm — the small false-positive rate just means occasionally doing an unnecessary real lookup, never missing an item that's actually there. text: Consistent Hashing Sources: Karger et al., "Consistent Hashing and Random Trees" (STOC 1997); DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store" (SOSP 2007) Problem it solves: In a distributed system with N servers, naive hashing (key % N) breaks when servers are added or removed — almost all keys need remapping. Consistent hashing ensures only K/N keys are remapped when a server changes (K = total keys, N = servers). How it works: 1. Place servers on a circular ring using hash(server_id) 2. For each key: hash(key) → find the next server clockwise on the ring 3. Adding a server: only keys between new server and its predecessor move 4. Removing a server: only keys that mapped to it move to next server Virtual Nodes (vnodes): Each physical server gets multiple positions on the ring (e.g., 150 virtual nodes). Benefits: - More even load distribution - When a server fails, its load spreads across multiple servers (not just one) - Accounts for servers of different capacities (powerful server = more vnodes) Real-world usage: - Amazon DynamoDB: partitioning data across nodes - Apache Cassandra: distributing data across cluster - Discord: distributing chat messages - CDNs: routing requests to cache servers - Redis Cluster: slot assignment When to use: Use consistent hashing when you have a distributed cache or storage layer that needs to scale horizontally with minimal data movement on topology changes. Trade-offs: Pro: Minimal remapping when cluster changes Pro: Even distribution with virtual nodes Con: More complex than simple modulo hashing Con: Hot spots possible without virtual nodes

B-Tree index (the default, general-purpose case): Balanced tree structure, keeps data sorted, supports equality (=) and range (<, >, BETWEEN) queries efficiently, and supports ORDER BY without an extra sort step if the sort matches the index order. Faster than B-Tree for pure equality lookups in principle, but rarely used in practice because B-Tree covers equality well enough and also handles ranges — using a hash index means giving up range queries for a marginal equality speedup. Composite (multi-column) indexes and column order: An index on (user_id, created_at) can efficiently serve queries filtering on user_id alone, or user_id + created_at together — but NOT an efficient query on created_at alone, because the index is sorted by user_id first. text: Message Queues & Pub-Sub Sources: AWS SQS Developer Guide, RabbitMQ documentation, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) ch.11 What it is: A message queue decouples producers (services that create work) from consumers (services that process it). Producer pushes a message, queue holds it, consumer pulls and processes it whenever ready. Neither side needs the other to be online at the same instant. Why use one: Smooths traffic spikes — queue absorbs a burst, consumers drain it at their own pace. Decouples services — producer doesn't care if consumer is slow, down, or scaled to zero. Enables retries — failed messages can be redelivered instead of lost. Enables async workflows — user gets a fast response, heavy work happens in background (e.g. "order placed" returns instantly, email/invoice generation happens after). Point-to-point vs Pub/Sub: Point-to-point (queue): one message, one consumer. Used for task distribution — e.g. a pool of workers pulling image-resize jobs off a queue. Pub/Sub (topic): one message, many subscribers. Used for fan-out — e.g. "order placed" event notifies inventory service, billing service, and analytics service simultaneously. Delivery guarantees: At-most-once: message may be lost, never duplicated. Fastest, least safe. At-least-once: message guaranteed delivered, but may be duplicated on retry. Most systems (SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka) default to this — consumers must be idempotent. Exactly-once: hardest to guarantee in a distributed system; usually achieved by combining at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers (dedupe by message ID), not by the queue itself. Visibility timeout / ack: Consumer pulls a message; queue hides it from other consumers for a timeout window. Consumer processes it, then explicitly acknowledges (deletes) the message. If consumer crashes before ack, message becomes visible again and another consumer picks it up — this is why consumers must be idempotent, since a message could be processed twice. Dead-letter queues (DLQ): Messages that fail processing repeatedly (e.g. 5 retries) are moved to a separate DLQ instead of blocking the main queue forever. Lets you inspect and reprocess poison messages without stalling healthy traffic. Queue vs Kafka: Traditional queues (SQS, RabbitMQ) delete a message once consumed — it's gone. Kafka is a log: messages are retained for a configured period and consumers track their own offset, so multiple consumer groups can replay the same stream independently. Use a queue for simple task distribution; use Kafka when you need replay, ordering within a partition, or multiple independent consumers of the same event stream. Real-world example: E-commerce checkout: "order placed" event published to a topic. → Inventory service subscribes, decrements stock. → Billing service subscribes, charges card. → Notification service subscribes, sends confirmation email. Each subscriber processes independently; if the email service is down, the order still completes — the message just waits in that service's queue until it recovers.

text: Search & Indexing (Inverted Index) Sources: Elasticsearch documentation ("Inverted index"), Apache Lucene documentation What it is: Searching billions of documents for a keyword by scanning each one would be far too slow. Search engines instead build an inverted index ahead of time — a data structure that maps each word to the list of documents containing it — so a search becomes a fast lookup instead of a full scan. Forward index vs inverted index: Forward index: document → list of words it contains (this is the natural way you'd store a document, but useless for "find all docs containing X"). Inverted index: word → list of documents containing it. Flips the mapping so a query for a term is a single lookup, not a scan of every document. Building the index: 1. Tokenization: split text into individual terms ("The quick fox" → ["the", "quick", "fox"]). 2. Normalization: lowercase, remove punctuation, stemming (running → run) so "run", "runs", "running" all match the same index entry. 3. Stop word removal (optional): common words like "the", "is" are often excluded since they match nearly everything and add little search value. 4. For each remaining term, append the document ID (and often position within the document, for phrase search) to that term's posting list. Querying: A search for "quick fox" looks up the posting list for "quick" and for "fox", then intersects them — documents in both lists contain both words. Ranking (which result appears first) typically uses TF-IDF or BM25: term frequency (how often the word appears in this doc) weighted against inverse document frequency (how rare the word is across all docs) — a rare word matching is a stronger signal than a common word matching. Distributed search (how this scales to billions of documents): The full index doesn't fit on one machine. It's split into shards, each holding a subset of documents and its own local inverted index. A query fans out to every shard in parallel, each returns its top-N matches, and a coordinating node merges and re-ranks the combined results — this is exactly how Elasticsearch/Solr scale search across a cluster. Each shard is also typically replicated for both availability and to spread read (query) load across replicas. Real-time-ish updates: New documents don't need a full index rebuild — an update is added as a small new index segment; a background merge process periodically combines small segments into larger ones for query efficiency. This is why "just indexed" documents often show up in search within seconds, not instantly, and why search indexes trade a small delay for much better write throughput. Real-world example: An e-commerce product search: catalog of 50M products is sharded across many nodes. Searching "wireless headphones" fans out to every shard, each returns its best local matches ranked by BM25, coordinator merges and returns the final top 20 — the same pattern used by product search on any major e-commerce site or by Elasticsearch-backed log search internally at a company.

text: Caching Strategies — System Design Sources: AWS Caching Best Practices documentation, Redis documentation, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) Why cache: Database reads are slow (milliseconds). Cache reads are fast (microseconds). 80% of traffic typically reads 20% of data (Pareto principle). Cache that 20% and handle 80% of load without hitting the database. Cache Types: 1. Application Cache (in-memory, local): Stored in the application's own memory. Fastest possible. Problem: Not shared across servers. Each server has its own cache. Use for: static config, lookup tables that rarely change. 2. Distributed Cache (Redis, Memcached): Shared cache server all application servers connect to. Slightly slower than local cache but consistent across fleet. Redis supports rich data structures: strings, lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes. Use for: session data, rate limiting counters, leaderboards, pub/sub. 3. CDN Cache: Caches static assets (images, JS, CSS) at edge locations globally. Requests served from nearest edge node — dramatically lower latency. Use for: static files, video content, public API responses. Cache Invalidation Strategies (the hard problem): Write-through: Write to cache AND database simultaneously. Pro: Cache always consistent. Con: Write latency increases. Write-behind (Write-back): Write to cache first, async to database. Pro: Low write latency. Con: Data loss risk if cache crashes before DB write. Cache-aside (Lazy loading): Application checks cache first. Miss → read from DB → store in cache → return. Most common pattern. Pro: Only caches what's actually read. Con: First request after cache miss is slow (cache miss penalty). Read-through: Cache sits in front of DB. Cache handles DB reads automatically. Application only talks to cache. TTL (Time to Live): Every cached item should have an expiry time. Without TTL: stale data stays forever (cache poisoning risk). Set TTL based on how often data changes: - User session: 24 hours - Product price: 5 minutes - Static config: 1 hour Cache Eviction Policies (when cache is full): LRU (Least Recently Used): Evict item not accessed for longest time. Most common. LFU (Least Frequently Used): Evict item accessed fewest times. FIFO: Evict oldest item. Simple but often suboptimal. Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd): Problem: Popular cache key expires. 1000 requests all miss → all hit DB simultaneously → DB crashes. Solutions: 1. Mutex lock — only first request fetches from DB, others wait. 2. Background refresh — refresh cache before TTL expires. 3. Jitter — add random offset to TTL so keys don't expire simultaneously. Redis at Scale (Zepto, Swiggy use case): Redis Sentinel: High availability — automatic failover if primary fails. Redis Cluster: Horizontal scaling — data sharded across multiple Redis nodes. Read replicas: Route read-heavy workloads to replicas.

text: Facebook TAO & Memcache at Scale (Case Study) Sources: Bronson et al., "TAO: Facebook's Distributed Data Store for the Social Graph" (USENIX ATC 2013), Nishtala et al., "Scaling Memcache at Facebook" (NSDI 2013) The problem: Facebook's social graph (users, friendships, likes, comments — modeled as nodes and edges) is read far more often than it's written, at massive scale, and the underlying data lived in sharded MySQL. Serving graph reads directly from MySQL at that read volume was not feasible — the read/write ratio was extremely skewed toward reads. Scaling Memcache at Facebook (the caching layer): Facebook ran one of the largest memcached deployments in the world — trillions of items across many clusters. Key lessons from that paper: Look-aside cache pattern: application code checks memcache first, on a miss reads from MySQL and populates the cache — memcache itself has no knowledge of the database, it's purely a fast key-value layer in front of it. Thundering herd / cache stampede problem: if a popular key expires, many requests can miss simultaneously and all hit the database at once for the same key. Mitigated with a "lease" mechanism — only one request is allowed to go fetch from the database and repopulate the cache; other concurrent requests for the same key wait briefly rather than all hitting the DB. Invalidation across regions: when data changes, the region owning the write broadcasts invalidations to caches in other regions — because Facebook serves from multiple geographic regions, simply relying on TTL expiry alone would leave far-flung caches stale for too long. TAO (the graph-aware layer built on top of that caching experience): Rather than have every service reimplement "cache the graph efficiently," Facebook built TAO as a dedicated read-through cache purpose-built for the social graph's actual access patterns — objects (nodes: a post, a user) and associations (edges: "likes," "friends") — instead of a generic key-value cache that every team had to hand-tune for graph queries. Read-heavy optimization: TAO explicitly favors availability and low latency for reads over strict consistency — a "like" count might be very briefly stale across regions, an acceptable trade for the massive read volume TAO serves. Write-through with async replication: writes go to the region's master database, and are asynchronously replicated to other regions' caches — again prioritizing not blocking the write path on cross-region consistency. The general lesson (useful beyond Facebook specifically): Both papers describe the same underlying pattern: a very read-heavy workload at extreme scale is served by pushing reads into a cache layer tuned for the specific access pattern (generic key-value for Memcache, graph-specific for TAO), while accepting eventual/relaxed consistency as a deliberate trade-off for availability and latency — and building explicit mechanisms (leases, cross-region invalidation) to control exactly how stale the cache is allowed to get, rather than leaving it unbounded.

text: Caching Strategies — System Design Sources: AWS Caching Best Practices documentation, Redis documentation, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) Why cache: Database reads are slow (milliseconds). Cache reads are fast (microseconds). 80% of traffic typically reads 20% of data (Pareto principle). Cache that 20% and handle 80% of load without hitting the database. Cache Types: 1. Application Cache (in-memory, local): Stored in the application's own memory. Fastest possible. Problem: Not shared across servers. Each server has its own cache. Use for: static config, lookup tables that rarely change. 2. Distributed Cache (Redis, Memcached): Shared cache server all application servers connect to. Slightly slower than local cache but consistent across fleet. Redis supports rich data structures: strings, lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes. Use for: session data, rate limiting counters, leaderboards, pub/sub. 3. CDN Cache: Caches static assets (images, JS, CSS) at edge locations globally. Requests served from nearest edge node — dramatically lower latency. Use for: static files, video content, public API responses. Cache Invalidation Strategies (the hard problem): Write-through: Write to cache AND database simultaneously. Pro: Cache always consistent. Con: Write latency increases. Write-behind (Write-back): Write to cache first, async to database. Pro: Low write latency. Con: Data loss risk if cache crashes before DB write. Cache-aside (Lazy loading): Application checks cache first. Miss → read from DB → store in cache → return. Most common pattern. Pro: Only caches what's actually read. Con: First request after cache miss is slow (cache miss penalty). Read-through: Cache sits in front of DB. Cache handles DB reads automatically. Application only talks to cache. TTL (Time to Live): Every cached item should have an expiry time. Without TTL: stale data stays forever (cache poisoning risk). Set TTL based on how often data changes: - User session: 24 hours - Product price: 5 minutes - Static config: 1 hour Cache Eviction Policies (when cache is full): LRU (Least Recently Used): Evict item not accessed for longest time. Most common. LFU (Least Frequently Used): Evict item accessed fewest times. FIFO: Evict oldest item. Simple but often suboptimal. Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd): Problem: Popular cache key expires. 1000 requests all miss → all hit DB simultaneously → DB crashes. Solutions: 1. Mutex lock — only first request fetches from DB, others wait. 2. Background refresh — refresh cache before TTL expires. 3. Jitter — add random offset to TTL so keys don't expire simultaneously. Redis at Scale (Zepto, Swiggy use case): Redis Sentinel: High availability — automatic failover if primary fails. Redis Cluster: Horizontal scaling — data sharded across multiple Redis nodes. Read replicas: Route read-heavy workloads to replicas.

text: Rate Limiter System Design Sources: Stripe API documentation (Rate Limiters), Cloudflare Learning Center (Rate Limiting) What it is: A rate limiter controls how many requests a client can make in a given time window. Critical for APIs to prevent abuse, ensure fair usage, and protect backend services. Used by every major API: Twitter, Stripe, Razorpay, GitHub. Algorithms: 1. Token Bucket (most common): Each user gets a bucket with N tokens. Each request consumes one token. Tokens refill at a fixed rate. If bucket empty, request rejected. Allows short bursts (use all tokens at once) but limits sustained rate. Used by: AWS API Gateway, Stripe. 2. Sliding Window Log: Store timestamp of every request in a sorted set (Redis). On each request, remove timestamps older than window, count remaining. If count >= limit, reject. Accurate but memory-intensive. 3. Fixed Window Counter: Simple counter per user per time window (e.g., per minute). Reset counter at window boundary. Fast and memory efficient. Problem: burst at window boundary (double the rate for a brief moment). 4. Leaky Bucket: Requests enter a queue (bucket). Processed at fixed rate. Smooths out bursts. Good for output rate limiting. Implementation with Redis: Redis is ideal for rate limiting because: - Atomic operations (INCR, EXPIRE) prevent race conditions - Sub-millisecond latency - Distributed — works across multiple API server instances Redis token bucket implementation: INCR user:123:requests EXPIRE user:123:requests 60 If value > limit: reject request Where to implement: - API Gateway layer (before hitting your services) - Middleware in FastAPI/Express - Nginx level for simple cases Distributed Rate Limiting Challenge: With multiple servers, each server has its own counter. Solution: Centralized Redis store shared across all servers. Trade-off: Redis becomes a bottleneck — use Redis Cluster for scale. Real example — Razorpay API: 100 requests per minute per API key. Exceeded: HTTP 429 Too Many Requests. Headers returned: X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset.

text: CAP THEOREM AND DISTRIBUTED SYSTEMS CONSISTENCY Sources: Eric Brewer, "CAP Twelve Years Later: How the 'Rules' Have Changed" (IEEE Computer, 2012); Gilbert & Lynch, "Brewer's Conjecture and the Feasibility of Consistent, Available, Partition-Tolerant Web Services" (2002) Overview: The CAP theorem states that a distributed database system can only guarantee two of three properties simultaneously: Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance. Understanding CAP is fundamental to system design — every database and architectural decision involves these trade-offs. The Three Properties: C — Consistency: Every read returns the most recent write (or an error). If you write a value on node 1 and immediately read it from node 2, you get the updated value. This is "strong consistency." Example: bank account balance — you must see the current balance, not a stale one. A — Availability: Every request receives a response (not an error), though it might not be the most recent data. The system keeps responding even if some nodes are down. Example: Netflix shows you recommendations even if their recommendation engine is partially down. P — Partition Tolerance: The system continues operating even if network messages are lost or delayed between nodes. A "partition" = network split where nodes can't communicate. In reality: you cannot opt out of P. Networks fail. Partitions happen. You MUST handle partitions. The Real Choice — CP or AP: Since P is mandatory, the real choice is: when a partition occurs, do you sacrifice C or A? CP (Consistency + Partition Tolerance): - When partition happens: refuse to answer rather than return stale data - Some requests get errors during partition - But when you respond, you're always correct - Examples: ZooKeeper, HBase, Google Spanner, MongoDB (with journaling), traditional relational databases AP (Availability + Partition Tolerance): - When partition happens: respond with possibly stale data - System always responds, never returns error - Data might be outdated temporarily - Examples: Cassandra, DynamoDB, CouchDB, DNS Neither CP nor AP fully — just P: - Technically, traditional SQL in a single datacenter: gives up P (can't run across partitions) - Rarely applicable in modern distributed systems Consistency Models (Spectrum): Strong Consistency (Linearizability): - Every read sees the most recent write - As if there's only one copy of data - Slowest — requires synchronization - Example: Google Spanner uses atomic clocks to achieve this globally Sequential Consistency: - All nodes see operations in same order, but might lag - Operations appear instantaneous but may not be truly real-time Causal Consistency: - Causally related operations are seen in order - "If you see my reply, you must have seen my original post" - Used by some distributed databases Eventual Consistency: - If no new updates, all nodes will eventually have the same value - Queries may return stale data temporarily - Highest availability, used by: DynamoDB, Cassandra, S3 - Most common choice for high-scale systems Read-Your-Own-Writes: - You always see your own updates (even if others don't yet) - Instagram: after you post a photo, you see it even

text: Load Balancer System Design Sources: AWS Elastic Load Balancing documentation, NGINX documentation (Load Balancing) What it is: A load balancer distributes incoming network traffic across multiple servers. Prevents any single server from becoming a bottleneck. Essential for high availability and horizontal scaling. Types of Load Balancers: 1. Layer 4 (Transport Layer): Routes based on IP and TCP/UDP port. Fast, no content inspection. Cannot route based on URL path or headers. Example: AWS Network Load Balancer. 2. Layer 7 (Application Layer): Routes based on HTTP content — URL, headers, cookies. Can do path-based routing (/api → API servers, /static → CDN). Example: AWS Application Load Balancer, Nginx. Load Balancing Algorithms: Round Robin: Requests distributed evenly in order. Simple, works well when servers have equal capacity. Weighted Round Robin: Servers get requests proportional to weight. Used when servers have different capacities. Least Connections: New request goes to server with fewest active connections. Better for long-lived connections (WebSockets, streaming). IP Hash: Client IP hashed to always hit same server. Useful for session stickiness (user always hits same server). Problem: uneven distribution if many users share an IP (NAT). Consistent Hashing: Used for distributed cache and storage routing. Minimizes remapping when servers are added or removed. Health Checks: Load balancer pings each server every few seconds. If server fails health check, removed from rotation automatically. When server recovers, added back automatically. This is how zero-downtime deployments work. Session Stickiness (Sticky Sessions): Problem: User login session stored on Server A. Request goes to Server B — user logged out. Solution 1: Sticky sessions — same user always hits same server (IP hash). Solution 2: Externalize sessions to Redis — any server can read any session. Solution 2 is better for true stateless servers. Real-world stack for Swiggy scale: DNS → AWS Route53 (global traffic routing) → AWS CloudFront (CDN + DDoS protection) → AWS ALB (Layer 7, path-based routing) → Auto Scaling Groups (EC2 instances) → Services

text: Database Replication & Failover Sources: PostgreSQL documentation (Replication), MySQL documentation (Replication), "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) ch.5 What it is: Replication keeps copies of the same data on multiple database nodes. Goals: survive a node failure without data loss, serve more read traffic than one machine can handle, and keep data closer to users in different regions. Leader-follower (primary-replica) replication: One node (leader) accepts all writes. Writes are streamed to one or more followers, which apply them and can serve read traffic. Most common setup for relational databases (Postgres, MySQL). Synchronous vs asynchronous replication: Synchronous: leader waits for follower to confirm the write before acknowledging the client. Zero data loss on failover, but write latency includes network round-trip to the follower, and the leader stalls if the follower is slow/down. Asynchronous: leader acknowledges the client immediately, follower catches up in the background. Fast writes, but a leader crash before replication completes means recent writes are lost. Semi-synchronous: at least one follower confirms synchronously, rest are async — common middle ground (used by MySQL semi-sync replication). Replication lag: The delay between a write on the leader and it appearing on a follower. Causes "read-your-own-writes" bugs: user updates their profile, immediately reloads the page, request is routed to a lagging follower, sees stale data. Fixed by: routing a user's own reads to the leader for a short window after they write, or reading from the same replica they just wrote through. Failover: When the leader dies, a follower must be promoted to leader. Manual failover: safer, slower — human confirms the old leader is really dead before promoting, avoiding split-brain. Automatic failover: faster recovery, but risk of split-brain — if the network partition means the old leader is alive but unreachable, promoting a new leader means two leaders may accept writes simultaneously, causing conflicting data. Tools like Patroni (Postgres) or Orchestrator (MySQL) use a consensus store (etcd/ZooKeeper) to agree on the new leader safely. Multi-leader and leaderless replication: Multi-leader: multiple nodes accept writes, used across data centers — but requires conflict resolution when the same record is written in two places. Leaderless (e.g. Cassandra, DynamoDB style): client writes to several replicas directly and reads from several, using quorum (W + R > N) to guarantee it sees the latest write. No single leader means no failover pause, but consistency is weaker and requires read-repair for divergent replicas. Real-world example: A typical production Postgres setup: one primary handles all writes, two read replicas serve read-heavy endpoints (e.g. product catalog browsing). Patroni monitors primary health via etcd; if the primary fails a health check, etcd elects a new leader from the replicas and updates DNS/proxy routing automatically — this is what "high availability" means for a database in practice.

text: CAP THEOREM AND DISTRIBUTED SYSTEMS CONSISTENCY Sources: Eric Brewer, "CAP Twelve Years Later: How the 'Rules' Have Changed" (IEEE Computer, 2012); Gilbert & Lynch, "Brewer's Conjecture and the Feasibility of Consistent, Available, Partition-Tolerant Web Services" (2002) Overview: The CAP theorem states that a distributed database system can only guarantee two of three properties simultaneously: Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance. Understanding CAP is fundamental to system design — every database and architectural decision involves these trade-offs. The Three Properties: C — Consistency: Every read returns the most recent write (or an error). If you write a value on node 1 and immediately read it from node 2, you get the updated value. This is "strong consistency." Example: bank account balance — you must see the current balance, not a stale one. A — Availability: Every request receives a response (not an error), though it might not be the most recent data. The system keeps responding even if some nodes are down. Example: Netflix shows you recommendations even if their recommendation engine is partially down. P — Partition Tolerance: The system continues operating even if network messages are lost or delayed between nodes. A "partition" = network split where nodes can't communicate. In reality: you cannot opt out of P. Networks fail. Partitions happen. You MUST handle partitions. The Real Choice — CP or AP: Since P is mandatory, the real choice is: when a partition occurs, do you sacrifice C or A? CP (Consistency + Partition Tolerance): - When partition happens: refuse to answer rather than return stale data - Some requests get errors during partition - But when you respond, you're always correct - Examples: ZooKeeper, HBase, Google Spanner, MongoDB (with journaling), traditional relational databases AP (Availability + Partition Tolerance): - When partition happens: respond with possibly stale data - System always responds, never returns error - Data might be outdated temporarily - Examples: Cassandra, DynamoDB, CouchDB, DNS Neither CP nor AP fully — just P: - Technically, traditional SQL in a single datacenter: gives up P (can't run across partitions) - Rarely applicable in modern distributed systems Consistency Models (Spectrum): Strong Consistency (Linearizability): - Every read sees the most recent write - As if there's only one copy of data - Slowest — requires synchronization - Example: Google Spanner uses atomic clocks to achieve this globally Sequential Consistency: - All nodes see operations in same order, but might lag - Operations appear instantaneous but may not be truly real-time Causal Consistency: - Causally related operations are seen in order - "If you see my reply, you must have seen my original post" - Used by some distributed databases Eventual Consistency: - If no new updates, all nodes will eventually have the same value - Queries may return stale data temporarily - Highest availability, used by: DynamoDB, Cassandra, S3 - Most common choice for high-scale systems Read-Your-Own-Writes: - You always see your own updates (even if others don't yet) - Instagram: after you post a photo, you see it even

text: Amazon Dynamo (Case Study) Sources: DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store" (SOSP 2007) Why it was built: Amazon's shopping cart service needed to always accept a write — even during a network partition or node failure — because a customer being unable to add to their cart is a direct lost sale. Traditional strongly-consistent databases prioritize consistency over availability during a partition; Dynamo inverted that priority for this specific use case. Core design goal: always writable. Dynamo chose availability and partition tolerance over strict consistency (the AP side of CAP) — a write should never be rejected because some replicas are temporarily unreachable. This means the system can end up with temporarily conflicting versions of the same data, which it must reconcile later rather than prevent up front. Consistent hashing for partitioning: Data is partitioned across nodes using consistent hashing (each node owns a range on a hash ring). Adding or removing a node only reshuffles the data immediately adjacent to it on the ring, not the entire dataset — critical for a system meant to scale nodes up/down without a massive rebalancing event. Sloppy quorum & hinted handoff: Normally a write requires acknowledgment from W replicas and a read from R replicas (with W + R > N giving strong-ish consistency). But if some of the "correct" replica nodes are down, Dynamo still accepts the write on a different, temporarily-substituting node ("sloppy quorum") rather than rejecting it — the substitute node holds a "hint" to hand the data back to the rightful replica once it recovers (hinted handoff). This is the core mechanism of the "always writable" guarantee. Vector clocks for conflict resolution: Because writes can be accepted by different replicas independently during a partition, the same key can end up with multiple conflicting versions. Dynamo tags each version with a vector clock (tracks which node made which update, in what order) so it can determine if one version is a strict descendant of another (safe to auto-merge) or if they're genuinely concurrent conflicting writes (must be reconciled — Dynamo pushes this reconciliation to the application, e.g. "merge the two shopping carts," since only the application knows how to correctly merge domain data). Read-repair & anti-entropy: When a read encounters divergent versions across replicas, the coordinator can push the resolved/latest version back to the stale replicas ("read repair") instead of waiting for a separate background process — keeps replicas converging toward consistency without blocking writes to do so. Legacy and influence: Dynamo's design (consistent hashing, eventual consistency, vector clocks, "AP over CP" for write availability) directly influenced Cassandra, Riak, and Amazon's own managed DynamoDB — this paper is one of the most cited references in distributed systems design precisely because it made an explicit, well-justified trade-off (availability over consistency) that became a standard pattern to reference when discussing CAP theorem trade-offs in interviews.

text: SQL VS NOSQL — WHEN TO USE WHICH Sources: MongoDB documentation, PostgreSQL documentation, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) ch.2-3 Overview: One of the most common system design interview questions is "what database would you use?" There's no universal answer — the right choice depends on your data model, access patterns, consistency requirements, and scale. Understanding the trade-offs is more important than memorizing which is "better." SQL (Relational Databases): Examples: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, Oracle Core Characteristics: - Data organized in tables with fixed schemas (columns defined upfront) - ACID transactions: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability - SQL query language — powerful, joins, aggregations, subqueries - Strong consistency — reads always reflect latest writes - Relations between tables via foreign keys - Vertical scaling primarily (add more CPU/RAM to one server) When to use SQL: - Complex relationships between entities (users → orders → products → inventory) - Need ACID transactions (banking, e-commerce, healthcare) - Data structure is well-defined and unlikely to change frequently - Need complex queries with joins and aggregations - Team knows SQL well (most developers do) - Compliance requirements (many regulations require ACID) NoSQL (Non-Relational Databases): Four types: Document, Key-Value, Column-Family, Graph 1. Document Stores (MongoDB, CouchDB, Firestore): - Data stored as JSON/BSON documents - Flexible schema: different documents can have different fields - Good for: product catalogs, user profiles, content management - Example: MongoDB stores restaurant menus — each restaurant has different menu structure - Query: rich queries on nested fields, but no joins across collections 2. Key-Value Stores (Redis, DynamoDB, Memcached): - Simplest NoSQL: key → value - Extremely fast (O(1) lookup) - Good for: caching, session storage, rate limiting, leaderboards (Redis sorted sets) - Limited query capability — only lookup by key (or key prefix) - Redis extra: supports list, set, hash, sorted set, stream data structures 3. Wide-Column / Column-Family (Cassandra, HBase, DynamoDB): - Rows with flexible columns, organized by partition key - Data spread across nodes by partition key — horizontally scalable - Good for: time-series data, IoT data, message history, activity logs - Cassandra strengths: write-heavy workloads, no single point of failure - Query: must specify partition key; range queries on sort key; no arbitrary queries 4. Graph Databases (Neo4j, Amazon Neptune, JanusGraph): - Data stored as nodes and edges (relationships) - Optimized for traversing relationships - Good for: social networks (friends-of-friends), recommendation engines, fraud detection - Query: Cypher (Neo4j), Gremlin — traverse graph relationships - Overkill for simple use cases; excellent for complex relationship queries Comparison Table: Property | SQL (PostgreSQL) | Document (MongoDB) | Wide-Column (Cassandra) | Key-Value (Redis) Schema | Fixed | Flexible | Flexible columns | None (any value) Transactions | Full ACID | Multi-doc ACID | Lightweight batch only | Basic (MULTI/EXEC) Query Language | SQL (very powerful) | MQL (moderate) | CQL (limited) | Commands only Horizontal Scale | Hard (sharding) | Built-in sharding | Native (ring) | Cluster mode Consistency | Strong | Tunable | Tunable (eventual) | Strong (single) / Eventual (cluster) Best for

text: Database Indexing & Query Optimization Sources: PostgreSQL documentation (Indexes), "Use The Index, Luke" (use-the-index-luke.com) What an index is: Without an index, finding a row matching a WHERE clause means scanning every row in the table (a "sequential scan" / "full table scan") — O(n). An index is a separate data structure that lets the database jump straight to matching rows, typically O(log n), at the cost of extra storage and slower writes (the index must be updated on every insert/update/delete too). B-Tree index (the default, general-purpose case): Balanced tree structure, keeps data sorted, supports equality (=) and range (<, >, BETWEEN) queries efficiently, and supports ORDER BY without an extra sort step if the sort matches the index order. This is what you get by default when you index a column in Postgres/MySQL. Hash index: Only supports exact-match equality lookups (=), not ranges. Faster than B-Tree for pure equality lookups in principle, but rarely used in practice because B-Tree covers equality well enough and also handles ranges — using a hash index means giving up range queries for a marginal equality speedup. Composite (multi-column) indexes and column order: An index on (user_id, created_at) can efficiently serve queries filtering on user_id alone, or user_id + created_at together — but NOT an efficient query on created_at alone, because the index is sorted by user_id first. Rule of thumb: put the column used for equality filters first, range/sort columns after — column order in a composite index is not arbitrary. Covering index: An index that includes every column a query needs (in the index itself, via an INCLUDE clause or by being a composite index) lets the database answer the query directly from the index without touching the actual table rows at all ("index-only scan") — this is the fastest possible read path. When an index is NOT used (common surprise): Applying a function to the indexed column in the WHERE clause (WHERE LOWER(email) = 'x') prevents the index from being used unless there's a matching functional index — the database can't know LOWER(email) matches the sorted order of the raw email index. Leading wildcard LIKE ('%foo') can't use a standard B-Tree index either, since the sort order doesn't help when the match could start anywhere. The cost of indexes: Every index must be updated on every write to the table — a table with 10 indexes writes is measurably slower than one with 2, because each insert touches 10 separate structures. This is why indexes aren't added blindly; each one is a real trade-off between read speed and write speed. text: Load Balancer System Design Sources: AWS Elastic Load Balancing documentation, NGINX documentation (Load Balancing) What it is: A load balancer distributes incoming network traffic across multiple servers. Prevents any single server from becoming a bottleneck. Essential for high availability and horizontal scaling. Types of Load Balancers: 1. Layer 4 (Transport Layer): Routes based on IP and TCP/UDP port. Fast, no content inspection. Cannot route based on URL path or headers. Example: AWS Network Load Balancer. 2. Layer 7 (Application Layer): Routes based on HTTP content — URL, headers, cookies. Can do path-based routing (/api → API servers, /static → CDN). Example: AWS Application Load Balancer, Nginx. Load Balancing Algorithms: Round Robin: Requests distributed evenly in order. Simple, works well when servers have equal capacity. Weighted Round Robin: Servers get requests proportional to weight. Used when servers have different capacities. Least Connections: New request goes to server with fewest active connections. Better for long-lived connections (WebSockets, streaming). IP Hash: Client IP hashed to always hit same server. Useful for session stickiness (user always hits same server). Problem: uneven distribution if many users share an IP (NAT). Consistent Hashing: Used for distributed cache and storage routing. Minimizes remapping when servers are added or removed. Health Checks: Load balancer pings each server every few seconds. If server fails health check, removed from rotation automatically. When server recovers, added back automatically. This is how zero-downtime deployments work. Session Stickiness (Sticky Sessions): Problem: User login session stored on Server A. Request goes to Server B — user logged out. Solution 1: Sticky sessions — same user always hits same server (IP hash). Solution 2: Externalize sessions to Redis — any server can read any session. Solution 2 is better for true stateless servers. Real-world stack for Swiggy scale: DNS → AWS Route53 (global traffic routing) → AWS CloudFront (CDN + DDoS protection) → AWS ALB (Layer 7, path-based routing) → Auto Scaling Groups (EC2 instances) → Services

text: Caching Strategies — System Design Sources: AWS Caching Best Practices documentation, Redis documentation, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) Why cache: Database reads are slow (milliseconds). Cache reads are fast (microseconds). 80% of traffic typically reads 20% of data (Pareto principle). Cache that 20% and handle 80% of load without hitting the database. Cache Types: 1. Application Cache (in-memory, local): Stored in the application's own memory. Fastest possible. Problem: Not shared across servers. Each server has its own cache. Use for: static config, lookup tables that rarely change. 2. Distributed Cache (Redis, Memcached): Shared cache server all application servers connect to. Slightly slower than local cache but consistent across fleet. Redis supports rich data structures: strings, lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes. Use for: session data, rate limiting counters, leaderboards, pub/sub. 3. CDN Cache: Caches static assets (images, JS, CSS) at edge locations globally. Requests served from nearest edge node — dramatically lower latency. Use for: static files, video content, public API responses. Cache Invalidation Strategies (the hard problem): Write-through: Write to cache AND database simultaneously. Pro: Cache always consistent. Con: Write latency increases. Write-behind (Write-back): Write to cache first, async to database. Pro: Low write latency. Con: Data loss risk if cache crashes before DB write. Cache-aside (Lazy loading): Application checks cache first. Miss → read from DB → store in cache → return. Most common pattern. Pro: Only caches what's actually read. Con: First request after cache miss is slow (cache miss penalty). Read-through: Cache sits in front of DB. Cache handles DB reads automatically. Application only talks to cache. TTL (Time to Live): Every cached item should have an expiry time. Without TTL: stale data stays forever (cache poisoning risk). Set TTL based on how often data changes: - User session: 24 hours - Product price: 5 minutes - Static config: 1 hour Cache Eviction Policies (when cache is full): LRU (Least Recently Used): Evict item not accessed for longest time. Most common. LFU (Least Frequently Used): Evict item accessed fewest times. FIFO: Evict oldest item. Simple but often suboptimal. Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd): Problem: Popular cache key expires. 1000 requests all miss → all hit DB simultaneously → DB crashes. Solutions: 1. Mutex lock — only first request fetches from DB, others wait. 2. Background refresh — refresh cache before TTL expires. 3. Jitter — add random offset to TTL so keys don't expire simultaneously. Redis at Scale (Zepto, Swiggy use case): Redis Sentinel: High availability — automatic failover if primary fails. Redis Cluster: Horizontal scaling — data sharded across multiple Redis nodes. Read replicas: Route read-heavy workloads to replicas.

text: Database Indexing & Query Optimization Sources: PostgreSQL documentation (Indexes), "Use The Index, Luke" (use-the-index-luke.com) What an index is: Without an index, finding a row matching a WHERE clause means scanning every row in the table (a "sequential scan" / "full table scan") — O(n). An index is a separate data structure that lets the database jump straight to matching rows, typically O(log n), at the cost of extra storage and slower writes (the index must be updated on every insert/update/delete too). B-Tree index (the default, general-purpose case): Balanced tree structure, keeps data sorted, supports equality (=) and range (<, >, BETWEEN) queries efficiently, and supports ORDER BY without an extra sort step if the sort matches the index order. This is what you get by default when you index a column in Postgres/MySQL. Hash index: Only supports exact-match equality lookups (=), not ranges. Faster than B-Tree for pure equality lookups in principle, but rarely used in practice because B-Tree covers equality well enough and also handles ranges — using a hash index means giving up range queries for a marginal equality speedup. Composite (multi-column) indexes and column order: An index on (user_id, created_at) can efficiently serve queries filtering on user_id alone, or user_id + created_at together — but NOT an efficient query on created_at alone, because the index is sorted by user_id first. Rule of thumb: put the column used for equality filters first, range/sort columns after — column order in a composite index is not arbitrary. Covering index: An index that includes every column a query needs (in the index itself, via an INCLUDE clause or by being a composite index) lets the database answer the query directly from the index without touching the actual table rows at all ("index-only scan") — this is the fastest possible read path. When an index is NOT used (common surprise): Applying a function to the indexed column in the WHERE clause (WHERE LOWER(email) = 'x') prevents the index from being used unless there's a matching functional index — the database can't know LOWER(email) matches the sorted order of the raw email index. Leading wildcard LIKE ('%foo') can't use a standard B-Tree index either, since the sort order doesn't help when the match could start anywhere. The cost of indexes: Every index must be updated on every write to the table — a table with 10 indexes writes is measurably slower than one with 2, because each insert touches 10 separate structures. This is why indexes aren't added blindly; each one is a real trade-off between read speed and write speed. text: Search & Indexing (Inverted Index) Sources: Elasticsearch documentation ("Inverted index"), Apache Lucene documentation What it is: Searching billions of documents for a keyword by scanning each one would be far too slow. Search engines instead build an inverted index ahead of time — a data structure that maps each word to the list of documents containing it — so a search becomes a fast lookup instead of a full scan. Forward index vs inverted index: Forward index: document → list of words it contains (this is the natural way you'd store a document, but useless for "find all docs containing X"). Inverted index: word → list of documents containing it. Flips the mapping so a query for a term is a single lookup, not a scan of every document. Building the index: 1. Tokenization: split text into individual terms ("The quick fox" → ["the", "quick", "fox"]). 2. Normalization: lowercase, remove punctuation, stemming (running → run) so "run", "runs", "running" all match the same index entry. 3. Stop word removal (optional): common words like "the", "is" are often excluded since they match nearly everything and add little search value. 4. For each remaining term, append the document ID (and often position within the document, for phrase search) to that term's posting list. Querying: A search for "quick fox" looks up the posting list for "quick" and for "fox", then intersects them — documents in both lists contain both words. Ranking (which result appears first) typically uses TF-IDF or BM25: term frequency (how often the word appears in this doc) weighted against inverse document frequency (how rare the word is across all docs) — a rare word matching is a stronger signal than a common word matching. Distributed search (how this scales to billions of documents): The full index doesn't fit on one machine. It's split into shards, each holding a subset of documents and its own local inverted index. A query fans out to every shard in parallel, each returns its top-N matches, and a coordinating node merges and re-ranks the combined results — this is exactly how Elasticsearch/Solr scale search across a cluster. Each shard is also typically replicated for both availability and to spread read (query) load across replicas. Real-time-ish updates: New documents don't need a full index rebuild — an update is added as a small new index segment; a background merge process periodically combines small segments into larger ones for query efficiency. This is why "just indexed" documents often show up in search within seconds, not instantly, and why search indexes trade a small delay for much better write throughput. Real-world example: An e-commerce product search: catalog of 50M products is sharded across many nodes. Searching "wireless headphones" fans out to every shard, each returns its best local matches ranked by BM25, coordinator merges and returns the final top 20 — the same pattern used by product search on any major e-commerce site or by Elasticsearch-backed log search internally at a company.

text: SQL VS NOSQL — WHEN TO USE WHICH Sources: MongoDB documentation, PostgreSQL documentation, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) ch.2-3 Overview: One of the most common system design interview questions is "what database would you use?" There's no universal answer — the right choice depends on your data model, access patterns, consistency requirements, and scale. Understanding the trade-offs is more important than memorizing which is "better." SQL (Relational Databases): Examples: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, Oracle Core Characteristics: - Data organized in tables with fixed schemas (columns defined upfront) - ACID transactions: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability - SQL query language — powerful, joins, aggregations, subqueries - Strong consistency — reads always reflect latest writes - Relations between tables via foreign keys - Vertical scaling primarily (add more CPU/RAM to one server) When to use SQL: - Complex relationships between entities (users → orders → products → inventory) - Need ACID transactions (banking, e-commerce, healthcare) - Data structure is well-defined and unlikely to change frequently - Need complex queries with joins and aggregations - Team knows SQL well (most developers do) - Compliance requirements (many regulations require ACID) NoSQL (Non-Relational Databases): Four types: Document, Key-Value, Column-Family, Graph 1. Document Stores (MongoDB, CouchDB, Firestore): - Data stored as JSON/BSON documents - Flexible schema: different documents can have different fields - Good for: product catalogs, user profiles, content management - Example: MongoDB stores restaurant menus — each restaurant has different menu structure - Query: rich queries on nested fields, but no joins across collections 2. Key-Value Stores (Redis, DynamoDB, Memcached): - Simplest NoSQL: key → value - Extremely fast (O(1) lookup) - Good for: caching, session storage, rate limiting, leaderboards (Redis sorted sets) - Limited query capability — only lookup by key (or key prefix) - Redis extra: supports list, set, hash, sorted set, stream data structures 3. Wide-Column / Column-Family (Cassandra, HBase, DynamoDB): - Rows with flexible columns, organized by partition key - Data spread across nodes by partition key — horizontally scalable - Good for: time-series data, IoT data, message history, activity logs - Cassandra strengths: write-heavy workloads, no single point of failure - Query: must specify partition key; range queries on sort key; no arbitrary queries 4. text: API Gateway Sources: AWS API Gateway Developer Guide, Kong Gateway documentation What it is: A single entry point that sits in front of a collection of backend services (especially in a microservices architecture) and routes each incoming request to the right service. Clients talk to one gateway instead of knowing about every individual service's address. What it handles (so individual services don't have to): Routing: maps a path/method to the right backend service (/users → user-service, /orders → order-service). Authentication: validates JWT/API keys once at the edge, so downstream services trust the gateway instead of each re-implementing auth. Rate limiting: throttles per-client request rate before it ever reaches backend services, protecting them from being overwhelmed. Request/response transformation: e.g. converting a legacy SOAP backend response to JSON for modern clients, without changing the backend. Aggregation: combining calls to multiple services into a single client-facing response (sometimes called the "backend for frontend" pattern) — a mobile app screen might need data from 3 services, gateway can fan out and merge. Observability: single place to log, trace, and monitor all API traffic instead of instrumenting every service separately. TLS termination: gateway handles HTTPS, internal traffic between gateway and services can be plain HTTP within a trusted network. Gateway vs Load Balancer: A load balancer (L4/L7) distributes traffic across replicas of the *same* service based on IP/path. An API gateway routes across *different* services and adds application-level concerns (auth, rate limiting, transformation) on top — they're often used together: gateway routes to a service name, load balancer distributes across that service's replicas. Failure mode to watch for: Single point of failure — if the gateway goes down, every service behind it is unreachable even if they're all healthy. Mitigated by running multiple gateway instances behind their own load balancer, and keeping the gateway itself stateless so any instance can handle any request. Backend for Frontend (BFF) pattern: Instead of one generic gateway for all clients, run a dedicated gateway per client type (mobile-BFF, web-BFF) — each shaped to that client's specific data needs, avoiding a single gateway trying to please every consumer with one generic contract. Real-world example: A ride-sharing app's mobile client hits a single gateway endpoint. Gateway validates the JWT, then calls trip-service, pricing-service, and driver-location-service in parallel, merges their responses into one JSON payload the app expects — the mobile client never needs to know these are three separate backend services, or that pricing-service might be redeployed independently tomorrow.

text: Database Replication & Failover Sources: PostgreSQL documentation (Replication), MySQL documentation (Replication), "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) ch.5 What it is: Replication keeps copies of the same data on multiple database nodes. Goals: survive a node failure without data loss, serve more read traffic than one machine can handle, and keep data closer to users in different regions. Leader-follower (primary-replica) replication: One node (leader) accepts all writes. Writes are streamed to one or more followers, which apply them and can serve read traffic. Most common setup for relational databases (Postgres, MySQL). Synchronous vs asynchronous replication: Synchronous: leader waits for follower to confirm the write before acknowledging the client. Zero data loss on failover, but write latency includes network round-trip to the follower, and the leader stalls if the follower is slow/down. Asynchronous: leader acknowledges the client immediately, follower catches up in the background. Fast writes, but a leader crash before replication completes means recent writes are lost. Semi-synchronous: at least one follower confirms synchronously, rest are async — common middle ground (used by MySQL semi-sync replication). Replication lag: The delay between a write on the leader and it appearing on a follower. Causes "read-your-own-writes" bugs: user updates their profile, immediately reloads the page, request is routed to a lagging follower, sees stale data. Fixed by: routing a user's own reads to the leader for a short window after they write, or reading from the same replica they just wrote through. Failover: When the leader dies, a follower must be promoted to leader. Manual failover: safer, slower — human confirms the old leader is really dead before promoting, avoiding split-brain. Automatic failover: faster recovery, but risk of split-brain — if the network partition means the old leader is alive but unreachable, promoting a new leader means two leaders may accept writes simultaneously, causing conflicting data. Tools like Patroni (Postgres) or Orchestrator (MySQL) use a consensus store (etcd/ZooKeeper) to agree on the new leader safely. Multi-leader and leaderless replication: Multi-leader: multiple nodes accept writes, used across data centers — but requires conflict resolution when the same record is written in two places. Leaderless (e.g. Cassandra, DynamoDB style): client writes to several replicas directly and reads from several, using quorum (W + R > N) to guarantee it sees the latest write. No single leader means no failover pause, but consistency is weaker and requires read-repair for divergent replicas. Real-world example: A typical production Postgres setup: one primary handles all writes, two read replicas serve read-heavy endpoints (e.g. product catalog browsing). Patroni monitors primary health via etcd; if the primary fails a health check, etcd elects a new leader from the replicas and updates DNS/proxy routing automatically — this is what "high availability" means for a database in practice.

text: CAP THEOREM AND DISTRIBUTED SYSTEMS CONSISTENCY Sources: Eric Brewer, "CAP Twelve Years Later: How the 'Rules' Have Changed" (IEEE Computer, 2012); Gilbert & Lynch, "Brewer's Conjecture and the Feasibility of Consistent, Available, Partition-Tolerant Web Services" (2002) Overview: The CAP theorem states that a distributed database system can only guarantee two of three properties simultaneously: Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance. Understanding CAP is fundamental to system design — every database and architectural decision involves these trade-offs. The Three Properties: C — Consistency: Every read returns the most recent write (or an error). If you write a value on node 1 and immediately read it from node 2, you get the updated value. This is "strong consistency." Example: bank account balance — you must see the current balance, not a stale one. A — Availability: Every request receives a response (not an error), though it might not be the most recent data. The system keeps responding even if some nodes are down. Example: Netflix shows you recommendations even if their recommendation engine is partially down. P — Partition Tolerance: The system continues operating even if network messages are lost or delayed between nodes. A "partition" = network split where nodes can't communicate.
