text: Event-Driven Architecture & CQRS Sources: Martin Fowler's blog (martinfowler.com — "CQRS", "Event Sourcing"), Microsoft Azure Architecture Center (CQRS pattern, Event-driven architecture style) What event-driven architecture is: Services communicate by emitting events ("OrderPlaced", "PaymentFailed") to a broker (Kafka, SNS, RabbitMQ) rather than calling each other's APIs directly. Interested services subscribe to the events they care about and react independently. Producer doesn't know or care who's listening. Why use it over direct service-to-service calls: Loose coupling — order-service doesn't need to know inventory-service, billing-service, and analytics-service exist; it just publishes "OrderPlaced". Adding a new consumer (e.g. a new fraud-detection service) requires zero changes to the producer. Resilience — if notification-service is down, the event waits in its queue; order-service isn't blocked waiting on a slow downstream call. CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation): Split the model used for writes (commands) from the model used for reads (queries) — instead of one model trying to serve both efficiently. Write side: optimized for validating and persisting a change (e.g. normalized relational tables, enforcing invariants). Read side: optimized for how the data is actually queried (e.g. a denormalized, pre-joined view tailored to a specific screen). The two are kept in sync via events — write side publishes an event on every change, read side subscribes and updates its own denormalized copy. Why CQRS pairs with event-driven design: The event stream that keeps read models in sync *is* the event-driven mechanism — a write triggers an event, one or more read models rebuild themselves from it, independently and asynchronously. Trade-off: eventual consistency. Because the read model updates asynchronously after the write event, there's a window where a query might return stale data (read model hasn't caught up yet). This is fine for a lot of use cases (a "likes count" being one event behind is not a problem) but wrong for anything requiring strict consistency (reading your own bank balance right after a transfer). Event Sourcing (often paired with CQRS, but a separate concept): Instead of storing current state and overwriting it, store the full sequence of events that led to the current state ("AccountOpened", "Deposited $100", "Withdrew $30"). Current state is derived by replaying events. Benefit: full audit trail for free, and you can rebuild any past state or fix a bug in projection logic by replaying history with corrected logic. Cost: replaying a long event history to get current state is slow without periodic snapshots; more operational complexity than just storing current state. Real-world example: An e-commerce order system publishes "OrderPlaced" on write. A dedicated "OrderSummaryView" read model (denormalized, stored in a fast key-value store) subscribes and updates itself — this is the exact table the "My Orders" page in the app queries, pre-shaped for that screen, entirely separate from the normalized orders/line_items tables used to validate and place the order in the first place.

text: Message Queues & Pub-Sub Sources: AWS SQS Developer Guide, RabbitMQ documentation, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) ch.11 What it is: A message queue decouples producers (services that create work) from consumers (services that process it). Producer pushes a message, queue holds it, consumer pulls and processes it whenever ready. Neither side needs the other to be online at the same instant. Why use one: Smooths traffic spikes — queue absorbs a burst, consumers drain it at their own pace. Decouples services — producer doesn't care if consumer is slow, down, or scaled to zero. Enables retries — failed messages can be redelivered instead of lost. Enables async workflows — user gets a fast response, heavy work happens in background (e.g. "order placed" returns instantly, email/invoice generation happens after). Point-to-point vs Pub/Sub: Point-to-point (queue): one message, one consumer. Used for task distribution — e.g. a pool of workers pulling image-resize jobs off a queue. Pub/Sub (topic): one message, many subscribers. Used for fan-out — e.g. "order placed" event notifies inventory service, billing service, and analytics service simultaneously. Delivery guarantees: At-most-once: message may be lost, never duplicated. Fastest, least safe. At-least-once: message guaranteed delivered, but may be duplicated on retry. Most systems (SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka) default to this — consumers must be idempotent. Exactly-once: hardest to guarantee in a distributed system; usually achieved by combining at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers (dedupe by message ID), not by the queue itself. Visibility timeout / ack: Consumer pulls a message; queue hides it from other consumers for a timeout window. Consumer processes it, then explicitly acknowledges (deletes) the message. If consumer crashes before ack, message becomes visible again and another consumer picks it up — this is why consumers must be idempotent, since a message could be processed twice. Dead-letter queues (DLQ): Messages that fail processing repeatedly (e.g. 5 retries) are moved to a separate DLQ instead of blocking the main queue forever. Lets you inspect and reprocess poison messages without stalling healthy traffic. Queue vs Kafka: Traditional queues (SQS, RabbitMQ) delete a message once consumed — it's gone. Kafka is a log: messages are retained for a configured period and consumers track their own offset, so multiple consumer groups can replay the same stream independently. Use a queue for simple task distribution; use Kafka when you need replay, ordering within a partition, or multiple independent consumers of the same event stream. Real-world example: E-commerce checkout: "order placed" event published to a topic. → Inventory service subscribes, decrements stock. → Billing service subscribes, charges card. → Notification service subscribes, sends confirmation email. Each subscriber processes independently; if the email service is down, the order still completes — the message just waits in that service's queue until it recovers.

text: API Gateway Sources: AWS API Gateway Developer Guide, Kong Gateway documentation What it is: A single entry point that sits in front of a collection of backend services (especially in a microservices architecture) and routes each incoming request to the right service. Clients talk to one gateway instead of knowing about every individual service's address. What it handles (so individual services don't have to): Routing: maps a path/method to the right backend service (/users → user-service, /orders → order-service). Authentication: validates JWT/API keys once at the edge, so downstream services trust the gateway instead of each re-implementing auth. Rate limiting: throttles per-client request rate before it ever reaches backend services, protecting them from being overwhelmed. Request/response transformation: e.g. converting a legacy SOAP backend response to JSON for modern clients, without changing the backend. Aggregation: combining calls to multiple services into a single client-facing response (sometimes called the "backend for frontend" pattern) — a mobile app screen might need data from 3 services, gateway can fan out and merge. Observability: single place to log, trace, and monitor all API traffic instead of instrumenting every service separately. TLS termination: gateway handles HTTPS, internal traffic between gateway and services can be plain HTTP within a trusted network. Gateway vs Load Balancer: A load balancer (L4/L7) distributes traffic across replicas of the *same* service based on IP/path. An API gateway routes across *different* services and adds application-level concerns (auth, rate limiting, transformation) on top — they're often used together: gateway routes to a service name, load balancer distributes across that service's replicas. Failure mode to watch for: Single point of failure — if the gateway goes down, every service behind it is unreachable even if they're all healthy. Mitigated by running multiple gateway instances behind their own load balancer, and keeping the gateway itself stateless so any instance can handle any request. Backend for Frontend (BFF) pattern: Instead of one generic gateway for all clients, run a dedicated gateway per client type (mobile-BFF, web-BFF) — each shaped to that client's specific data needs, avoiding a single gateway trying to please every consumer with one generic contract. Real-world example: A ride-sharing app's mobile client hits a single gateway endpoint. Gateway validates the JWT, then calls trip-service, pricing-service, and driver-location-service in parallel, merges their responses into one JSON payload the app expects — the mobile client never needs to know these are three separate backend services, or that pricing-service might be redeployed independently tomorrow.

text: Database Replication & Failover Sources: PostgreSQL documentation (Replication), MySQL documentation (Replication), "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) ch.5 What it is: Replication keeps copies of the same data on multiple database nodes. Goals: survive a node failure without data loss, serve more read traffic than one machine can handle, and keep data closer to users in different regions. Leader-follower (primary-replica) replication: One node (leader) accepts all writes. Writes are streamed to one or more followers, which apply them and can serve read traffic. Most common setup for relational databases (Postgres, MySQL). Synchronous vs asynchronous replication: Synchronous: leader waits for follower to confirm the write before acknowledging the client. Zero data loss on failover, but write latency includes network round-trip to the follower, and the leader stalls if the follower is slow/down. Asynchronous: leader acknowledges the client immediately, follower catches up in the background. Fast writes, but a leader crash before replication completes means recent writes are lost. Semi-synchronous: at least one follower confirms synchronously, rest are async — common middle ground (used by MySQL semi-sync replication). Replication lag: The delay between a write on the leader and it appearing on a follower. Causes "read-your-own-writes" bugs: user updates their profile, immediately reloads the page, request is routed to a lagging follower, sees stale data. Fixed by: routing a user's own reads to the leader for a short window after they write, or reading from the same replica they just wrote through. Failover: When the leader dies, a follower must be promoted to leader. Manual failover: safer, slower — human confirms the old leader is really dead before promoting, avoiding split-brain. Automatic failover: faster recovery, but risk of split-brain — if the network partition means the old leader is alive but unreachable, promoting a new leader means two leaders may accept writes simultaneously, causing conflicting data. Tools like Patroni (Postgres) or Orchestrator (MySQL) use a consensus store (etcd/ZooKeeper) to agree on the new leader safely. Multi-leader and leaderless replication: Multi-leader: multiple nodes accept writes, used across data centers — but requires conflict resolution when the same record is written in two places. Leaderless (e.g. Cassandra, DynamoDB style): client writes to several replicas directly and reads from several, using quorum (W + R > N) to guarantee it sees the latest write. No single leader means no failover pause, but consistency is weaker and requires read-repair for divergent replicas. Real-world example: A typical production Postgres setup: one primary handles all writes, two read replicas serve read-heavy endpoints (e.g. product catalog browsing). Patroni monitors primary health via etcd; if the primary fails a health check, etcd elects a new leader from the replicas and updates DNS/proxy routing automatically — this is what "high availability" means for a database in practice.

Each key is assigned to the nearest server clockwise - Adding a server: only the keys between the new server and its predecessor move - Removing a server: only its keys move to the next server - On average: only K/N keys need to move (K = total keys, N = number of servers) Virtual nodes (vnodes): - text: Pinterest System Design (Case Study) Sources: Pinterest Engineering Blog (medium.com/pinterest-engineering) Core challenge: Pinterest's home feed and search need to serve a highly visual, read-heavy product (billions of "pins," each with images) with personalized ranking, at a read:write ratio that's extremely skewed toward reads — most users browse far more pins than they create. Sharded MySQL as the source of truth: Pinterest's engineering blog has documented using sharded MySQL for core data (pins, boards, users) — sharding by a key like user_id so a given user's data mostly lives on one shard, keeping most queries scoped to a single shard rather than fanning out across all of them. This is a common pattern for reaching MySQL-scale-and-beyond throughput without abandoning a relational model the team already knows well. The feed fan-out problem: When a user follows thousands of boards/users, generating their home feed by querying all of those sources at read time (fan-out on read) is expensive per-request. Alternatively, pre-computing each follower's feed at write time (fan-out on write, i.e. when a pin is created, push it into every follower's precomputed feed) is fast to read but expensive for users with huge numbers of followers (a "celebrity" pinner writing once means fanning out to millions of followers' feeds). Pinterest (like Twitter, Instagram) uses a hybrid: fan-out on write for most users, with a separate fan-out on read path merged in at request time for accounts with very large follower counts — avoiding the write amplification blowup for the small number of accounts where fan-out on write would be disproportionately expensive. Image storage and serving: Billions of images at multiple resolutions (thumbnail, feed-size, full-size) are stored in blob storage and served through a CDN — the application database stores only metadata and a reference/URL to the image, never the image bytes themselves, keeping the relational database small and fast while a purpose-built object store and CDN handle the actual (much larger) binary content and its geographic distribution to users. Personalized ranking: Unlike a purely chronological feed, Pinterest's home feed is ranked by a recommendation model considering a user's past engagement — this ranking step is a separate service/pipeline from the raw "fetch candidate pins" step, following the general large-scale feed pattern of candidate generation (get a broad pool of possibly-relevant pins cheaply) followed by ranking (score and reorder a smaller candidate set more expensively) — doing expensive ML ranking over the entire pin corpus per request would not be feasible, so cheap retrieval narrows the set before expensive ranking runs on it. Real-world takeaway for interviews: "Design Pinterest/Instagram feed" questions center on the fan-out on write vs read trade-off (and the hybrid approach for high-follower accounts), plus the candidate-generation-then-ranking split for personalization — both are reusable patterns that show up across most large-scale social feed system designs, not Pinterest-specific tricks.

text: DATABASE SHARDING AND PARTITIONING Sources: MongoDB documentation (Sharding), Vitess documentation (originally built at YouTube) Overview: When a single database server can't handle the load (too many queries, too much data), you scale horizontally by splitting data across multiple servers. This is called sharding (horizontal partitioning). Understanding sharding is critical for system design interviews — almost every large-scale system uses it. Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling: - Vertical (scale up): add more CPU/RAM/disk to existing server. Simple but has limits. - Horizontal (scale out): add more servers. Complex but theoretically unlimited scale. - Sharding is horizontal scaling for databases. Types of Partitioning: 1. Horizontal Partitioning (Sharding): - Split rows across multiple tables/servers - Different rows in different places - Example: users 1-1M on server 1, users 1M-2M on server 2 - Most common type when people say "sharding" 2. Vertical Partitioning: - Split columns across multiple tables/servers - User profile (name, email) on one server, user media (photos, videos) on another - Good for separating hot (frequently accessed) from cold data Sharding Strategies: 1. Range-Based Sharding: - Partition by value range: users A-M on shard 1, N-Z on shard 2 - Or by ID range: IDs 0-1M on shard 1, 1M-2M on shard 2 - Pros: simple to implement, range queries easy - Cons: uneven distribution (many users start with common letters), hot shards 2. Hash-Based Sharding: - shard_id = hash(shard_key) % num_shards - Example: user_id=123 → hash(123) % 4 → shard 2 - Pros: even distribution, simple routing - Cons: range queries hard, adding/removing shards requires resharding 3. Directory-Based Sharding: - Lookup table: shard_key → shard_id - Example: user_id=123 → shard_id=3 (looked up from directory) - Pros: flexible, can move data between shards easily - Cons: lookup table is a bottleneck/single point of failure 4. Geographic Sharding: - Users in India → India shard, users in US → US shard - Good for data residency requirements and low latency - Cons: cross-region queries are slow Choosing the Shard Key (Critical Decision): The shard key determines how data is distributed. A bad shard key causes hot spots. text: Example: sharding tweets by author_id — Elon Musk's shard gets all the traffic - Solution: split hot shards further, add sub-sharding for popular entities Consistent Hashing (Solves the Resharding Problem): Problem with hash(key) % N: - If you add a shard (N+1): almost all keys need to move to a new shard - Moving data is slow and disruptive Consistent hashing: - Imagine a ring (0 to 2^32) - Both servers and keys are hashed onto this ring - Each key is assigned to the nearest server clockwise - Adding a server: only the keys between the new server and its predecessor move - Removing a server: only its keys move to the next server - On average: only K/N keys need to move (K = total keys, N = number of servers) Virtual nodes (vnodes): - Each physical server owns multiple positions on the ring (virtual nodes) - More even distribution - When a server is added/removed, impact is spread across all remaining servers - Used by: Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak Cross-Shard Queries (The Pain): Query: "find all users who signed up in January" (no shard key filter) - Must query ALL shards - Merge and sort results in application layer - Called "scatter-gather" or "fan-out query" - Expensive — avoid if possible Solution 1: Denormalize and duplicate data for query patterns Solution 2: Maintain a separate query service (Elasticsearch) for cross-shard queries Solution 3: Accept that cross-shard queries are slow, avoid them in hot paths Cross-Shard Joins: - Traditional SQL joins work within a shard - Cross-shard joins must be done in application code - Fetch data from shard A, fetch data from shard B, join in application memory - Very expensive — usually avoided by denormalization Cross-Shard Transactions: - ACID transactions across multiple shards require 2-Phase Commit (2PC) - 2PC is slow and can deadlock - Most distributed systems avoid this: - Use eventual consistency instead of strong consistency - Partition data such that transactions stay within one shard - Use saga pattern for multi-step transactions Resharding: When a shard is too large (data grown) or too hot (traffic grown): 1. Create two new shards 2. Copy half the data from old shard to each new shard 3. Redirect new writes to new shards 4. Let old shard drain (serve reads while migration happens) 5. Decommission old shard This is operationally complex — minimize resharding by: - Choosing shard count 10x what you need today (shards don't need to have equal hardware) - Planning for horizontal expansion within a shard (replication before sharding) Examples of Sharding in Real Systems: Instagram (PostgreSQL Sharding): - Shard key: user_id - Shard ID embedded in all object IDs using Postgres sequence trick - Instagram ran on sharded PostgreSQL for years — proof SQL can scale Discord (Message Sharding): - Shard key: channel_id (all messages in same channel on same Cassandra partition) - This makes "get last N messages in channel" extremely fast — single partition read Twitter (Gizzard): - Custom sharding framework

text: Distributed Transactions: 2PC & Saga Pattern Sources: "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) ch.9, microservices.io (Chris Richardson) — "Saga pattern" The problem: A single database transaction (BEGIN...COMMIT) guarantees all-or-nothing across tables in one database. But a "place order" flow in a microservices system might need to update order-service's DB, decrement inventory-service's DB, and charge payment-service's DB — three separate databases, no single transaction can span all of them. Two-Phase Commit (2PC): A coordinator asks every participant to "prepare" (lock resources, confirm it *can* commit, but don't commit yet). If all participants vote yes, coordinator tells everyone to commit. If any vote no, coordinator tells everyone to abort. Guarantees atomicity across multiple resources — either all commit or all abort. Why 2PC is avoided in practice at scale: Blocking: if the coordinator crashes after participants have "prepared" but before sending commit/abort, participants are stuck holding locks indefinitely, waiting for a coordinator that may never come back. Latency: every participant must stay locked and waiting through two full round-trips before any of them can proceed — slow, and doesn't scale well across services owned by different teams with independent uptime. Tight coupling: all participants must be available simultaneously; one slow or down service blocks the whole transaction for everyone. Saga pattern (the common alternative in microservices): Break the transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each with its own compensating action to undo it if a later step fails. Example: (1) order-service creates order [compensate: cancel order], (2) inventory-service reserves stock [compensate: release stock], (3) payment-service charges card [compensate: refund]. If step 3 fails, the saga runs compensations for steps 2 and 1 in reverse — no single distributed lock is ever held across all three. Choreography vs Orchestration (two ways to coordinate a saga): Choreography: each service publishes an event when its step completes, next service reacts to that event — fully decentralized, no single point of control, but harder to see the overall flow/state of "which step is this order on." Orchestration: a central saga orchestrator explicitly tells each service what to do next and tracks the saga's state — easier to reason about and debug, but the orchestrator becomes a piece of infrastructure every saga depends on. Key trade-off vs 2PC: Sagas give up strict atomicity (there IS a window where inventory is reserved but payment hasn't happened yet — visible partial state) in exchange for no blocking locks held across services and independent service availability. This is why sagas are preferred in practice: partial visibility for a short window is an acceptable trade for not letting one service's outage freeze every other service's transactions. Real-world example: Booking a flight + hotel as one "trip" transaction: reserve flight seat, reserve hotel room, charge card. If the hotel is sold out by the time that step runs, the saga triggers a compensating action to release the flight seat that was already reserved — the user never ends up charged for a trip that couldn't be fully booked, without ever holding a lock

text: Example: sharding tweets by author_id — Elon Musk's shard gets all the traffic - Solution: split hot shards further, add sub-sharding for popular entities Consistent Hashing (Solves the Resharding Problem): Problem with hash(key) % N: - If you add a shard (N+1): almost all keys need to move to a new shard - Moving data is slow and disruptive Consistent hashing: - Imagine a ring (0 to 2^32) - Both servers and keys are hashed onto this ring - Each key is assigned to the nearest server clockwise - Adding a server: only the keys between the new server and its predecessor move - Removing a server: only its keys move to the next server - On average: only K/N keys need to move (K = total keys, N = number of servers) Virtual nodes (vnodes): - Each physical server owns multiple positions on the ring (virtual nodes) - More even distribution - When a server is added/removed, impact is spread across all remaining servers - Used by: Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak Cross-Shard Queries (The Pain): Query: "find all users who signed up in January" (no shard key filter) - Must query ALL shards - Merge and sort results in application layer - Called "scatter-gather" or "fan-out query" - Expensive — avoid if possible Solution 1: Denormalize and duplicate data for query patterns Solution 2: Maintain a separate query service (Elasticsearch) for cross-shard queries Solution 3: Accept that cross-shard queries are slow, avoid them in hot paths Cross-Shard Joins: - Traditional SQL joins work within a shard - Cross-shard joins must be done in application code - Fetch data from shard A, fetch data from shard B, join in application memory - Very expensive — usually avoided by denormalization Cross-Shard Transactions: - ACID transactions across multiple shards require 2-Phase Commit (2PC) - 2PC is slow and can deadlock - Most distributed systems avoid this: - Use eventual consistency instead of strong consistency - Partition data such that transactions stay within one shard - Use saga pattern for multi-step transactions Resharding: When a shard is too large (data grown) or too hot (traffic grown): 1. Create two new shards 2. Copy half the data from old shard to each new shard 3. Redirect new writes to new shards 4. Let old shard drain (serve reads while migration happens) 5. Decommission old shard This is operationally complex — minimize resharding by: - Choosing shard count 10x what you need today (shards don't need to have equal hardware) - Planning for horizontal expansion within a shard (replication before sharding) Examples of Sharding in Real Systems: Instagram (PostgreSQL Sharding): - Shard key: user_id - Shard ID embedded in all object IDs using Postgres sequence trick - Instagram ran on sharded PostgreSQL for years — proof SQL can scale Discord (Message Sharding): - Shard key: channel_id (all messages in same channel on same Cassandra partition) - This makes "get last N messages in channel" extremely fast — single partition read Twitter (Gizzard): - Custom sharding framework

text: Consistent Hashing Sources: Karger et al., "Consistent Hashing and Random Trees" (STOC 1997); DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store" (SOSP 2007) Problem it solves: In a distributed system with N servers, naive hashing (key % N) breaks when servers are added or removed — almost all keys need remapping. Consistent hashing ensures only K/N keys are remapped when a server changes (K = total keys, N = servers). How it works: 1. Place servers on a circular ring using hash(server_id) 2. For each key: hash(key) → find the next server clockwise on the ring 3. Adding a server: only keys between new server and its predecessor move 4. Removing a server: only keys that mapped to it move to next server Virtual Nodes (vnodes): Each physical server gets multiple positions on the ring (e.g., 150 virtual nodes). Benefits: - More even load distribution - When a server fails, its load spreads across multiple servers (not just one) - Accounts for servers of different capacities (powerful server = more vnodes) Real-world usage: - Amazon DynamoDB: partitioning data across nodes - Apache Cassandra: distributing data across cluster - Discord: distributing chat messages - CDNs: routing requests to cache servers - Redis Cluster: slot assignment When to use: Use consistent hashing when you have a distributed cache or storage layer that needs to scale horizontally with minimal data movement on topology changes. Trade-offs: Pro: Minimal remapping when cluster changes Pro: Even distribution with virtual nodes Con: More complex than simple modulo hashing Con: Hot spots possible without virtual nodes

Horizontal Partitioning (Sharding): - Split rows across multiple tables/servers - Different rows in different places - Example: users 1-1M on server 1, users 1M-2M on server 2 - Most common type when people say "sharding" 2. Vertical Partitioning: - Split columns across multiple tables/servers - User profile (name, email) on one server, user media (photos, videos) on another - Good for separating hot (frequently accessed) from cold data Sharding Strategies: 1. Range-Based Sharding: - Partition by value range: users A-M on shard 1, N-Z on shard 2 - Or by ID range: IDs 0-1M on shard 1, 1M-2M on shard 2 - Pros: simple to implement, range queries easy - Cons: uneven distribution (many users start with common letters), hot shards 2. text: Amazon Dynamo (Case Study) Sources: DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store" (SOSP 2007) Why it was built: Amazon's shopping cart service needed to always accept a write — even during a network partition or node failure — because a customer being unable to add to their cart is a direct lost sale. Traditional strongly-consistent databases prioritize consistency over availability during a partition; Dynamo inverted that priority for this specific use case. Core design goal: always writable. Dynamo chose availability and partition tolerance over strict consistency (the AP side of CAP) — a write should never be rejected because some replicas are temporarily unreachable. This means the system can end up with temporarily conflicting versions of the same data, which it must reconcile later rather than prevent up front. Consistent hashing for partitioning: Data is partitioned across nodes using consistent hashing (each node owns a range on a hash ring). Adding or removing a node only reshuffles the data immediately adjacent to it on the ring, not the entire dataset — critical for a system meant to scale nodes up/down without a massive rebalancing event. Sloppy quorum & hinted handoff: Normally a write requires acknowledgment from W replicas and a read from R replicas (with W + R > N giving strong-ish consistency). But if some of the "correct" replica nodes are down, Dynamo still accepts the write on a different, temporarily-substituting node ("sloppy quorum") rather than rejecting it — the substitute node holds a "hint" to hand the data back to the rightful replica once it recovers (hinted handoff). This is the core mechanism of the "always writable" guarantee. Vector clocks for conflict resolution: Because writes can be accepted by different replicas independently during a partition, the same key can end up with multiple conflicting versions. Dynamo tags each version with a vector clock (tracks which node made which update, in what order) so it can determine if one version is a strict descendant of another (safe to auto-merge) or if they're genuinely concurrent conflicting writes (must be reconciled — Dynamo pushes this reconciliation to the application, e.g. "merge the two shopping carts," since only the application knows how to correctly merge domain data). Read-repair & anti-entropy: When a read encounters divergent versions across replicas, the coordinator can push the resolved/latest version back to the stale replicas ("read repair") instead of waiting for a separate background process — keeps replicas converging toward consistency without blocking writes to do so. Legacy and influence: Dynamo's design (consistent hashing, eventual consistency, vector clocks, "AP over CP" for write availability) directly influenced Cassandra, Riak, and Amazon's own managed DynamoDB — this paper is one of the most cited references in distributed systems design precisely because it made an explicit, well-justified trade-off (availability over consistency) that became a standard pattern to reference when discussing CAP theorem trade-offs in interviews.

Each key is assigned to the nearest server clockwise - Adding a server: only the keys between the new server and its predecessor move - Removing a server: only its keys move to the next server - On average: only K/N keys need to move (K = total keys, N = number of servers) Virtual nodes (vnodes): - Each physical server owns multiple positions on the ring (virtual nodes) - More even distribution - When a server is added/removed, impact is spread across all remaining servers - Used by: Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak Cross-Shard Queries (The Pain): Query: "find all users who signed up in January" (no shard key filter) - Must query ALL shards - Merge and sort results in application layer - Called "scatter-gather" or "fan-out query" - Expensive — avoid if possible Solution 1: Denormalize and duplicate data for query patterns Solution 2: Maintain a separate query service (Elasticsearch) for cross-shard queries Solution 3: Accept that cross-shard queries are slow, avoid them in hot paths Cross-Shard Joins: - Traditional SQL joins work within a shard - Cross-shard joins must be done in application code - Fetch data from shard A, fetch data from shard B, join in application memory - Very expensive — usually avoided by denormalization Cross-Shard Transactions: - ACID transactions across multiple shards require 2-Phase Commit (2PC) - 2PC is slow and can deadlock - Most distributed systems avoid this: - Use eventual consistency instead of strong consistency - Partition data such that transactions stay within one shard - Use saga pattern for multi-step transactions Resharding: When a shard is too large (data grown) or too hot (traffic grown): 1. Create two new shards 2. Copy half the data from old shard to each new shard 3. Redirect new writes to new shards 4. Let old shard drain (serve reads while migration happens) 5. Decommission old shard This is operationally complex — minimize resharding by: - Choosing shard count 10x what you need today (shards don't need to have equal hardware) - Planning for horizontal expansion within a shard (replication before sharding) Examples of Sharding in Real Systems: Instagram (PostgreSQL Sharding): - Shard key: user_id - Shard ID embedded in all object IDs using Postgres sequence trick - Instagram ran on sharded PostgreSQL for years — proof SQL can scale Discord (Message Sharding): - Shard key: channel_id (all messages in same channel on same Cassandra partition) - This makes "get last N messages in channel" extremely fast — single partition read Twitter (Gizzard): - Custom sharding framework

text: Pinterest System Design (Case Study) Sources: Pinterest Engineering Blog (medium.com/pinterest-engineering) Core challenge: Pinterest's home feed and search need to serve a highly visual, read-heavy product (billions of "pins," each with images) with personalized ranking, at a read:write ratio that's extremely skewed toward reads — most users browse far more pins than they create. Sharded MySQL as the source of truth: Pinterest's engineering blog has documented using sharded MySQL for core data (pins, boards, users) — sharding by a key like user_id so a given user's data mostly lives on one shard, keeping most queries scoped to a single shard rather than fanning out across all of them. This is a common pattern for reaching MySQL-scale-and-beyond throughput without abandoning a relational model the team already knows well. The feed fan-out problem: When a user follows thousands of boards/users, generating their home feed by querying all of those sources at read time (fan-out on read) is expensive per-request. Alternatively, pre-computing each follower's feed at write time (fan-out on write, i.e. when a pin is created, push it into every follower's precomputed feed) is fast to read but expensive for users with huge numbers of followers (a "celebrity" pinner writing once means fanning out to millions of followers' feeds). Pinterest (like Twitter, Instagram) uses a hybrid: fan-out on write for most users, with a separate fan-out on read path merged in at request time for accounts with very large follower counts — avoiding the write amplification blowup for the small number of accounts where fan-out on write would be disproportionately expensive. Image storage and serving: Billions of images at multiple resolutions (thumbnail, feed-size, full-size) are stored in blob storage and served through a CDN — the application database stores only metadata and a reference/URL to the image, never the image bytes themselves, keeping the relational database small and fast while a purpose-built object store and CDN handle the actual (much larger) binary content and its geographic distribution to users. Personalized ranking: Unlike a purely chronological feed, Pinterest's home feed is ranked by a recommendation model considering a user's past engagement — this ranking step is a separate service/pipeline from the raw "fetch candidate pins" step, following the general large-scale feed pattern of candidate generation (get a broad pool of possibly-relevant pins cheaply) followed by ranking (score and reorder a smaller candidate set more expensively) — doing expensive ML ranking over the entire pin corpus per request would not be feasible, so cheap retrieval narrows the set before expensive ranking runs on it. Real-world takeaway for interviews: "Design Pinterest/Instagram feed" questions center on the fan-out on write vs read trade-off (and the hybrid approach for high-follower accounts), plus the candidate-generation-then-ranking split for personalization — both are reusable patterns that show up across most large-scale social feed system designs, not Pinterest-specific tricks.

text: Slack System Design (Case Study) Sources: Slack Engineering Blog (slack.engineering) Core challenge: Real-time message delivery to potentially thousands of connected clients per workspace, while keeping full message history durable and searchable, and keeping every client's view of a channel consistent as new messages, edits, and reactions arrive. Real-time delivery via WebSockets: Each connected client holds a persistent WebSocket connection to a gateway server. When a message is sent, it's written to the durable store first, then fanned out over the open WebSocket connections of every client currently viewing that channel — the WebSocket is for live delivery to already-connected clients, not the system of record; a client reconnecting after being offline fetches missed history from the durable store via a normal API call, not by expecting to replay it from the socket. The "gateway holds connections, backend holds truth" split: Gateway/connection servers are relatively lightweight and mostly hold open sockets and route messages; the actual message data, ordering, and history lives in the backend datastore. This separation lets Slack scale the number of concurrent open connections independently from the storage/query layer — a spike in simultaneous online users stresses connection servers, not necessarily the database. Sharding by workspace/channel: Slack's engineering blog has discussed sharding message storage by team/channel, since most reads and writes for a given message are scoped to one channel — this keeps related data (a channel's message history) together on the same shard, so a typical "load channel history" query hits one shard rather than fanning out across the whole dataset. Historical MySQL scaling (Vitess): Slack has written about outgrowing a single large MySQL setup and adopting Vitess (a MySQL sharding middleware, originally built at YouTube) to shard their relational data horizontally while keeping the MySQL query interface application code already relied on — an example of solving a scaling problem by adding a sharding layer in front of an existing database technology, rather than fully rewriting onto a different database. Presence (online/offline/typing indicators): Presence state changes extremely frequently (far more often than actual messages) and is far less critical to get perfectly right — a "typing..." indicator being a second late or occasionally wrong is a minor UX blemish, not a correctness bug. This makes presence a good candidate for the most relaxed consistency and heaviest batching/throttling in the whole system, illustrating that not every real-time-feeling feature needs the same delivery guarantees as the actual message content. Real-world takeaway for interviews: "Design Slack/a chat app" questions hinge on separating three different problems that are easy to conflate: durable message storage (needs to be correct and never lost), real-time fan-out to online clients (needs to be fast, some staleness on reconnect is fine since history backfills it), and ephemeral presence state (needs to be cheap and fast, correctness is optional) — each deserves a different consistency/durability trade-off.

End-to-End Encryption: Signal protocol. Keys stored only on devices. Server never has access to message plaintext. This is a deliberate trade-off: cannot do server-side spam filtering. Scalability: Erlang/OTP chosen specifically because one Erlang process per connection scales to millions of concurrent connections per server. WhatsApp ran 2 million connections on a single server using Erlang. Trade-offs: No server-side message storage after delivery → cannot restore lost messages E2E encryption → cannot do content moderation Presence accuracy traded off for scale — last seen may lag slightly

text: WhatsApp System Design Sources: WhatsApp Engineering (public talks/posts on Erlang-based scaling), Meta Engineering Blog Overview: WhatsApp handles 100 billion messages per day across 2 billion users. Core challenges: real-time message delivery, end-to-end encryption, presence (online/offline), and media delivery at scale. Core Components: - Connection Service: Maintains persistent WebSocket connections per user - Message Service: Stores and routes messages between users - Presence Service: Tracks online/offline/last-seen status - Push Notification Service: Delivers messages to offline users via APNs/FCM - Media Service: Handles image, video, audio upload and delivery - Group Service: Manages group membership and fan-out Protocol: WebSocket for persistent bidirectional connection. XMPP protocol adapted by WhatsApp for message framing. Each user device maintains one persistent TCP connection to the server. Message Delivery Flow: Sender sends message → Server receives → Stores in queue → If recipient online: deliver via WebSocket immediately → If offline: store in database, send push notification → Recipient comes online: fetch pending messages, delete from queue Database Choice: Messages: Erlang Mnesia (in-memory) for active sessions + Cassandra for persistence Media: Distributed object storage (similar to S3) User data: MySQL for profiles and contacts Messages are NOT stored long-term on server after delivery (privacy design). End-to-End Encryption: Signal protocol. Keys stored only on devices. Server never has access to message plaintext. This is a deliberate trade-off: cannot do server-side spam filtering. Scalability: Erlang/OTP chosen specifically because one Erlang process per connection scales to millions of concurrent connections per server. WhatsApp ran 2 million connections on a single server using Erlang. Trade-offs: No server-side message storage after delivery → cannot restore lost messages E2E encryption → cannot do content moderation Presence accuracy traded off for scale — last seen may lag slightly

text: Slack System Design (Case Study) Sources: Slack Engineering Blog (slack.engineering) Core challenge: Real-time message delivery to potentially thousands of connected clients per workspace, while keeping full message history durable and searchable, and keeping every client's view of a channel consistent as new messages, edits, and reactions arrive. Real-time delivery via WebSockets: Each connected client holds a persistent WebSocket connection to a gateway server. When a message is sent, it's written to the durable store first, then fanned out over the open WebSocket connections of every client currently viewing that channel — the WebSocket is for live delivery to already-connected clients, not the system of record; a client reconnecting after being offline fetches missed history from the durable store via a normal API call, not by expecting to replay it from the socket. The "gateway holds connections, backend holds truth" split: Gateway/connection servers are relatively lightweight and mostly hold open sockets and route messages; the actual message data, ordering, and history lives in the backend datastore. This separation lets Slack scale the number of concurrent open connections independently from the storage/query layer — a spike in simultaneous online users stresses connection servers, not necessarily the database. Sharding by workspace/channel: Slack's engineering blog has discussed sharding message storage by team/channel, since most reads and writes for a given message are scoped to one channel — this keeps related data (a channel's message history) together on the same shard, so a typical "load channel history" query hits one shard rather than fanning out across the whole dataset. Historical MySQL scaling (Vitess): Slack has written about outgrowing a single large MySQL setup and adopting Vitess (a MySQL sharding middleware, originally built at YouTube) to shard their relational data horizontally while keeping the MySQL query interface application code already relied on — an example of solving a scaling problem by adding a sharding layer in front of an existing database technology, rather than fully rewriting onto a different database. Presence (online/offline/typing indicators): Presence state changes extremely frequently (far more often than actual messages) and is far less critical to get perfectly right — a "typing..." indicator being a second late or occasionally wrong is a minor UX blemish, not a correctness bug. This makes presence a good candidate for the most relaxed consistency and heaviest batching/throttling in the whole system, illustrating that not every real-time-feeling feature needs the same delivery guarantees as the actual message content. Real-world takeaway for interviews: "Design Slack/a chat app" questions hinge on separating three different problems that are easy to conflate: durable message storage (needs to be correct and never lost), real-time fan-out to online clients (needs to be fast, some staleness on reconnect is fine since history backfills it), and ephemeral presence state (needs to be cheap and fast, correctness is optional) — each deserves a different consistency/durability trade-off.

text: APACHE KAFKA — SYSTEM DESIGN DEEP DIVE Sources: Apache Kafka documentation, Kreps, Narkhede, Rao — "Kafka: a Distributed Messaging System for Log Processing" (NetDB 2011) Overview: Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform. Think of it as a highly durable, infinitely scalable message queue where producers write events and consumers read them. It's used in almost every large-scale system: Uber uses it for location updates, LinkedIn (who built Kafka) uses it for activity feeds, Netflix uses it for analytics pipeline. Core Concepts: Event/Message: A piece of data — "user_id: 123 placed order_id: 456 at timestamp: 1234567890" Topic: A named log of events. Like a table in a database. E.g., "order-events" topic Producer: Writes events to a topic Consumer: Reads events from a topic Broker: A Kafka server that stores events Cluster: Multiple brokers working together Partition: A topic is split into partitions for parallelism Offset: A sequential ID for each event in a partition (like array index) Consumer Group: Multiple consumers sharing the work of reading a topic Why Kafka? (vs Traditional Message Queues like RabbitMQ): Traditional queue: event consumed → deleted from queue Kafka: events retained for configurable period (default 7 days) → multiple consumers can independently read the same events This is transformative: - Add a new consumer without affecting existing ones - Replay events from past (debugging, backfilling new systems) - Decouple producers from consumers completely Kafka vs RabbitMQ: - RabbitMQ: message broker, push model, messages deleted after consumption, good for task queues - Kafka: event log, pull model, messages retained, good for event streaming and data pipelines - Choose Kafka when: multiple consumers need the same events, need event replay, high throughput - Choose RabbitMQ when: complex routing, guaranteed message ordering per consumer, task-queue pattern Architecture Deep Dive: Topics and Partitions: - Topic "order-events" might have 12 partitions - Each partition is an ordered, immutable log of events - Partitions distributed across brokers (partition 0 on broker 1, partition 1 on broker 2, etc.) - Events within a partition are strictly ordered - Events across partitions have no guaranteed order Partition Key: - Producer specifies a key per event: order.send(key="user_123", value=event) - All events with same key go to same partition - Guarantees ordering for events with same key (e.g., all events for user_123 are ordered) - Without key: round-robin across partitions Replication: - Each partition has a leader and N replicas on different brokers (N = replication factor) - Default replication factor: 3 (1 leader + 2 replicas) - All reads/writes go to leader - Replicas passively sync from leader - If leader fails, a replica is automatically elected as new leader (ZooKeeper or KRaft consensus) - Durability: Kafka can acknowledge write only after all replicas confirm receipt (acks=all) Consumer Groups: - Multiple consumers in a group share partitions - Each partition assigned to exactly one consumer in a group - 12 partitions + 6 consumers = 2 partitions per consumer (parallelism) - 12 partitions + 12 consumers = 1 partition per consumer (max parallelism)

text: Slack System Design (Case Study) Sources: Slack Engineering Blog (slack.engineering) Core challenge: Real-time message delivery to potentially thousands of connected clients per workspace, while keeping full message history durable and searchable, and keeping every client's view of a channel consistent as new messages, edits, and reactions arrive. Real-time delivery via WebSockets: Each connected client holds a persistent WebSocket connection to a gateway server. When a message is sent, it's written to the durable store first, then fanned out over the open WebSocket connections of every client currently viewing that channel — the WebSocket is for live delivery to already-connected clients, not the system of record; a client reconnecting after being offline fetches missed history from the durable store via a normal API call, not by expecting to replay it from the socket. The "gateway holds connections, backend holds truth" split: Gateway/connection servers are relatively lightweight and mostly hold open sockets and route messages; the actual message data, ordering, and history lives in the backend datastore. This separation lets Slack scale the number of concurrent open connections independently from the storage/query layer — a spike in simultaneous online users stresses connection servers, not necessarily the database. Sharding by workspace/channel: Slack's engineering blog has discussed sharding message storage by team/channel, since most reads and writes for a given message are scoped to one channel — this keeps related data (a channel's message history) together on the same shard, so a typical "load channel history" query hits one shard rather than fanning out across the whole dataset. Historical MySQL scaling (Vitess): Slack has written about outgrowing a single large MySQL setup and adopting Vitess (a MySQL sharding middleware, originally built at YouTube) to shard their relational data horizontally while keeping the MySQL query interface application code already relied on — an example of solving a scaling problem by adding a sharding layer in front of an existing database technology, rather than fully rewriting onto a different database. Presence (online/offline/typing indicators): Presence state changes extremely frequently (far more often than actual messages) and is far less critical to get perfectly right — a "typing..." indicator being a second late or occasionally wrong is a minor UX blemish, not a correctness bug. This makes presence a good candidate for the most relaxed consistency and heaviest batching/throttling in the whole system, illustrating that not every real-time-feeling feature needs the same delivery guarantees as the actual message content. Real-world takeaway for interviews: "Design Slack/a chat app" questions hinge on separating three different problems that are easy to conflate: durable message storage (needs to be correct and never lost), real-time fan-out to online clients (needs to be fast, some staleness on reconnect is fine since history backfills it), and ephemeral presence state (needs to be cheap and fast, correctness is optional) — each deserves a different consistency/durability trade-off.

Understanding CAP is fundamental to system design — every database and architectural decision involves these trade-offs. The Three Properties: C — Consistency: Every read returns the most recent write (or an error). If you write a value on node 1 and immediately read it from node 2, you get the updated value. This is "strong consistency." Example: bank account balance — you must see the current balance, not a stale one. A — Availability: Every request receives a response (not an error), though it might not be the most recent data. The system keeps responding even if some nodes are down. Example: Netflix shows you recommendations even if their recommendation engine is partially down. P — Partition Tolerance: The system continues operating even if network messages are lost or delayed between nodes. A "partition" = network split where nodes can't communicate. In reality: you cannot opt out of P. Networks fail. Partitions happen. You MUST handle partitions. The Real Choice — CP or AP: Since P is mandatory, the real choice is: when a partition occurs, do you sacrifice C or A? CP (Consistency + Partition Tolerance): - When partition happens: refuse to answer rather than return stale data - Some requests get errors during partition - But when you respond, you're always correct - Examples: ZooKeeper, HBase, Google Spanner, MongoDB (with journaling), traditional relational databases AP (Availability + Partition Tolerance): - When partition happens: respond with possibly stale data - System always responds, never returns error - Data might be outdated temporarily - Examples: Cassandra, DynamoDB, CouchDB, DNS Neither CP nor AP fully — just P: - Technically, traditional SQL in a single datacenter: gives up P (can't run across partitions) - Rarely applicable in modern distributed systems Consistency Models (Spectrum): Strong Consistency (Linearizability): - Every read sees the most recent write - As if there's only one copy of data - Slowest — requires synchronization - Example: Google Spanner uses atomic clocks to achieve this globally Sequential Consistency: - All nodes see operations in same order, but might lag - Operations appear instantaneous but may not be truly real-time Causal Consistency: - Causally related operations are seen in order - "If you see my reply, you must have seen my original post" - Used by some distributed databases Eventual Consistency: - If no new updates, all nodes will eventually have the same value - Queries may return stale data temporarily - Highest availability, used by: DynamoDB, Cassandra, S3 - Most common choice for high-scale systems Read-Your-Own-Writes: - You always see your own updates (even if others don't yet) - Instagram: after you post a photo, you see it even

text: Distributed Locks & Leader Election Sources: Redis documentation (Distributed Locks with Redis / Redlock), Apache ZooKeeper documentation, etcd documentation What it is: A distributed lock lets multiple processes across different machines coordinate so only one of them does a particular piece of work at a time — e.g. only one instance of a cron job runs, or only one node processes a given task. A regular in-process lock (mutex) doesn't work here because the "processes" are on different machines with no shared memory. Why you need one: Running the same scheduled job twice (duplicate emails sent, duplicate charges). Two nodes both thinking they're the "leader" and both writing conflicting data. Preventing two workers from picking up and processing the same queue item. Redis-based locks (simple case): SET a key with a unique value and an expiry (SET lock_key unique_id NX EX 30). NX means "only set if not exists" — this is the actual locking mechanism. Expiry (EX) prevents a deadlock if the holder crashes before releasing. Release by checking the value matches before deleting (via a Lua script, to make compare-and-delete atomic) — otherwise you might delete a lock some other process acquired after your expiry. Limitation: single Redis node is a single point of failure. If it fails over to a replica before the write is replicated, two clients could both believe they hold the lock. Redlock (multi-node Redis locking): Acquire the lock on a majority of independent Redis nodes (e.g. 3 of 5) within a time budget. Considered "acquired" only if majority succeeds before the clock runs out. More resilient to a single node failing, though it has been debated (Martin Kleppmann's critique) as not being fully safe under clock drift/GC pauses — good enough for "efficiency" locks (avoid duplicate work), not for correctness-critical locks (avoid data corruption). ZooKeeper / etcd-based locks (correctness-critical case): Both are consensus-based stores (using ZAB / Raft respectively) — a write is only acknowledged once a majority of nodes agree, which is much stronger than a single Redis node's guarantee. Leader election pattern: each candidate creates an ephemeral sequential node; the candidate with the lowest sequence number is the leader. If the leader's session dies (crash, network partition), its ephemeral node disappears automatically and the next-lowest candidate becomes leader. Use this when correctness matters more than latency — e.g. only one node should ever be allowed to write to a given shard. Fencing tokens: Even with a "correct" lock, a paused process (GC pause, slow disk) can wake up after its lock has expired and still think it holds the lock, then write stale data. Fix: every time a lock is granted, issue a monotonically increasing fencing token. The resource being protected (e.g. storage service) rejects any write that comes with an older token than the last one it saw — this is the actual fix for "lock expired but process is still running" bugs, the lock alone is not sufficient. text: Distributed Transactions: 2PC & Saga Pattern Sources: "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) ch.9, microservices.io (Chris Richardson) — "Saga pattern" The problem: A single database transaction (BEGIN...COMMIT) guarantees all-or-nothing across tables in one database. But a "place order" flow in a microservices system might need to update order-service's DB, decrement inventory-service's DB, and charge payment-service's DB — three separate databases, no single transaction can span all of them. Two-Phase Commit (2PC): A coordinator asks every participant to "prepare" (lock resources, confirm it *can* commit, but don't commit yet). If all participants vote yes, coordinator tells everyone to commit. If any vote no, coordinator tells everyone to abort. Guarantees atomicity across multiple resources — either all commit or all abort. Why 2PC is avoided in practice at scale: Blocking: if the coordinator crashes after participants have "prepared" but before sending commit/abort, participants are stuck holding locks indefinitely, waiting for a coordinator that may never come back. Latency: every participant must stay locked and waiting through two full round-trips before any of them can proceed — slow, and doesn't scale well across services owned by different teams with independent uptime. Tight coupling: all participants must be available simultaneously; one slow or down service blocks the whole transaction for everyone. Saga pattern (the common alternative in microservices): Break the transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each with its own compensating action to undo it if a later step fails. Example: (1) order-service creates order [compensate: cancel order], (2) inventory-service reserves stock [compensate: release stock], (3) payment-service charges card [compensate: refund]. If step 3 fails, the saga runs compensations for steps 2 and 1 in reverse — no single distributed lock is ever held across all three. Choreography vs Orchestration (two ways to coordinate a saga): Choreography: each service publishes an event when its step completes, next service reacts to that event — fully decentralized, no single point of control, but harder to see the overall flow/state of "which step is this order on." Orchestration: a central saga orchestrator explicitly tells each service what to do next and tracks the saga's state — easier to reason about and debug, but the orchestrator becomes a piece of infrastructure every saga depends on. Key trade-off vs 2PC: Sagas give up strict atomicity (there IS a window where inventory is reserved but payment hasn't happened yet — visible partial state) in exchange for no blocking locks held across services and independent service availability. This is why sagas are preferred in practice: partial visibility for a short window is an acceptable trade for not letting one service's outage freeze every other service's transactions. Real-world example: Booking a flight + hotel as one "trip" transaction: reserve flight seat, reserve hotel room, charge card. If the hotel is sold out by the time that step runs, the saga triggers a compensating action to release the flight seat that was already reserved — the user never ends up charged for a trip that couldn't be fully booked, without ever holding a lock

text: Database Replication & Failover Sources: PostgreSQL documentation (Replication), MySQL documentation (Replication), "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) ch.5 What it is: Replication keeps copies of the same data on multiple database nodes. Goals: survive a node failure without data loss, serve more read traffic than one machine can handle, and keep data closer to users in different regions. Leader-follower (primary-replica) replication: One node (leader) accepts all writes. Writes are streamed to one or more followers, which apply them and can serve read traffic. Most common setup for relational databases (Postgres, MySQL). Synchronous vs asynchronous replication: Synchronous: leader waits for follower to confirm the write before acknowledging the client. Zero data loss on failover, but write latency includes network round-trip to the follower, and the leader stalls if the follower is slow/down. Asynchronous: leader acknowledges the client immediately, follower catches up in the background. Fast writes, but a leader crash before replication completes means recent writes are lost. Semi-synchronous: at least one follower confirms synchronously, rest are async — common middle ground (used by MySQL semi-sync replication). Replication lag: The delay between a write on the leader and it appearing on a follower. Causes "read-your-own-writes" bugs: user updates their profile, immediately reloads the page, request is routed to a lagging follower, sees stale data. Fixed by: routing a user's own reads to the leader for a short window after they write, or reading from the same replica they just wrote through. Failover: When the leader dies, a follower must be promoted to leader. Manual failover: safer, slower — human confirms the old leader is really dead before promoting, avoiding split-brain. Automatic failover: faster recovery, but risk of split-brain — if the network partition means the old leader is alive but unreachable, promoting a new leader means two leaders may accept writes simultaneously, causing conflicting data. Tools like Patroni (Postgres) or Orchestrator (MySQL) use a consensus store (etcd/ZooKeeper) to agree on the new leader safely. Multi-leader and leaderless replication: Multi-leader: multiple nodes accept writes, used across data centers — but requires conflict resolution when the same record is written in two places. Leaderless (e.g. Cassandra, DynamoDB style): client writes to several replicas directly and reads from several, using quorum (W + R > N) to guarantee it sees the latest write. No single leader means no failover pause, but consistency is weaker and requires read-repair for divergent replicas. Real-world example: A typical production Postgres setup: one primary handles all writes, two read replicas serve read-heavy endpoints (e.g. product catalog browsing). Patroni monitors primary health via etcd; if the primary fails a health check, etcd elects a new leader from the replicas and updates DNS/proxy routing automatically — this is what "high availability" means for a database in practice.

But a "place order" flow in a microservices system might need to update order-service's DB, decrement inventory-service's DB, and charge payment-service's DB — three separate databases, no single transaction can span all of them. Two-Phase Commit (2PC): A coordinator asks every participant to "prepare" (lock resources, confirm it *can* commit, but don't commit yet). If all participants vote yes, coordinator tells everyone to commit. If any vote no, coordinator tells everyone to abort. Guarantees atomicity across multiple resources — either all commit or all abort. Why 2PC is avoided in practice at scale: Blocking: if the coordinator crashes after participants have "prepared" but before sending commit/abort, participants are stuck holding locks indefinitely, waiting for a coordinator that may never come back. Latency: every participant must stay locked and waiting through two full round-trips before any of them can proceed — slow, and doesn't scale well across services owned by different teams with independent uptime. Tight coupling: all participants must be available simultaneously; one slow or down service blocks the whole transaction for everyone. Saga pattern (the common alternative in microservices): Break the transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each with its own compensating action to undo it if a later step fails. Example: (1) order-service creates order [compensate: cancel order], (2) inventory-service reserves stock [compensate: release stock], (3) payment-service charges card [compensate: refund]. If step 3 fails, the saga runs compensations for steps 2 and 1 in reverse — no single distributed lock is ever held across all three. Orchestration: a central saga orchestrator explicitly tells each service what to do next and tracks the saga's state — easier to reason about and debug, but the orchestrator becomes a piece of infrastructure every saga depends on. Key trade-off vs 2PC: Sagas give up strict atomicity (there IS a window where inventory is reserved but payment hasn't happened yet — visible partial state) in exchange for no blocking locks held across services and independent service availability. This is why sagas are preferred in practice: partial visibility for a short window is an acceptable trade for not letting one service's outage freeze every other service's transactions. text: CAP THEOREM AND DISTRIBUTED SYSTEMS CONSISTENCY Sources: Eric Brewer, "CAP Twelve Years Later: How the 'Rules' Have Changed" (IEEE Computer, 2012); Gilbert & Lynch, "Brewer's Conjecture and the Feasibility of Consistent, Available, Partition-Tolerant Web Services" (2002) Overview: The CAP theorem states that a distributed database system can only guarantee two of three properties simultaneously: Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance. Understanding CAP is fundamental to system design — every database and architectural decision involves these trade-offs. The Three Properties: C — Consistency: Every read returns the most recent write (or an error). If you write a value on node 1 and immediately read it from node 2, you get the updated value. This is "strong consistency." Example: bank account balance — you must see the current balance, not a stale one. A — Availability: Every request receives a response (not an error), though it might not be the most recent data. The system keeps responding even if some nodes are down. Example: Netflix shows you recommendations even if their recommendation engine is partially down. P — Partition Tolerance: The system continues operating even if network messages are lost or delayed between nodes. A "partition" = network split where nodes can't communicate. In reality: you cannot opt out of P. Networks fail. Partitions happen. You MUST handle partitions. The Real Choice — CP or AP: Since P is mandatory, the real choice is: when a partition occurs, do you sacrifice C or A? text: Airbnb System Design (Case Study) Sources: Airbnb Engineering Blog (medium.com/airbnb-engineering) Core challenge: Airbnb's central hard problem isn't just "store listings and bookings" — it's preventing double-booking of the same property for overlapping dates while serving a search experience (browsing available listings by location, dates, price) that needs to be fast across millions of listings. Preventing double bookings: The booking write path needs a strong consistency guarantee: two guests must not both successfully book the same listing for overlapping dates. This is handled with a transactional check-and-reserve against the availability calendar for that listing — the specific listing's availability is the unit that needs strict consistency, even though the overall system is large and distributed. This is a good illustration of a general system design principle: you don't need every part of a large system to be strongly consistent, only the specific slice where correctness actually matters (here: one listing's calendar), while other parts (search, browsing) can be eventually consistent. Search (a different consistency requirement than booking): Search/browse needs to be fast and handle huge read volume, but a search result showing a listing that was juuust booked a few seconds ago by someone else is a minor, acceptable inconsistency — corrected when the user actually tries to book and hits the strongly-consistent availability check. This split (fast/loose for search, strict for the actual booking transaction) is why the search index can be a denormalized, eventually-consistent copy updated asynchronously from the source-of-truth booking/listing data, rather than the search path querying the strongly consistent store directly. Service-Oriented Architecture migration: Airbnb's engineering blog has documented moving from a large Ruby on Rails monolith to a service-oriented architecture as the company scaled — driven by the same forces most large monoliths eventually hit: independent teams needing to deploy independently, and different parts of the system (search vs booking vs payments) having very different scaling and consistency needs that a single monolithic app and database struggled to serve well simultaneously. Experimentation infrastructure: Because pricing, search ranking, and UI changes all materially affect booking conversion (real revenue), Airbnb built significant internal infrastructure for A/B testing at scale — a recurring theme in their engineering blog is treating experimentation itself as core infrastructure, not an afterthought bolted onto the product. Real-world takeaway for interviews: "Design Airbnb" is a common system design interview question specifically because it forces you to identify which part of the system needs strong consistency (the booking transaction against one listing's calendar) versus which parts can be eventually consistent (search results, listing browsing) — correctly drawing that line is the core of the answer, not just listing components.

text: DROPBOX / GOOGLE DRIVE SYSTEM DESIGN Sources: Dropbox Tech Blog (dropbox.tech) Overview: Dropbox is a cloud file storage and synchronization service. Users can store files in the cloud and access them from multiple devices, with changes synced automatically. Core challenges: (1) efficient sync — only send what changed, not the entire file, (2) handle concurrent edits from multiple devices, (3) store and retrieve petabytes of files reliably. Scale Numbers (Dropbox): - 700+ million registered users - 600,000+ business customers - 500 petabytes of data stored - 1 billion files uploaded per day - 10 million concurrent connected devices Core Features: 1. Upload files to cloud storage 2. Sync files across multiple devices 3. Share files and folders with others 4. Version history (restore deleted/older files) 5. Offline access (local cache) 6. Real-time collaboration (Google Docs style, for Google Drive) The Sync Problem — This is Everything: Naive approach: When file changes, upload entire file. Problem: A 10GB video with a 1KB edit = waste 10GB of bandwidth. Unacceptable. Chunking (Block-Level Sync): 1. File is split into fixed-size blocks (4MB default) 2. Each block is hashed (SHA-256) 3.
