text: Event-Driven Architecture & CQRS Sources: Martin Fowler's blog (martinfowler.com — "CQRS", "Event Sourcing"), Microsoft Azure Architecture Center (CQRS pattern, Event-driven architecture style) What event-driven architecture is: Services communicate by emitting events ("OrderPlaced", "PaymentFailed") to a broker (Kafka, SNS, RabbitMQ) rather than calling each other's APIs directly. Interested services subscribe to the events they care about and react independently. Producer doesn't know or care who's listening. Why use it over direct service-to-service calls: Loose coupling — order-service doesn't need to know inventory-service, billing-service, and analytics-service exist; it just publishes "OrderPlaced". Adding a new consumer (e.g. a new fraud-detection service) requires zero changes to the producer. Resilience — if notification-service is down, the event waits in its queue; order-service isn't blocked waiting on a slow downstream call. CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation): Split the model used for writes (commands) from the model used for reads (queries) — instead of one model trying to serve both efficiently. Write side: optimized for validating and persisting a change (e.g. normalized relational tables, enforcing invariants). Read side: optimized for how the data is actually queried (e.g. a denormalized, pre-joined view tailored to a specific screen). The two are kept in sync via events — write side publishes an event on every change, read side subscribes and updates its own denormalized copy. Why CQRS pairs with event-driven design: The event stream that keeps read models in sync *is* the event-driven mechanism — a write triggers an event, one or more read models rebuild themselves from it, independently and asynchronously. Trade-off: eventual consistency. Because the read model updates asynchronously after the write event, there's a window where a query might return stale data (read model hasn't caught up yet). This is fine for a lot of use cases (a "likes count" being one event behind is not a problem) but wrong for anything requiring strict consistency (reading your own bank balance right after a transfer). Event Sourcing (often paired with CQRS, but a separate concept): Instead of storing current state and overwriting it, store the full sequence of events that led to the current state ("AccountOpened", "Deposited $100", "Withdrew $30"). Current state is derived by replaying events. Benefit: full audit trail for free, and you can rebuild any past state or fix a bug in projection logic by replaying history with corrected logic. Cost: replaying a long event history to get current state is slow without periodic snapshots; more operational complexity than just storing current state. Real-world example: An e-commerce order system publishes "OrderPlaced" on write. A dedicated "OrderSummaryView" read model (denormalized, stored in a fast key-value store) subscribes and updates itself — this is the exact table the "My Orders" page in the app queries, pre-shaped for that screen, entirely separate from the normalized orders/line_items tables used to validate and place the order in the first place.

query: How does Facebook scale Memcache?
text: Facebook TAO & Memcache at Scale (Case Study) Sources: Bronson et al., "TAO: Facebook's Distributed Data Store for the Social Graph" (USENIX ATC 2013), Nishtala et al., "Scaling Memcache at Facebook" (NSDI 2013) The problem: Facebook's social graph (users, friendships, likes, comments — modeled as nodes and edges) is read far more often than it's written, at massive scale, and the underlying data lived in sharded MySQL. Serving graph reads directly from MySQL at that read volume was not feasible — the read/write ratio was extremely skewed toward reads. Scaling Memcache at Facebook (the caching layer): Facebook ran one of the largest memcached deployments in the world — trillions of items across many clusters. Key lessons from that paper: Look-aside cache pattern: application code checks memcache first, on a miss reads from MySQL and populates the cache — memcache itself has no knowledge of the database, it's purely a fast key-value layer in front of it. Thundering herd / cache stampede problem: if a popular key expires, many requests can miss simultaneously and all hit the database at once for the same key. Mitigated with a "lease" mechanism — only one request is allowed to go fetch from the database and repopulate the cache; other concurrent requests for the same key wait briefly rather than all hitting the DB. Invalidation across regions: when data changes, the region owning the write broadcasts invalidations to caches in other regions — because Facebook serves from multiple geographic regions, simply relying on TTL expiry alone would leave far-flung caches stale for too long. TAO (the graph-aware layer built on top of that caching experience): Rather than have every service reimplement "cache the graph efficiently," Facebook built TAO as a dedicated read-through cache purpose-built for the social graph's actual access patterns — objects (nodes: a post, a user) and associations (edges: "likes," "friends") — instead of a generic key-value cache that every team had to hand-tune for graph queries. Read-heavy optimization: TAO explicitly favors availability and low latency for reads over strict consistency — a "like" count might be very briefly stale across regions, an acceptable trade for the massive read volume TAO serves. Write-through with async replication: writes go to the region's master database, and are asynchronously replicated to other regions' caches — again prioritizing not blocking the write path on cross-region consistency. The general lesson (useful beyond Facebook specifically): Both papers describe the same underlying pattern: a very read-heavy workload at extreme scale is served by pushing reads into a cache layer tuned for the specific access pattern (generic key-value for Memcache, graph-specific for TAO), while accepting eventual/relaxed consistency as a deliberate trade-off for availability and latency — and building explicit mechanisms (leases, cross-region invalidation) to control exactly how stale the cache is allowed to get, rather than leaving it unbounded.

text: Caching Strategies — System Design Sources: AWS Caching Best Practices documentation, Redis documentation, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) Why cache: Database reads are slow (milliseconds). Cache reads are fast (microseconds). 80% of traffic typically reads 20% of data (Pareto principle). Cache that 20% and handle 80% of load without hitting the database. Cache Types: 1. Application Cache (in-memory, local): Stored in the application's own memory. Fastest possible. Problem: Not shared across servers. Each server has its own cache. Use for: static config, lookup tables that rarely change. 2. Distributed Cache (Redis, Memcached): Shared cache server all application servers connect to. Slightly slower than local cache but consistent across fleet. Redis supports rich data structures: strings, lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes. Use for: session data, rate limiting counters, leaderboards, pub/sub. 3. CDN Cache: Caches static assets (images, JS, CSS) at edge locations globally. Requests served from nearest edge node — dramatically lower latency. Use for: static files, video content, public API responses. Cache Invalidation Strategies (the hard problem): Write-through: Write to cache AND database simultaneously. Pro: Cache always consistent. Con: Write latency increases. Write-behind (Write-back): Write to cache first, async to database. Pro: Low write latency. Con: Data loss risk if cache crashes before DB write. Cache-aside (Lazy loading): Application checks cache first. Miss → read from DB → store in cache → return. Most common pattern. Pro: Only caches what's actually read. Con: First request after cache miss is slow (cache miss penalty). Read-through: Cache sits in front of DB. Cache handles DB reads automatically. Application only talks to cache. TTL (Time to Live): Every cached item should have an expiry time. Without TTL: stale data stays forever (cache poisoning risk). Set TTL based on how often data changes: - User session: 24 hours - Product price: 5 minutes - Static config: 1 hour Cache Eviction Policies (when cache is full): LRU (Least Recently Used): Evict item not accessed for longest time. Most common. LFU (Least Frequently Used): Evict item accessed fewest times. FIFO: Evict oldest item. Simple but often suboptimal. Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd): Problem: Popular cache key expires. 1000 requests all miss → all hit DB simultaneously → DB crashes. Solutions: 1. Mutex lock — only first request fetches from DB, others wait. 2. Background refresh — refresh cache before TTL expires. 3. Jitter — add random offset to TTL so keys don't expire simultaneously. Redis at Scale (Zepto, Swiggy use case): Redis Sentinel: High availability — automatic failover if primary fails. Redis Cluster: Horizontal scaling — data sharded across multiple Redis nodes. Read replicas: Route read-heavy workloads to replicas.

text: Consistent Hashing Sources: Karger et al., "Consistent Hashing and Random Trees" (STOC 1997); DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store" (SOSP 2007) Problem it solves: In a distributed system with N servers, naive hashing (key % N) breaks when servers are added or removed — almost all keys need remapping. Consistent hashing ensures only K/N keys are remapped when a server changes (K = total keys, N = servers). How it works: 1. Place servers on a circular ring using hash(server_id) 2. For each key: hash(key) → find the next server clockwise on the ring 3. Adding a server: only keys between new server and its predecessor move 4. Removing a server: only keys that mapped to it move to next server Virtual Nodes (vnodes): Each physical server gets multiple positions on the ring (e.g., 150 virtual nodes). Benefits: - More even load distribution - When a server fails, its load spreads across multiple servers (not just one) - Accounts for servers of different capacities (powerful server = more vnodes) Real-world usage: - Amazon DynamoDB: partitioning data across nodes - Apache Cassandra: distributing data across cluster - Discord: distributing chat messages - CDNs: routing requests to cache servers - Redis Cluster: slot assignment When to use: Use consistent hashing when you have a distributed cache or storage layer that needs to scale horizontally with minimal data movement on topology changes. Trade-offs: Pro: Minimal remapping when cluster changes Pro: Even distribution with virtual nodes Con: More complex than simple modulo hashing Con: Hot spots possible without virtual nodes

text: Search & Indexing (Inverted Index) Sources: Elasticsearch documentation ("Inverted index"), Apache Lucene documentation What it is: Searching billions of documents for a keyword by scanning each one would be far too slow. Search engines instead build an inverted index ahead of time — a data structure that maps each word to the list of documents containing it — so a search becomes a fast lookup instead of a full scan. Forward index vs inverted index: Forward index: document → list of words it contains (this is the natural way you'd store a document, but useless for "find all docs containing X"). Inverted index: word → list of documents containing it. Flips the mapping so a query for a term is a single lookup, not a scan of every document. Building the index: 1. Tokenization: split text into individual terms ("The quick fox" → ["the", "quick", "fox"]). 2. Normalization: lowercase, remove punctuation, stemming (running → run) so "run", "runs", "running" all match the same index entry. 3. Stop word removal (optional): common words like "the", "is" are often excluded since they match nearly everything and add little search value. 4. For each remaining term, append the document ID (and often position within the document, for phrase search) to that term's posting list. Querying: A search for "quick fox" looks up the posting list for "quick" and for "fox", then intersects them — documents in both lists contain both words. Ranking (which result appears first) typically uses TF-IDF or BM25: term frequency (how often the word appears in this doc) weighted against inverse document frequency (how rare the word is across all docs) — a rare word matching is a stronger signal than a common word matching. Distributed search (how this scales to billions of documents): The full index doesn't fit on one machine. It's split into shards, each holding a subset of documents and its own local inverted index. A query fans out to every shard in parallel, each returns its top-N matches, and a coordinating node merges and re-ranks the combined results — this is exactly how Elasticsearch/Solr scale search across a cluster. Each shard is also typically replicated for both availability and to spread read (query) load across replicas. Real-time-ish updates: New documents don't need a full index rebuild — an update is added as a small new index segment; a background merge process periodically combines small segments into larger ones for query efficiency. This is why "just indexed" documents often show up in search within seconds, not instantly, and why search indexes trade a small delay for much better write throughput. Real-world example: An e-commerce product search: catalog of 50M products is sharded across many nodes. Searching "wireless headphones" fans out to every shard, each returns its best local matches ranked by BM25, coordinator merges and returns the final top 20 — the same pattern used by product search on any major e-commerce site or by Elasticsearch-backed log search internally at a company.

Sharded MySQL as the source of truth: Pinterest's engineering blog has documented using sharded MySQL for core data (pins, boards, users) — sharding by a key like user_id so a given user's data mostly lives on one shard, keeping most queries scoped to a single shard rather than fanning out across all of them. This is a common pattern for reaching MySQL-scale-and-beyond throughput without abandoning a relational model the team already knows well. The feed fan-out problem: When a user follows thousands of boards/users, generating their home feed by querying all of those sources at read time (fan-out on read) is expensive per-request. Alternatively, pre-computing each follower's feed at write time (fan-out on write, i.e. when a pin is created, push it into every follower's precomputed feed) is fast to read but expensive for users with huge numbers of followers (a "celebrity" pinner writing once means fanning out to millions of followers' feeds). Pinterest (like Twitter, Instagram) uses a hybrid: fan-out on write for most users, with a separate fan-out on read path merged in at request time for accounts with very large follower counts — avoiding the write amplification blowup for the small number of accounts where fan-out on write would be disproportionately expensive. Image storage and serving: Billions of images at multiple resolutions (thumbnail, feed-size, full-size) are stored in blob storage and served through a CDN — the application database stores only metadata and a reference/URL to the image, never the image bytes themselves, keeping the relational database small and fast while a purpose-built object store and CDN handle the actual (much larger) binary content and its geographic distribution to users. Personalized ranking: Unlike a purely chronological feed, Pinterest's home feed is ranked by a recommendation model considering a user's past engagement — this ranking step is a separate service/pipeline from the raw "fetch candidate pins" step, following the general large-scale feed pattern of candidate generation (get a broad pool of possibly-relevant pins cheaply) followed by ranking (score and reorder a smaller candidate set more expensively) — doing expensive ML ranking over the entire pin corpus per request would not be feasible, so cheap retrieval narrows the set before expensive ranking runs on it. Real-world takeaway for interviews: "Design Pinterest/Instagram feed" questions center on the fan-out on write vs read trade-off (and the hybrid approach for high-follower accounts), plus the candidate-generation-then-ranking split for personalization — both are reusable patterns that show up across most large-scale social feed system designs, not Pinterest-specific tricks.

text: Search & Indexing (Inverted Index) Sources: Elasticsearch documentation ("Inverted index"), Apache Lucene documentation What it is: Searching billions of documents for a keyword by scanning each one would be far too slow. Search engines instead build an inverted index ahead of time — a data structure that maps each word to the list of documents containing it — so a search becomes a fast lookup instead of a full scan. Forward index vs inverted index: Forward index: document → list of words it contains (this is the natural way you'd store a document, but useless for "find all docs containing X"). Inverted index: word → list of documents containing it. Flips the mapping so a query for a term is a single lookup, not a scan of every document. Building the index: 1. Tokenization: split text into individual terms ("The quick fox" → ["the", "quick", "fox"]). 2. Normalization: lowercase, remove punctuation, stemming (running → run) so "run", "runs", "running" all match the same index entry. 3. Stop word removal (optional): common words like "the", "is" are often excluded since they match nearly everything and add little search value. 4. For each remaining term, append the document ID (and often position within the document, for phrase search) to that term's posting list. Querying: A search for "quick fox" looks up the posting list for "quick" and for "fox", then intersects them — documents in both lists contain both words. Ranking (which result appears first) typically uses TF-IDF or BM25: term frequency (how often the word appears in this doc) weighted against inverse document frequency (how rare the word is across all docs) — a rare word matching is a stronger signal than a common word matching. Distributed search (how this scales to billions of documents): The full index doesn't fit on one machine. It's split into shards, each holding a subset of documents and its own local inverted index. A query fans out to every shard in parallel, each returns its top-N matches, and a coordinating node merges and re-ranks the combined results — this is exactly how Elasticsearch/Solr scale search across a cluster. Each shard is also typically replicated for both availability and to spread read (query) load across replicas. Real-time-ish updates: New documents don't need a full index rebuild — an update is added as a small new index segment; a background merge process periodically combines small segments into larger ones for query efficiency. This is why "just indexed" documents often show up in search within seconds, not instantly, and why search indexes trade a small delay for much better write throughput. Real-world example: An e-commerce product search: catalog of 50M products is sharded across many nodes. Searching "wireless headphones" fans out to every shard, each returns its best local matches ranked by BM25, coordinator merges and returns the final top 20 — the same pattern used by product search on any major e-commerce site or by Elasticsearch-backed log search internally at a company.

text: Airbnb System Design (Case Study) Sources: Airbnb Engineering Blog (medium.com/airbnb-engineering) Core challenge: Airbnb's central hard problem isn't just "store listings and bookings" — it's preventing double-booking of the same property for overlapping dates while serving a search experience (browsing available listings by location, dates, price) that needs to be fast across millions of listings. Preventing double bookings: The booking write path needs a strong consistency guarantee: two guests must not both successfully book the same listing for overlapping dates. This is handled with a transactional check-and-reserve against the availability calendar for that listing — the specific listing's availability is the unit that needs strict consistency, even though the overall system is large and distributed. This is a good illustration of a general system design principle: you don't need every part of a large system to be strongly consistent, only the specific slice where correctness actually matters (here: one listing's calendar), while other parts (search, browsing) can be eventually consistent. Search (a different consistency requirement than booking): Search/browse needs to be fast and handle huge read volume, but a search result showing a listing that was juuust booked a few seconds ago by someone else is a minor, acceptable inconsistency — corrected when the user actually tries to book and hits the strongly-consistent availability check. This split (fast/loose for search, strict for the actual booking transaction) is why the search index can be a denormalized, eventually-consistent copy updated asynchronously from the source-of-truth booking/listing data, rather than the search path querying the strongly consistent store directly. Service-Oriented Architecture migration: Airbnb's engineering blog has documented moving from a large Ruby on Rails monolith to a service-oriented architecture as the company scaled — driven by the same forces most large monoliths eventually hit: independent teams needing to deploy independently, and different parts of the system (search vs booking vs payments) having very different scaling and consistency needs that a single monolithic app and database struggled to serve well simultaneously. Experimentation infrastructure: Because pricing, search ranking, and UI changes all materially affect booking conversion (real revenue), Airbnb built significant internal infrastructure for A/B testing at scale — a recurring theme in their engineering blog is treating experimentation itself as core infrastructure, not an afterthought bolted onto the product. Real-world takeaway for interviews: "Design Airbnb" is a common system design interview question specifically because it forces you to identify which part of the system needs strong consistency (the booking transaction against one listing's calendar) versus which parts can be eventually consistent (search results, listing browsing) — correctly drawing that line is the core of the answer, not just listing components.

text: Search & Indexing (Inverted Index) Sources: Elasticsearch documentation ("Inverted index"), Apache Lucene documentation What it is: Searching billions of documents for a keyword by scanning each one would be far too slow. Search engines instead build an inverted index ahead of time — a data structure that maps each word to the list of documents containing it — so a search becomes a fast lookup instead of a full scan. Forward index vs inverted index: Forward index: document → list of words it contains (this is the natural way you'd store a document, but useless for "find all docs containing X"). Inverted index: word → list of documents containing it. Flips the mapping so a query for a term is a single lookup, not a scan of every document. Building the index: 1. Tokenization: split text into individual terms ("The quick fox" → ["the", "quick", "fox"]). 2. Normalization: lowercase, remove punctuation, stemming (running → run) so "run", "runs", "running" all match the same index entry. 3. Stop word removal (optional): common words like "the", "is" are often excluded since they match nearly everything and add little search value. 4. For each remaining term, append the document ID (and often position within the document, for phrase search) to that term's posting list. Querying: A search for "quick fox" looks up the posting list for "quick" and for "fox", then intersects them — documents in both lists contain both words. Ranking (which result appears first) typically uses TF-IDF or BM25: term frequency (how often the word appears in this doc) weighted against inverse document frequency (how rare the word is across all docs) — a rare word matching is a stronger signal than a common word matching. Distributed search (how this scales to billions of documents): The full index doesn't fit on one machine. It's split into shards, each holding a subset of documents and its own local inverted index. A query fans out to every shard in parallel, each returns its top-N matches, and a coordinating node merges and re-ranks the combined results — this is exactly how Elasticsearch/Solr scale search across a cluster. Each shard is also typically replicated for both availability and to spread read (query) load across replicas. Real-time-ish updates: New documents don't need a full index rebuild — an update is added as a small new index segment; a background merge process periodically combines small segments into larger ones for query efficiency. This is why "just indexed" documents often show up in search within seconds, not instantly, and why search indexes trade a small delay for much better write throughput. Real-world example: An e-commerce product search: catalog of 50M products is sharded across many nodes. Searching "wireless headphones" fans out to every shard, each returns its best local matches ranked by BM25, coordinator merges and returns the final top 20 — the same pattern used by product search on any major e-commerce site or by Elasticsearch-backed log search internally at a company.

query: How does Google detect search spam?
text: Web Crawler Design Sources: S. Brin & L. Page, "The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine" (1998), standard system design interview treatment (Alex Xu, "System Design Interview") What it does: Starts from a set of seed URLs, downloads each page, extracts new links from it, and adds those links to a queue to be crawled next — recursively discovering and downloading a large portion of the web. Core components: Seed URLs: the starting set of pages to crawl. Frontier (URL queue): the set of URLs discovered but not yet fetched — this is the main piece of shared state the whole system revolves around. Fetcher: downloads the page content for a URL. Parser/Extractor: pulls new links out of the downloaded HTML, plus whatever content the crawler is actually collecting (text for a search index, prices for a shopping comparison site, etc.). Duplicate detector: avoids re-crawling and re-storing content already seen. Storage: the downloaded content and metadata. Avoiding duplicate work: Two different URLs often point to the same content (mobile vs desktop URL, tracking params, http vs https). Hash the normalized content (not just the URL) to detect "we've already stored this page" even if the URL differs. A Bloom filter is commonly used to cheaply check "have we already queued this URL" before adding it to the frontier, without needing to store every full URL in memory to check. Politeness (this is a hard requirement, not an optimization): Crawling a site too fast can look like — or actually be — a denial-of-service attack, and can get the crawler's IP banned. Rules: respect robots.txt (tells the crawler which paths it's not allowed to fetch), and rate-limit per domain (e.g. max 1 request/second to a given host), typically using a separate queue or delay per domain rather than one global rate limit. Priority / freshness: Not all pages are equal — a news homepage changes hourly, a static about-page almost never. Crawlers assign a re-crawl priority per URL based on how often it has historically changed and how important it is (e.g. via inbound link count, an early precursor to PageRank), rather than crawling everything on a fixed schedule. Scaling the frontier: A single machine's queue can't hold "every URL on the web" and a single fetcher can't download fast enough. The frontier is partitioned (e.g. by domain hash) across many worker machines, each responsible for fetching a subset of URLs — this also naturally helps enforce per-domain politeness, since all URLs for one domain land on the same worker's queue. Handling crawler traps and infinite spaces: Some sites generate infinite URLs dynamically (e.g. a calendar with a "next month" link that goes on forever). Crawlers cap max depth per site and max pages per domain to avoid getting stuck indefinitely on a single site's infinite link structure. Real-world example: Building a search engine's crawler: seed with a list of popular domains, fetcher pool downloads pages respecting robots.txt and per-domain rate limits, parser extracts text (for the search index)

text: Pinterest System Design (Case Study) Sources: Pinterest Engineering Blog (medium.com/pinterest-engineering) Core challenge: Pinterest's home feed and search need to serve a highly visual, read-heavy product (billions of "pins," each with images) with personalized ranking, at a read:write ratio that's extremely skewed toward reads — most users browse far more pins than they create. Sharded MySQL as the source of truth: Pinterest's engineering blog has documented using sharded MySQL for core data (pins, boards, users) — sharding by a key like user_id so a given user's data mostly lives on one shard, keeping most queries scoped to a single shard rather than fanning out across all of them. This is a common pattern for reaching MySQL-scale-and-beyond throughput without abandoning a relational model the team already knows well. The feed fan-out problem: When a user follows thousands of boards/users, generating their home feed by querying all of those sources at read time (fan-out on read) is expensive per-request. Alternatively, pre-computing each follower's feed at write time (fan-out on write, i.e. when a pin is created, push it into every follower's precomputed feed) is fast to read but expensive for users with huge numbers of followers (a "celebrity" pinner writing once means fanning out to millions of followers' feeds). Pinterest (like Twitter, Instagram) uses a hybrid: fan-out on write for most users, with a separate fan-out on read path merged in at request time for accounts with very large follower counts — avoiding the write amplification blowup for the small number of accounts where fan-out on write would be disproportionately expensive. Image storage and serving: Billions of images at multiple resolutions (thumbnail, feed-size, full-size) are stored in blob storage and served through a CDN — the application database stores only metadata and a reference/URL to the image, never the image bytes themselves, keeping the relational database small and fast while a purpose-built object store and CDN handle the actual (much larger) binary content and its geographic distribution to users. Personalized ranking: Unlike a purely chronological feed, Pinterest's home feed is ranked by a recommendation model considering a user's past engagement — this ranking step is a separate service/pipeline from the raw "fetch candidate pins" step, following the general large-scale feed pattern of candidate generation (get a broad pool of possibly-relevant pins cheaply) followed by ranking (score and reorder a smaller candidate set more expensively) — doing expensive ML ranking over the entire pin corpus per request would not be feasible, so cheap retrieval narrows the set before expensive ranking runs on it. Real-world takeaway for interviews: "Design Pinterest/Instagram feed" questions center on the fan-out on write vs read trade-off (and the hybrid approach for high-follower accounts), plus the candidate-generation-then-ranking split for personalization — both are reusable patterns that show up across most large-scale social feed system designs, not Pinterest-specific tricks.

text: Amazon Dynamo (Case Study) Sources: DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store" (SOSP 2007) Why it was built: Amazon's shopping cart service needed to always accept a write — even during a network partition or node failure — because a customer being unable to add to their cart is a direct lost sale. Traditional strongly-consistent databases prioritize consistency over availability during a partition; Dynamo inverted that priority for this specific use case. Core design goal: always writable. Dynamo chose availability and partition tolerance over strict consistency (the AP side of CAP) — a write should never be rejected because some replicas are temporarily unreachable. This means the system can end up with temporarily conflicting versions of the same data, which it must reconcile later rather than prevent up front. Consistent hashing for partitioning: Data is partitioned across nodes using consistent hashing (each node owns a range on a hash ring). Adding or removing a node only reshuffles the data immediately adjacent to it on the ring, not the entire dataset — critical for a system meant to scale nodes up/down without a massive rebalancing event. Sloppy quorum & hinted handoff: Normally a write requires acknowledgment from W replicas and a read from R replicas (with W + R > N giving strong-ish consistency). But if some of the "correct" replica nodes are down, Dynamo still accepts the write on a different, temporarily-substituting node ("sloppy quorum") rather than rejecting it — the substitute node holds a "hint" to hand the data back to the rightful replica once it recovers (hinted handoff). This is the core mechanism of the "always writable" guarantee. Vector clocks for conflict resolution: Because writes can be accepted by different replicas independently during a partition, the same key can end up with multiple conflicting versions. Dynamo tags each version with a vector clock (tracks which node made which update, in what order) so it can determine if one version is a strict descendant of another (safe to auto-merge) or if they're genuinely concurrent conflicting writes (must be reconciled — Dynamo pushes this reconciliation to the application, e.g. "merge the two shopping carts," since only the application knows how to correctly merge domain data). Read-repair & anti-entropy: When a read encounters divergent versions across replicas, the coordinator can push the resolved/latest version back to the stale replicas ("read repair") instead of waiting for a separate background process — keeps replicas converging toward consistency without blocking writes to do so. Legacy and influence: Dynamo's design (consistent hashing, eventual consistency, vector clocks, "AP over CP" for write availability) directly influenced Cassandra, Riak, and Amazon's own managed DynamoDB — this paper is one of the most cited references in distributed systems design precisely because it made an explicit, well-justified trade-off (availability over consistency) that became a standard pattern to reference when discussing CAP theorem trade-offs in interviews.

text: APACHE KAFKA — SYSTEM DESIGN DEEP DIVE Sources: Apache Kafka documentation, Kreps, Narkhede, Rao — "Kafka: a Distributed Messaging System for Log Processing" (NetDB 2011) Overview: Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform. Think of it as a highly durable, infinitely scalable message queue where producers write events and consumers read them. It's used in almost every large-scale system: Uber uses it for location updates, LinkedIn (who built Kafka) uses it for activity feeds, Netflix uses it for analytics pipeline. Core Concepts: Event/Message: A piece of data — "user_id: 123 placed order_id: 456 at timestamp: 1234567890" Topic: A named log of events. Like a table in a database. E.g., "order-events" topic Producer: Writes events to a topic Consumer: Reads events from a topic Broker: A Kafka server that stores events Cluster: Multiple brokers working together Partition: A topic is split into partitions for parallelism Offset: A sequential ID for each event in a partition (like array index) Consumer Group: Multiple consumers sharing the work of reading a topic Why Kafka? (vs Traditional Message Queues like RabbitMQ): Traditional queue: event consumed → deleted from queue Kafka: events retained for configurable period (default 7 days) → multiple consumers can independently read the same events This is transformative: - Add a new consumer without affecting existing ones - Replay events from past (debugging, backfilling new systems) - Decouple producers from consumers completely Kafka vs RabbitMQ: - RabbitMQ: message broker, push model, messages deleted after consumption, good for task queues - Kafka: event log, pull model, messages retained, good for event streaming and data pipelines - Choose Kafka when: multiple consumers need the same events, need event replay, high throughput - Choose RabbitMQ when: complex routing, guaranteed message ordering per consumer, task-queue pattern Architecture Deep Dive: Topics and Partitions: - Topic "order-events" might have 12 partitions - Each partition is an ordered, immutable log of events - Partitions distributed across brokers (partition 0 on broker 1, partition 1 on broker 2, etc.) - Events within a partition are strictly ordered - Events across partitions have no guaranteed order Partition Key: - Producer specifies a key per event: order.send(key="user_123", value=event) - All events with same key go to same partition - Guarantees ordering for events with same key (e.g., all events for user_123 are ordered) - Without key: round-robin across partitions Replication: - Each partition has a leader and N replicas on different brokers (N = replication factor) - Default replication factor: 3 (1 leader + 2 replicas) - All reads/writes go to leader - Replicas passively sync from leader - If leader fails, a replica is automatically elected as new leader (ZooKeeper or KRaft consensus) - Durability: Kafka can acknowledge write only after all replicas confirm receipt (acks=all) Consumer Groups: - Multiple consumers in a group share partitions - Each partition assigned to exactly one consumer in a group - 12 partitions + 6 consumers = 2 partitions per consumer (parallelism) - 12 partitions + 12 consumers = 1 partition per consumer (max parallelism)

text: LinkedIn & the Origin of Kafka (Case Study) Sources: LinkedIn Engineering Blog, Kreps, Narkhede, Rao — "Kafka: a Distributed Messaging System for Log Processing" (NetDB 2011) The problem LinkedIn had: By the early 2010s, LinkedIn had many separate systems that needed the same underlying activity data — the news feed, search indexing, relevance/ML pipelines, monitoring, and analytics all needed a feed of user activity events (page views, connections made, likes). Each consumer had built its own point-to-point pipeline to get this data, resulting in an N×M mess of custom, fragile integrations between every producer and every consumer. Why existing message queues weren't a fit: Traditional queues (JMS-style brokers) were built for low-throughput, transactional messaging, not the sustained high-throughput firehose of activity events LinkedIn needed to move (hundreds of billions of events/day at LinkedIn's later scale). They also typically delete a message once consumed, so a second, independent consumer couldn't replay the same stream. Kafka's core design choices (as a direct response to that problem): Log-based storage: instead of deleting messages after delivery, Kafka retains them for a configured period (or forever) as an append-only log. Multiple independent consumer groups can each read the same stream at their own pace, tracking their own offset — this single change is what let LinkedIn support many different downstream consumers off one shared pipeline instead of N separate point-to-point integrations. Partitioning: each topic is split into partitions, each handled independently and in order, allowing horizontal scaling of both writes and reads by adding more partitions and consumers. Sequential disk I/O: Kafka relies on sequential reads/writes to disk (fast, even on spinning disks) plus OS page cache, rather than random access — this is why Kafka achieves very high throughput despite persisting everything. Pull-based consumption: consumers pull at their own pace and track their own offset, rather than the broker pushing and needing to track per-consumer state — simplifies the broker and lets slow consumers fall behind without overwhelming themselves, catching up later from their last offset. Outcome: LinkedIn open-sourced Kafka in 2011 and it became an Apache project; it's now the de facto standard for high-throughput event streaming across the industry (adopted by Netflix, Uber, and most large-scale systems that need a durable, replayable, multi-consumer event backbone) — a direct example of solving an internal integration problem generally enough that it became foundational infrastructure well beyond its original use case. Relevance to system design interviews: "Why Kafka over a traditional queue" is a common follow-up question — the answer is precisely this history: replayability (log retention, multiple independent consumer groups) and throughput (partitioning + sequential I/O), not just "it's a queue but faster."

text: Message Queues & Pub-Sub Sources: AWS SQS Developer Guide, RabbitMQ documentation, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) ch.11 What it is: A message queue decouples producers (services that create work) from consumers (services that process it). Producer pushes a message, queue holds it, consumer pulls and processes it whenever ready. Neither side needs the other to be online at the same instant. Why use one: Smooths traffic spikes — queue absorbs a burst, consumers drain it at their own pace. Decouples services — producer doesn't care if consumer is slow, down, or scaled to zero. Enables retries — failed messages can be redelivered instead of lost. Enables async workflows — user gets a fast response, heavy work happens in background (e.g. "order placed" returns instantly, email/invoice generation happens after). Point-to-point vs Pub/Sub: Point-to-point (queue): one message, one consumer. Used for task distribution — e.g. a pool of workers pulling image-resize jobs off a queue. Pub/Sub (topic): one message, many subscribers. Used for fan-out — e.g. "order placed" event notifies inventory service, billing service, and analytics service simultaneously. Delivery guarantees: At-most-once: message may be lost, never duplicated. Fastest, least safe. At-least-once: message guaranteed delivered, but may be duplicated on retry. Most systems (SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka) default to this — consumers must be idempotent. Exactly-once: hardest to guarantee in a distributed system; usually achieved by combining at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers (dedupe by message ID), not by the queue itself. Visibility timeout / ack: Consumer pulls a message; queue hides it from other consumers for a timeout window. Consumer processes it, then explicitly acknowledges (deletes) the message. If consumer crashes before ack, message becomes visible again and another consumer picks it up — this is why consumers must be idempotent, since a message could be processed twice. Dead-letter queues (DLQ): Messages that fail processing repeatedly (e.g. 5 retries) are moved to a separate DLQ instead of blocking the main queue forever. Lets you inspect and reprocess poison messages without stalling healthy traffic. Queue vs Kafka: Traditional queues (SQS, RabbitMQ) delete a message once consumed — it's gone. Kafka is a log: messages are retained for a configured period and consumers track their own offset, so multiple consumer groups can replay the same stream independently. Use a queue for simple task distribution; use Kafka when you need replay, ordering within a partition, or multiple independent consumers of the same event stream. Real-world example: E-commerce checkout: "order placed" event published to a topic. → Inventory service subscribes, decrements stock. → Billing service subscribes, charges card. → Notification service subscribes, sends confirmation email. Each subscriber processes independently; if the email service is down, the order still completes — the message just waits in that service's queue until it recovers.

query: What are some common use cases for Kafka and how does it achieve high throughput?
text: LinkedIn & the Origin of Kafka (Case Study) Sources: LinkedIn Engineering Blog, Kreps, Narkhede, Rao — "Kafka: a Distributed Messaging System for Log Processing" (NetDB 2011) The problem LinkedIn had: By the early 2010s, LinkedIn had many separate systems that needed the same underlying activity data — the news feed, search indexing, relevance/ML pipelines, monitoring, and analytics all needed a feed of user activity events (page views, connections made, likes). Each consumer had built its own point-to-point pipeline to get this data, resulting in an N×M mess of custom, fragile integrations between every producer and every consumer. Why existing message queues weren't a fit: Traditional queues (JMS-style brokers) were built for low-throughput, transactional messaging, not the sustained high-throughput firehose of activity events LinkedIn needed to move (hundreds of billions of events/day at LinkedIn's later scale). They also typically delete a message once consumed, so a second, independent consumer couldn't replay the same stream. Kafka's core design choices (as a direct response to that problem): Log-based storage: instead of deleting messages after delivery, Kafka retains them for a configured period (or forever) as an append-only log. Multiple independent consumer groups can each read the same stream at their own pace, tracking their own offset — this single change is what let LinkedIn support many different downstream consumers off one shared pipeline instead of N separate point-to-point integrations. Partitioning: each topic is split into partitions, each handled independently and in order, allowing horizontal scaling of both writes and reads by adding more partitions and consumers. Sequential disk I/O: Kafka relies on sequential reads/writes to disk (fast, even on spinning disks) plus OS page cache, rather than random access — this is why Kafka achieves very high throughput despite persisting everything. Pull-based consumption: consumers pull at their own pace and track their own offset, rather than the broker pushing and needing to track per-consumer state — simplifies the broker and lets slow consumers fall behind without overwhelming themselves, catching up later from their last offset. Outcome: LinkedIn open-sourced Kafka in 2011 and it became an Apache project; it's now the de facto standard for high-throughput event streaming across the industry (adopted by Netflix, Uber, and most large-scale systems that need a durable, replayable, multi-consumer event backbone) — a direct example of solving an internal integration problem generally enough that it became foundational infrastructure well beyond its original use case. Relevance to system design interviews: "Why Kafka over a traditional queue" is a common follow-up question — the answer is precisely this history: replayability (log retention, multiple independent consumer groups) and throughput (partitioning + sequential I/O), not just "it's a queue but faster."

text: Message Queues & Pub-Sub Sources: AWS SQS Developer Guide, RabbitMQ documentation, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) ch.11 What it is: A message queue decouples producers (services that create work) from consumers (services that process it). Producer pushes a message, queue holds it, consumer pulls and processes it whenever ready. Neither side needs the other to be online at the same instant. Why use one: Smooths traffic spikes — queue absorbs a burst, consumers drain it at their own pace. Decouples services — producer doesn't care if consumer is slow, down, or scaled to zero. Enables retries — failed messages can be redelivered instead of lost. Enables async workflows — user gets a fast response, heavy work happens in background (e.g. "order placed" returns instantly, email/invoice generation happens after). Point-to-point vs Pub/Sub: Point-to-point (queue): one message, one consumer. Used for task distribution — e.g. a pool of workers pulling image-resize jobs off a queue. Pub/Sub (topic): one message, many subscribers. Used for fan-out — e.g. "order placed" event notifies inventory service, billing service, and analytics service simultaneously. Delivery guarantees: At-most-once: message may be lost, never duplicated. Fastest, least safe. At-least-once: message guaranteed delivered, but may be duplicated on retry. Most systems (SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka) default to this — consumers must be idempotent. Exactly-once: hardest to guarantee in a distributed system; usually achieved by combining at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers (dedupe by message ID), not by the queue itself. Visibility timeout / ack: Consumer pulls a message; queue hides it from other consumers for a timeout window. Consumer processes it, then explicitly acknowledges (deletes) the message. If consumer crashes before ack, message becomes visible again and another consumer picks it up — this is why consumers must be idempotent, since a message could be processed twice. Dead-letter queues (DLQ): Messages that fail processing repeatedly (e.g. 5 retries) are moved to a separate DLQ instead of blocking the main queue forever. Lets you inspect and reprocess poison messages without stalling healthy traffic. Queue vs Kafka: Traditional queues (SQS, RabbitMQ) delete a message once consumed — it's gone. Kafka is a log: messages are retained for a configured period and consumers track their own offset, so multiple consumer groups can replay the same stream independently. Use a queue for simple task distribution; use Kafka when you need replay, ordering within a partition, or multiple independent consumers of the same event stream. Real-world example: E-commerce checkout: "order placed" event published to a topic. → Inventory service subscribes, decrements stock. → Billing service subscribes, charges card. → Notification service subscribes, sends confirmation email. Each subscriber processes independently; if the email service is down, the order still completes — the message just waits in that service's queue until it recovers.

text: LinkedIn & the Origin of Kafka (Case Study) Sources: LinkedIn Engineering Blog, Kreps, Narkhede, Rao — "Kafka: a Distributed Messaging System for Log Processing" (NetDB 2011) The problem LinkedIn had: By the early 2010s, LinkedIn had many separate systems that needed the same underlying activity data — the news feed, search indexing, relevance/ML pipelines, monitoring, and analytics all needed a feed of user activity events (page views, connections made, likes). Each consumer had built its own point-to-point pipeline to get this data, resulting in an N×M mess of custom, fragile integrations between every producer and every consumer. Why existing message queues weren't a fit: Traditional queues (JMS-style brokers) were built for low-throughput, transactional messaging, not the sustained high-throughput firehose of activity events LinkedIn needed to move (hundreds of billions of events/day at LinkedIn's later scale). They also typically delete a message once consumed, so a second, independent consumer couldn't replay the same stream. Multiple independent consumer groups can each read the same stream at their own pace, tracking their own offset — this single change is what let LinkedIn support many different downstream consumers off one shared pipeline instead of N separate point-to-point integrations. Sequential disk I/O: Kafka relies on sequential reads/writes to disk (fast, even on spinning disks) plus OS page cache, rather than random access — this is why Kafka achieves very high throughput despite persisting everything. Pull-based consumption: consumers pull at their own pace and track their own offset, rather than the broker pushing and needing to track per-consumer state — simplifies the broker and lets slow consumers fall behind without overwhelming themselves, catching up later from their last offset. text: Event-Driven Architecture & CQRS Sources: Martin Fowler's blog (martinfowler.com — "CQRS", "Event Sourcing"), Microsoft Azure Architecture Center (CQRS pattern, Event-driven architecture style) What event-driven architecture is: Services communicate by emitting events ("OrderPlaced", "PaymentFailed") to a broker (Kafka, SNS, RabbitMQ) rather than calling each other's APIs directly. Interested services subscribe to the events they care about and react independently. Producer doesn't know or care who's listening. Why use it over direct service-to-service calls: Loose coupling — order-service doesn't need to know inventory-service, billing-service, and analytics-service exist; it just publishes "OrderPlaced". Adding a new consumer (e.g. a new fraud-detection service) requires zero changes to the producer. Resilience — if notification-service is down, the event waits in its queue; order-service isn't blocked waiting on a slow downstream call. CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation): Split the model used for writes (commands) from the model used for reads (queries) — instead of one model trying to serve both efficiently. Write side: optimized for validating and persisting a change (e.g. normalized relational tables, enforcing invariants). Read side: optimized for how the data is actually queried (e.g. a denormalized, pre-joined view tailored to a specific screen). The two are kept in sync via events — write side publishes an event on every change, read side subscribes and updates its own denormalized copy. Why CQRS pairs with event-driven design: The event stream that keeps read models in sync *is* the event-driven mechanism — a write triggers an event, one or more read models rebuild themselves from it, independently and asynchronously. Trade-off: eventual consistency. Because the read model updates asynchronously after the write event, there's a window where a query might return stale data (read model hasn't caught up yet). This is fine for a lot of use cases (a "likes count" being one event behind is not a problem) but wrong for anything requiring strict consistency (reading your own bank balance right after a transfer). Event Sourcing (often paired with CQRS, but a separate concept): Instead of storing current state and overwriting it, store the full sequence of events that led to the current state ("AccountOpened", "Deposited $100", "Withdrew $30"). Current state is derived by replaying events. Benefit: full audit trail for free, and you can rebuild any past state or fix a bug in projection logic by replaying history with corrected logic. Cost: replaying a long event history to get current state is slow without periodic snapshots; more operational complexity than just storing current state. Real-world example: An e-commerce order system publishes "OrderPlaced" on write. A dedicated "OrderSummaryView" read model (denormalized, stored in a fast key-value store) subscribes and updates itself — this is the exact table the "My Orders" page in the app queries, pre-shaped for that screen, entirely separate from the normalized orders/line_items tables used to validate and place the order in the first place.

text: WhatsApp System Design Sources: WhatsApp Engineering (public talks/posts on Erlang-based scaling), Meta Engineering Blog Overview: WhatsApp handles 100 billion messages per day across 2 billion users. Core challenges: real-time message delivery, end-to-end encryption, presence (online/offline), and media delivery at scale. Core Components: - Connection Service: Maintains persistent WebSocket connections per user - Message Service: Stores and routes messages between users - Presence Service: Tracks online/offline/last-seen status - Push Notification Service: Delivers messages to offline users via APNs/FCM - Media Service: Handles image, video, audio upload and delivery - Group Service: Manages group membership and fan-out Protocol: WebSocket for persistent bidirectional connection. XMPP protocol adapted by WhatsApp for message framing. Each user device maintains one persistent TCP connection to the server. Message Delivery Flow: Sender sends message → Server receives → Stores in queue → If recipient online: deliver via WebSocket immediately → If offline: store in database, send push notification → Recipient comes online: fetch pending messages, delete from queue Database Choice: Messages: Erlang Mnesia (in-memory) for active sessions + Cassandra for persistence Media: Distributed object storage (similar to S3) User data: MySQL for profiles and contacts Messages are NOT stored long-term on server after delivery (privacy design). End-to-End Encryption: Signal protocol. Keys stored only on devices. Server never has access to message plaintext. This is a deliberate trade-off: cannot do server-side spam filtering. Scalability: Erlang/OTP chosen specifically because one Erlang process per connection scales to millions of concurrent connections per server. WhatsApp ran 2 million connections on a single server using Erlang. Trade-offs: No server-side message storage after delivery → cannot restore lost messages E2E encryption → cannot do content moderation Presence accuracy traded off for scale — last seen may lag slightly

text: Rate Limiter System Design Sources: Stripe API documentation (Rate Limiters), Cloudflare Learning Center (Rate Limiting) What it is: A rate limiter controls how many requests a client can make in a given time window. Critical for APIs to prevent abuse, ensure fair usage, and protect backend services. Used by every major API: Twitter, Stripe, Razorpay, GitHub. Algorithms: 1. Token Bucket (most common): Each user gets a bucket with N tokens. Each request consumes one token. Tokens refill at a fixed rate. If bucket empty, request rejected. Allows short bursts (use all tokens at once) but limits sustained rate. Used by: AWS API Gateway, Stripe. 2. Sliding Window Log: Store timestamp of every request in a sorted set (Redis). On each request, remove timestamps older than window, count remaining. If count >= limit, reject. Accurate but memory-intensive. 3. Fixed Window Counter: Simple counter per user per time window (e.g., per minute). Reset counter at window boundary. Fast and memory efficient. Problem: burst at window boundary (double the rate for a brief moment). 4. Leaky Bucket: Requests enter a queue (bucket). Processed at fixed rate. Smooths out bursts. Good for output rate limiting. Implementation with Redis: Redis is ideal for rate limiting because: - Atomic operations (INCR, EXPIRE) prevent race conditions - Sub-millisecond latency - Distributed — works across multiple API server instances Redis token bucket implementation: INCR user:123:requests EXPIRE user:123:requests 60 If value > limit: reject request Where to implement: - API Gateway layer (before hitting your services) - Middleware in FastAPI/Express - Nginx level for simple cases Distributed Rate Limiting Challenge: With multiple servers, each server has its own counter. Solution: Centralized Redis store shared across all servers. Trade-off: Redis becomes a bottleneck — use Redis Cluster for scale. Real example — Razorpay API: 100 requests per minute per API key. Exceeded: HTTP 429 Too Many Requests. Headers returned: X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset.

text: Message Queues & Pub-Sub Sources: AWS SQS Developer Guide, RabbitMQ documentation, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) ch.11 What it is: A message queue decouples producers (services that create work) from consumers (services that process it). Producer pushes a message, queue holds it, consumer pulls and processes it whenever ready. Neither side needs the other to be online at the same instant. Why use one: Smooths traffic spikes — queue absorbs a burst, consumers drain it at their own pace. Decouples services — producer doesn't care if consumer is slow, down, or scaled to zero. Enables retries — failed messages can be redelivered instead of lost. Enables async workflows — user gets a fast response, heavy work happens in background (e.g. "order placed" returns instantly, email/invoice generation happens after). Point-to-point vs Pub/Sub: Point-to-point (queue): one message, one consumer. Used for task distribution — e.g. a pool of workers pulling image-resize jobs off a queue. Pub/Sub (topic): one message, many subscribers. Used for fan-out — e.g. "order placed" event notifies inventory service, billing service, and analytics service simultaneously. Delivery guarantees: At-most-once: message may be lost, never duplicated. Fastest, least safe. At-least-once: message guaranteed delivered, but may be duplicated on retry. Most systems (SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka) default to this — consumers must be idempotent. Exactly-once: hardest to guarantee in a distributed system; usually achieved by combining at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers (dedupe by message ID), not by the queue itself. Visibility timeout / ack: Consumer pulls a message; queue hides it from other consumers for a timeout window. Consumer processes it, then explicitly acknowledges (deletes) the message. If consumer crashes before ack, message becomes visible again and another consumer picks it up — this is why consumers must be idempotent, since a message could be processed twice. Dead-letter queues (DLQ): Messages that fail processing repeatedly (e.g. 5 retries) are moved to a separate DLQ instead of blocking the main queue forever. Lets you inspect and reprocess poison messages without stalling healthy traffic. Queue vs Kafka: Traditional queues (SQS, RabbitMQ) delete a message once consumed — it's gone. Kafka is a log: messages are retained for a configured period and consumers track their own offset, so multiple consumer groups can replay the same stream independently. text: Bloom Filters Sources: Burton H. Bloom, "Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding with Allowable Errors" (1970), Redis documentation (Bloom Filter / probabilistic data structures) What it is: A probabilistic data structure that answers "have I possibly seen this item before?" using a fixed, tiny amount of memory — regardless of how many items have been added. Trades perfect accuracy for massive space savings. The guarantee (this is the important part): No false negatives: if the filter says "definitely not present," the item is genuinely not present. Possible false positives: if the filter says "possibly present," it might actually not be — the false positive rate is tunable (smaller filter / more items = higher false positive rate). It never says "definitely present" for something that was never added incorrectly in the wrong direction — the asymmetry only goes one way, which is what makes it usable: you only need a secondary, slower check for the "possibly present" case. How it works: A bit array of m bits, all initially 0, plus k independent hash functions. To add an item: hash it k times, set the k resulting bit positions to 1. To check an item: hash it the same k times, if ALL k bit positions are 1, report "possibly present"; if ANY bit is 0, report "definitely not present" (since adding that item would have set that bit). False positives happen because bits get shared/overwritten by other items' hashes — you can't tell whether a set bit was set by the item you're checking or by pure coincidence from other insertions. Why not just use a hash set: A hash set storing millions of actual keys uses far more memory (must store each key or at least its full hash) than a Bloom filter, which only needs a handful of bits per item regardless of key size. The trade is: a hash set has zero false positives, a Bloom filter accepts a small false-positive rate in exchange for a fraction of the memory. Cannot remove items (in the basic version): Because bits are shared across multiple items' hashes, clearing a bit to "remove" one item could break the correctness for other items that also set that bit. A Counting Bloom Filter (using small counters instead of single bits) supports removal at the cost of more memory — used when deletions are actually needed. Real-world example: A CDN or database wants to avoid an expensive disk/network lookup for keys that definitely don't exist (e.g. checking if a URL is on a known-malicious list, or if a cache key might exist before hitting disk). Check the Bloom filter first: if "definitely not present," skip the expensive lookup entirely. If "possibly present," do the real (slower, authoritative) lookup to confirm — the small false-positive rate just means occasionally doing an unnecessary real lookup, never missing an item that's actually there. This "fanout" problem is one of the hardest in distributed systems. Scale Numbers: - 350+ million monthly active users - 500 million tweets per day (~6000 tweets/second) - 150 million daily active users - Peak: Obama election tweet — 150,000 tweets/second - Average user follows 200 accounts - 1% of users have 1M+ followers (celebrities, news accounts) Core Features to Design: 1. text: Distributed Transactions: 2PC & Saga Pattern Sources: "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) ch.9, microservices.io (Chris Richardson) — "Saga pattern" The problem: A single database transaction (BEGIN...COMMIT) guarantees all-or-nothing across tables in one database. But a "place order" flow in a microservices system might need to update order-service's DB, decrement inventory-service's DB, and charge payment-service's DB — three separate databases, no single transaction can span all of them. Two-Phase Commit (2PC): A coordinator asks every participant to "prepare" (lock resources, confirm it *can* commit, but don't commit yet). If all participants vote yes, coordinator tells everyone to commit. If any vote no, coordinator tells everyone to abort. Guarantees atomicity across multiple resources — either all commit or all abort. Why 2PC is avoided in practice at scale: Blocking: if the coordinator crashes after participants have "prepared" but before sending commit/abort, participants are stuck holding locks indefinitely, waiting for a coordinator that may never come back. Latency: every participant must stay locked and waiting through two full round-trips before any of them can proceed — slow, and doesn't scale well across services owned by different teams with independent uptime. Tight coupling: all participants must be available simultaneously; one slow or down service blocks the whole transaction for everyone. Saga pattern (the common alternative in microservices): Break the transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each with its own compensating action to undo it if a later step fails. Example: (1) order-service creates order [compensate: cancel order], (2) inventory-service reserves stock [compensate: release stock], (3) payment-service charges card [compensate: refund]. If step 3 fails, the saga runs compensations for steps 2 and 1 in reverse — no single distributed lock is ever held across all three. Choreography vs Orchestration (two ways to coordinate a saga): Choreography: each service publishes an event when its step completes, next service reacts to that event — fully decentralized, no single point of control, but harder to see the overall flow/state of "which step is this order on." Orchestration: a central saga orchestrator explicitly tells each service what to do next and tracks the saga's state — easier to reason about and debug, but the orchestrator becomes a piece of infrastructure every saga depends on. Key trade-off vs 2PC: Sagas give up strict atomicity (there IS a window where inventory is reserved but payment hasn't happened yet — visible partial state) in exchange for no blocking locks held across services and independent service availability. This is why sagas are preferred in practice: partial visibility for a short window is an acceptable trade for not letting one service's outage freeze every other service's transactions. Real-world example: Booking a flight + hotel as one "trip" transaction: reserve flight seat, reserve hotel room, charge card. If the hotel is sold out by the time that step runs, the saga triggers a compensating action to release the flight seat that was already reserved — the user never ends up charged for a trip that couldn't be fully booked, without ever holding a lock

text: Event-Driven Architecture & CQRS Sources: Martin Fowler's blog (martinfowler.com — "CQRS", "Event Sourcing"), Microsoft Azure Architecture Center (CQRS pattern, Event-driven architecture style) What event-driven architecture is: Services communicate by emitting events ("OrderPlaced", "PaymentFailed") to a broker (Kafka, SNS, RabbitMQ) rather than calling each other's APIs directly. Interested services subscribe to the events they care about and react independently. Producer doesn't know or care who's listening. Why use it over direct service-to-service calls: Loose coupling — order-service doesn't need to know inventory-service, billing-service, and analytics-service exist; it just publishes "OrderPlaced". Adding a new consumer (e.g. a new fraud-detection service) requires zero changes to the producer. Resilience — if notification-service is down, the event waits in its queue; order-service isn't blocked waiting on a slow downstream call. CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation): Split the model used for writes (commands) from the model used for reads (queries) — instead of one model trying to serve both efficiently. Write side: optimized for validating and persisting a change (e.g. normalized relational tables, enforcing invariants). Read side: optimized for how the data is actually queried (e.g. a denormalized, pre-joined view tailored to a specific screen). The two are kept in sync via events — write side publishes an event on every change, read side subscribes and updates its own denormalized copy. Why CQRS pairs with event-driven design: The event stream that keeps read models in sync *is* the event-driven mechanism — a write triggers an event, one or more read models rebuild themselves from it, independently and asynchronously. Trade-off: eventual consistency. Because the read model updates asynchronously after the write event, there's a window where a query might return stale data (read model hasn't caught up yet). This is fine for a lot of use cases (a "likes count" being one event behind is not a problem) but wrong for anything requiring strict consistency (reading your own bank balance right after a transfer). Event Sourcing (often paired with CQRS, but a separate concept): Instead of storing current state and overwriting it, store the full sequence of events that led to the current state ("AccountOpened", "Deposited $100", "Withdrew $30"). Current state is derived by replaying events. Benefit: full audit trail for free, and you can rebuild any past state or fix a bug in projection logic by replaying history with corrected logic. Cost: replaying a long event history to get current state is slow without periodic snapshots; more operational complexity than just storing current state. Real-world example: An e-commerce order system publishes "OrderPlaced" on write. A dedicated "OrderSummaryView" read model (denormalized, stored in a fast key-value store) subscribes and updates itself — this is the exact table the "My Orders" page in the app queries, pre-shaped for that screen, entirely separate from the normalized orders/line_items tables used to validate and place the order in the first place.

text: Distributed Locks & Leader Election Sources: Redis documentation (Distributed Locks with Redis / Redlock), Apache ZooKeeper documentation, etcd documentation What it is: A distributed lock lets multiple processes across different machines coordinate so only one of them does a particular piece of work at a time — e.g. only one instance of a cron job runs, or only one node processes a given task. A regular in-process lock (mutex) doesn't work here because the "processes" are on different machines with no shared memory. Why you need one: Running the same scheduled job twice (duplicate emails sent, duplicate charges). Two nodes both thinking they're the "leader" and both writing conflicting data. Preventing two workers from picking up and processing the same queue item. Redis-based locks (simple case): SET a key with a unique value and an expiry (SET lock_key unique_id NX EX 30). NX means "only set if not exists" — this is the actual locking mechanism. Expiry (EX) prevents a deadlock if the holder crashes before releasing. Release by checking the value matches before deleting (via a Lua script, to make compare-and-delete atomic) — otherwise you might delete a lock some other process acquired after your expiry. Limitation: single Redis node is a single point of failure. If it fails over to a replica before the write is replicated, two clients could both believe they hold the lock. Redlock (multi-node Redis locking): Acquire the lock on a majority of independent Redis nodes (e.g. 3 of 5) within a time budget. Considered "acquired" only if majority succeeds before the clock runs out. More resilient to a single node failing, though it has been debated (Martin Kleppmann's critique) as not being fully safe under clock drift/GC pauses — good enough for "efficiency" locks (avoid duplicate work), not for correctness-critical locks (avoid data corruption). ZooKeeper / etcd-based locks (correctness-critical case): Both are consensus-based stores (using ZAB / Raft respectively) — a write is only acknowledged once a majority of nodes agree, which is much stronger than a single Redis node's guarantee. Leader election pattern: each candidate creates an ephemeral sequential node; the candidate with the lowest sequence number is the leader. If the leader's session dies (crash, network partition), its ephemeral node disappears automatically and the next-lowest candidate becomes leader. Use this when correctness matters more than latency — e.g. only one node should ever be allowed to write to a given shard. Fencing tokens: Even with a "correct" lock, a paused process (GC pause, slow disk) can wake up after its lock has expired and still think it holds the lock, then write stale data. Fix: every time a lock is granted, issue a monotonically increasing fencing token. The resource being protected (e.g. storage service) rejects any write that comes with an older token than the last one it saw — this is the actual fix for "lock expired but process is still running" bugs, the lock alone is not sufficient. Real-world example: A distributed cron system runs the same job definition

query: How do microservices handle inter-service communication and service discovery?
text: API Gateway Sources: AWS API Gateway Developer Guide, Kong Gateway documentation What it is: A single entry point that sits in front of a collection of backend services (especially in a microservices architecture) and routes each incoming request to the right service. Clients talk to one gateway instead of knowing about every individual service's address. What it handles (so individual services don't have to): Routing: maps a path/method to the right backend service (/users → user-service, /orders → order-service). Authentication: validates JWT/API keys once at the edge, so downstream services trust the gateway instead of each re-implementing auth. Rate limiting: throttles per-client request rate before it ever reaches backend services, protecting them from being overwhelmed. Request/response transformation: e.g. converting a legacy SOAP backend response to JSON for modern clients, without changing the backend. Aggregation: combining calls to multiple services into a single client-facing response (sometimes called the "backend for frontend" pattern) — a mobile app screen might need data from 3 services, gateway can fan out and merge. Observability: single place to log, trace, and monitor all API traffic instead of instrumenting every service separately. TLS termination: gateway handles HTTPS, internal traffic between gateway and services can be plain HTTP within a trusted network. Gateway vs Load Balancer: A load balancer (L4/L7) distributes traffic across replicas of the *same* service based on IP/path. An API gateway routes across *different* services and adds application-level concerns (auth, rate limiting, transformation) on top — they're often used together: gateway routes to a service name, load balancer distributes across that service's replicas. Failure mode to watch for: Single point of failure — if the gateway goes down, every service behind it is unreachable even if they're all healthy. Mitigated by running multiple gateway instances behind their own load balancer, and keeping the gateway itself stateless so any instance can handle any request. Backend for Frontend (BFF) pattern: Instead of one generic gateway for all clients, run a dedicated gateway per client type (mobile-BFF, web-BFF) — each shaped to that client's specific data needs, avoiding a single gateway trying to please every consumer with one generic contract. Real-world example: A ride-sharing app's mobile client hits a single gateway endpoint. Gateway validates the JWT, then calls trip-service, pricing-service, and driver-location-service in parallel, merges their responses into one JSON payload the app expects — the mobile client never needs to know these are three separate backend services, or that pricing-service might be redeployed independently tomorrow.
