Adding a new consumer (e.g. a new fraud-detection service) requires zero changes to the producer. Resilience — if notification-service is down, the event waits in its queue; order-service isn't blocked waiting on a slow downstream call. CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation): Split the model used for writes (commands) from the model used for reads (queries) — instead of one model trying to serve both efficiently. Write side: optimized for validating and persisting a change (e.g. normalized relational tables, enforcing invariants). Read side: optimized for how the data is actually queried (e.g. a denormalized, pre-joined view tailored to a specific screen). The two are kept in sync via events — write side publishes an event on every change, read side subscribes and updates its own denormalized copy. Why CQRS pairs with event-driven design: The event stream that keeps read models in sync *is* the event-driven mechanism — a write triggers an event, one or more read models rebuild themselves from it, independently and asynchronously. Trade-off: eventual consistency. Because the read model updates asynchronously after the write event, there's a window where a query might return stale data (read model hasn't caught up yet). This is fine for a lot of use cases (a "likes count" being one event behind is not a problem) but wrong for anything requiring strict consistency (reading your own bank balance right after a transfer). Event Sourcing (often paired with CQRS, but a separate concept): Instead of storing current state and overwriting it, store the full sequence of events that led to the current state ("AccountOpened", "Deposited $100", "Withdrew $30"). Current state is derived by replaying events. Benefit: full audit trail for free, and you can rebuild any past state or fix a bug in projection logic by replaying history with corrected logic. Cost: replaying a long event history to get current state is slow without periodic snapshots; more operational complexity than just storing current state. Real-world example: An e-commerce order system publishes "OrderPlaced" on write. A dedicated "OrderSummaryView" read model (denormalized, stored in a fast key-value store) subscribes and updates itself — this is the exact table the "My Orders" page in the app queries, pre-shaped for that screen, entirely separate from the normalized orders/line_items tables used to validate and place the order in the first place.

query: Explain the purpose of an API Gateway in microservices.
text: API Gateway Sources: AWS API Gateway Developer Guide, Kong Gateway documentation What it is: A single entry point that sits in front of a collection of backend services (especially in a microservices architecture) and routes each incoming request to the right service. Clients talk to one gateway instead of knowing about every individual service's address. What it handles (so individual services don't have to): Routing: maps a path/method to the right backend service (/users → user-service, /orders → order-service). Authentication: validates JWT/API keys once at the edge, so downstream services trust the gateway instead of each re-implementing auth. Rate limiting: throttles per-client request rate before it ever reaches backend services, protecting them from being overwhelmed. Request/response transformation: e.g. converting a legacy SOAP backend response to JSON for modern clients, without changing the backend. Aggregation: combining calls to multiple services into a single client-facing response (sometimes called the "backend for frontend" pattern) — a mobile app screen might need data from 3 services, gateway can fan out and merge. Observability: single place to log, trace, and monitor all API traffic instead of instrumenting every service separately. TLS termination: gateway handles HTTPS, internal traffic between gateway and services can be plain HTTP within a trusted network. Gateway vs Load Balancer: A load balancer (L4/L7) distributes traffic across replicas of the *same* service based on IP/path. An API gateway routes across *different* services and adds application-level concerns (auth, rate limiting, transformation) on top — they're often used together: gateway routes to a service name, load balancer distributes across that service's replicas. Failure mode to watch for: Single point of failure — if the gateway goes down, every service behind it is unreachable even if they're all healthy. Mitigated by running multiple gateway instances behind their own load balancer, and keeping the gateway itself stateless so any instance can handle any request. Backend for Frontend (BFF) pattern: Instead of one generic gateway for all clients, run a dedicated gateway per client type (mobile-BFF, web-BFF) — each shaped to that client's specific data needs, avoiding a single gateway trying to please every consumer with one generic contract. Real-world example: A ride-sharing app's mobile client hits a single gateway endpoint. Gateway validates the JWT, then calls trip-service, pricing-service, and driver-location-service in parallel, merges their responses into one JSON payload the app expects — the mobile client never needs to know these are three separate backend services, or that pricing-service might be redeployed independently tomorrow.

text: Rate Limiter System Design Sources: Stripe API documentation (Rate Limiters), Cloudflare Learning Center (Rate Limiting) What it is: A rate limiter controls how many requests a client can make in a given time window. Critical for APIs to prevent abuse, ensure fair usage, and protect backend services. Used by every major API: Twitter, Stripe, Razorpay, GitHub. Algorithms: 1. Token Bucket (most common): Each user gets a bucket with N tokens. Each request consumes one token. Tokens refill at a fixed rate. If bucket empty, request rejected. Allows short bursts (use all tokens at once) but limits sustained rate. Used by: AWS API Gateway, Stripe. 2. Sliding Window Log: Store timestamp of every request in a sorted set (Redis). On each request, remove timestamps older than window, count remaining. If count >= limit, reject. Accurate but memory-intensive. 3. Fixed Window Counter: Simple counter per user per time window (e.g., per minute). Reset counter at window boundary. Fast and memory efficient. Problem: burst at window boundary (double the rate for a brief moment). 4. Leaky Bucket: Requests enter a queue (bucket). Processed at fixed rate. Smooths out bursts. Good for output rate limiting. Implementation with Redis: Redis is ideal for rate limiting because: - Atomic operations (INCR, EXPIRE) prevent race conditions - Sub-millisecond latency - Distributed — works across multiple API server instances Redis token bucket implementation: INCR user:123:requests EXPIRE user:123:requests 60 If value > limit: reject request Where to implement: - API Gateway layer (before hitting your services) - Middleware in FastAPI/Express - Nginx level for simple cases Distributed Rate Limiting Challenge: With multiple servers, each server has its own counter. Solution: Centralized Redis store shared across all servers. Trade-off: Redis becomes a bottleneck — use Redis Cluster for scale. Real example — Razorpay API: 100 requests per minute per API key. Exceeded: HTTP 429 Too Many Requests. Headers returned: X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset.

text: Distributed Transactions: 2PC & Saga Pattern Sources: "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) ch.9, microservices.io (Chris Richardson) — "Saga pattern" The problem: A single database transaction (BEGIN...COMMIT) guarantees all-or-nothing across tables in one database. But a "place order" flow in a microservices system might need to update order-service's DB, decrement inventory-service's DB, and charge payment-service's DB — three separate databases, no single transaction can span all of them. Two-Phase Commit (2PC): A coordinator asks every participant to "prepare" (lock resources, confirm it *can* commit, but don't commit yet). If all participants vote yes, coordinator tells everyone to commit. If any vote no, coordinator tells everyone to abort. Guarantees atomicity across multiple resources — either all commit or all abort. Why 2PC is avoided in practice at scale: Blocking: if the coordinator crashes after participants have "prepared" but before sending commit/abort, participants are stuck holding locks indefinitely, waiting for a coordinator that may never come back. Latency: every participant must stay locked and waiting through two full round-trips before any of them can proceed — slow, and doesn't scale well across services owned by different teams with independent uptime. Tight coupling: all participants must be available simultaneously; one slow or down service blocks the whole transaction for everyone. Saga pattern (the common alternative in microservices): Break the transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each with its own compensating action to undo it if a later step fails. Example: (1) order-service creates order [compensate: cancel order], (2) inventory-service reserves stock [compensate: release stock], (3) payment-service charges card [compensate: refund]. If step 3 fails, the saga runs compensations for steps 2 and 1 in reverse — no single distributed lock is ever held across all three. Choreography vs Orchestration (two ways to coordinate a saga): Choreography: each service publishes an event when its step completes, next service reacts to that event — fully decentralized, no single point of control, but harder to see the overall flow/state of "which step is this order on." Orchestration: a central saga orchestrator explicitly tells each service what to do next and tracks the saga's state — easier to reason about and debug, but the orchestrator becomes a piece of infrastructure every saga depends on. Key trade-off vs 2PC: Sagas give up strict atomicity (there IS a window where inventory is reserved but payment hasn't happened yet — visible partial state) in exchange for no blocking locks held across services and independent service availability. This is why sagas are preferred in practice: partial visibility for a short window is an acceptable trade for not letting one service's outage freeze every other service's transactions. Real-world example: Booking a flight + hotel as one "trip" transaction: reserve flight seat, reserve hotel room, charge card. If the hotel is sold out by the time that step runs, the saga triggers a compensating action to release the flight seat that was already reserved — the user never ends up charged for a trip that couldn't be fully booked, without ever holding a lock

text: Event-Driven Architecture & CQRS Sources: Martin Fowler's blog (martinfowler.com — "CQRS", "Event Sourcing"), Microsoft Azure Architecture Center (CQRS pattern, Event-driven architecture style) What event-driven architecture is: Services communicate by emitting events ("OrderPlaced", "PaymentFailed") to a broker (Kafka, SNS, RabbitMQ) rather than calling each other's APIs directly. Interested services subscribe to the events they care about and react independently. Producer doesn't know or care who's listening. Why use it over direct service-to-service calls: Loose coupling — order-service doesn't need to know inventory-service, billing-service, and analytics-service exist; it just publishes "OrderPlaced". Adding a new consumer (e.g. a new fraud-detection service) requires zero changes to the producer. Resilience — if notification-service is down, the event waits in its queue; order-service isn't blocked waiting on a slow downstream call. CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation): Split the model used for writes (commands) from the model used for reads (queries) — instead of one model trying to serve both efficiently. Write side: optimized for validating and persisting a change (e.g. normalized relational tables, enforcing invariants). Read side: optimized for how the data is actually queried (e.g. a denormalized, pre-joined view tailored to a specific screen). The two are kept in sync via events — write side publishes an event on every change, read side subscribes and updates its own denormalized copy. Why CQRS pairs with event-driven design: The event stream that keeps read models in sync *is* the event-driven mechanism — a write triggers an event, one or more read models rebuild themselves from it, independently and asynchronously. Trade-off: eventual consistency. Because the read model updates asynchronously after the write event, there's a window where a query might return stale data (read model hasn't caught up yet). This is fine for a lot of use cases (a "likes count" being one event behind is not a problem) but wrong for anything requiring strict consistency (reading your own bank balance right after a transfer). Event Sourcing (often paired with CQRS, but a separate concept): Instead of storing current state and overwriting it, store the full sequence of events that led to the current state ("AccountOpened", "Deposited $100", "Withdrew $30"). Current state is derived by replaying events. Benefit: full audit trail for free, and you can rebuild any past state or fix a bug in projection logic by replaying history with corrected logic. Cost: replaying a long event history to get current state is slow without periodic snapshots; more operational complexity than just storing current state. Real-world example: An e-commerce order system publishes "OrderPlaced" on write. A dedicated "OrderSummaryView" read model (denormalized, stored in a fast key-value store) subscribes and updates itself — this is the exact table the "My Orders" page in the app queries, pre-shaped for that screen, entirely separate from the normalized orders/line_items tables used to validate and place the order in the first place.

text: Message Queues & Pub-Sub Sources: AWS SQS Developer Guide, RabbitMQ documentation, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) ch.11 What it is: A message queue decouples producers (services that create work) from consumers (services that process it). Producer pushes a message, queue holds it, consumer pulls and processes it whenever ready. Neither side needs the other to be online at the same instant. Why use one: Smooths traffic spikes — queue absorbs a burst, consumers drain it at their own pace. Decouples services — producer doesn't care if consumer is slow, down, or scaled to zero. Enables retries — failed messages can be redelivered instead of lost. Enables async workflows — user gets a fast response, heavy work happens in background (e.g. "order placed" returns instantly, email/invoice generation happens after). Point-to-point vs Pub/Sub: Point-to-point (queue): one message, one consumer. Used for task distribution — e.g. a pool of workers pulling image-resize jobs off a queue. Pub/Sub (topic): one message, many subscribers. Used for fan-out — e.g. "order placed" event notifies inventory service, billing service, and analytics service simultaneously. Delivery guarantees: At-most-once: message may be lost, never duplicated. Fastest, least safe. At-least-once: message guaranteed delivered, but may be duplicated on retry. Most systems (SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka) default to this — consumers must be idempotent. Exactly-once: hardest to guarantee in a distributed system; usually achieved by combining at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers (dedupe by message ID), not by the queue itself. Visibility timeout / ack: Consumer pulls a message; queue hides it from other consumers for a timeout window. Consumer processes it, then explicitly acknowledges (deletes) the message. If consumer crashes before ack, message becomes visible again and another consumer picks it up — this is why consumers must be idempotent, since a message could be processed twice. Dead-letter queues (DLQ): Messages that fail processing repeatedly (e.g. 5 retries) are moved to a separate DLQ instead of blocking the main queue forever. Lets you inspect and reprocess poison messages without stalling healthy traffic. Queue vs Kafka: Traditional queues (SQS, RabbitMQ) delete a message once consumed — it's gone. Kafka is a log: messages are retained for a configured period and consumers track their own offset, so multiple consumer groups can replay the same stream independently. Use a queue for simple task distribution; use Kafka when you need replay, ordering within a partition, or multiple independent consumers of the same event stream. Real-world example: E-commerce checkout: "order placed" event published to a topic. → Inventory service subscribes, decrements stock. → Billing service subscribes, charges card. → Notification service subscribes, sends confirmation email. Each subscriber processes independently; if the email service is down, the order still completes — the message just waits in that service's queue until it recovers.

text: Distributed Transactions: 2PC & Saga Pattern Sources: "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) ch.9, microservices.io (Chris Richardson) — "Saga pattern" The problem: A single database transaction (BEGIN...COMMIT) guarantees all-or-nothing across tables in one database. But a "place order" flow in a microservices system might need to update order-service's DB, decrement inventory-service's DB, and charge payment-service's DB — three separate databases, no single transaction can span all of them. Two-Phase Commit (2PC): A coordinator asks every participant to "prepare" (lock resources, confirm it *can* commit, but don't commit yet). If all participants vote yes, coordinator tells everyone to commit. If any vote no, coordinator tells everyone to abort. Guarantees atomicity across multiple resources — either all commit or all abort. Why 2PC is avoided in practice at scale: Blocking: if the coordinator crashes after participants have "prepared" but before sending commit/abort, participants are stuck holding locks indefinitely, waiting for a coordinator that may never come back. Latency: every participant must stay locked and waiting through two full round-trips before any of them can proceed — slow, and doesn't scale well across services owned by different teams with independent uptime. Tight coupling: all participants must be available simultaneously; one slow or down service blocks the whole transaction for everyone. Saga pattern (the common alternative in microservices): Break the transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each with its own compensating action to undo it if a later step fails. Example: (1) order-service creates order [compensate: cancel order], (2) inventory-service reserves stock [compensate: release stock], (3) payment-service charges card [compensate: refund]. If step 3 fails, the saga runs compensations for steps 2 and 1 in reverse — no single distributed lock is ever held across all three. Choreography vs Orchestration (two ways to coordinate a saga): Choreography: each service publishes an event when its step completes, next service reacts to that event — fully decentralized, no single point of control, but harder to see the overall flow/state of "which step is this order on." Orchestration: a central saga orchestrator explicitly tells each service what to do next and tracks the saga's state — easier to reason about and debug, but the orchestrator becomes a piece of infrastructure every saga depends on. Key trade-off vs 2PC: Sagas give up strict atomicity (there IS a window where inventory is reserved but payment hasn't happened yet — visible partial state) in exchange for no blocking locks held across services and independent service availability. This is why sagas are preferred in practice: partial visibility for a short window is an acceptable trade for not letting one service's outage freeze every other service's transactions. Real-world example: Booking a flight + hotel as one "trip" transaction: reserve flight seat, reserve hotel room, charge card. If the hotel is sold out by the time that step runs, the saga triggers a compensating action to release the flight seat that was already reserved — the user never ends up charged for a trip that couldn't be fully booked, without ever holding a lock

text: APACHE KAFKA — SYSTEM DESIGN DEEP DIVE Sources: Apache Kafka documentation, Kreps, Narkhede, Rao — "Kafka: a Distributed Messaging System for Log Processing" (NetDB 2011) Overview: Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform. Think of it as a highly durable, infinitely scalable message queue where producers write events and consumers read them. It's used in almost every large-scale system: Uber uses it for location updates, LinkedIn (who built Kafka) uses it for activity feeds, Netflix uses it for analytics pipeline. Core Concepts: Event/Message: A piece of data — "user_id: 123 placed order_id: 456 at timestamp: 1234567890" Topic: A named log of events. Like a table in a database. E.g., "order-events" topic Producer: Writes events to a topic Consumer: Reads events from a topic Broker: A Kafka server that stores events Cluster: Multiple brokers working together Partition: A topic is split into partitions for parallelism Offset: A sequential ID for each event in a partition (like array index) Consumer Group: Multiple consumers sharing the work of reading a topic Why Kafka? (vs Traditional Message Queues like RabbitMQ): Traditional queue: event consumed → deleted from queue Kafka: events retained for configurable period (default 7 days) → multiple consumers can independently read the same events This is transformative: - Add a new consumer without affecting existing ones - Replay events from past (debugging, backfilling new systems) - Decouple producers from consumers completely Kafka vs RabbitMQ: - RabbitMQ: message broker, push model, messages deleted after consumption, good for task queues - Kafka: event log, pull model, messages retained, good for event streaming and data pipelines - Choose Kafka when: multiple consumers need the same events, need event replay, high throughput - Choose RabbitMQ when: complex routing, guaranteed message ordering per consumer, task-queue pattern Architecture Deep Dive: Topics and Partitions: - Topic "order-events" might have 12 partitions - Each partition is an ordered, immutable log of events - Partitions distributed across brokers (partition 0 on broker 1, partition 1 on broker 2, etc.) - Events within a partition are strictly ordered - Events across partitions have no guaranteed order Partition Key: - Producer specifies a key per event: order.send(key="user_123", value=event) - All events with same key go to same partition - Guarantees ordering for events with same key (e.g., all events for user_123 are ordered) - Without key: round-robin across partitions Replication: - Each partition has a leader and N replicas on different brokers (N = replication factor) - Default replication factor: 3 (1 leader + 2 replicas) - All reads/writes go to leader - Replicas passively sync from leader - If leader fails, a replica is automatically elected as new leader (ZooKeeper or KRaft consensus) - Durability: Kafka can acknowledge write only after all replicas confirm receipt (acks=all) Consumer Groups: - Multiple consumers in a group share partitions - Each partition assigned to exactly one consumer in a group - 12 partitions + 6 consumers = 2 partitions per consumer (parallelism) - 12 partitions + 12 consumers = 1 partition per consumer (max parallelism)

text: MICROSERVICES ARCHITECTURE Sources: Martin Fowler & James Lewis, "Microservices" (martinfowler.com, 2014) Overview: Microservices is an architectural pattern where an application is built as a collection of small, independent services. Monolith vs Microservices: Monolith: - Single codebase: all features in one application - Single deployment: deploy everything together - Single database: all features share one database - Simple to develop initially - Hard to scale, hard to maintain at large size - One bug can take down entire application Microservices: - Multiple codebases: each service owns its feature - Independent deployment: deploy User Service without touching Order Service - Separate databases: each service owns its data - Complex to develop (distributed systems problems) - Easy to scale: scale only the services that need it - Failure isolation: Order Service failure doesn't affect User Service When to use Microservices: - Team is large (multiple teams working on same codebase causes conflicts) - Different components need to scale independently - Different components have different tech requirements - Already have a working monolith that needs to grow When NOT to use Microservices: - Early stage startup (monolith first, microservices when you have real scale problems) - Small team (distributed systems overhead is too high) - Uncertain requirements (microservice boundaries hard to change later) Core Microservices Concepts: Service Boundaries (Domain-Driven Design): Each microservice should own one "bounded context" — a coherent piece of business logic. text: SQL VS NOSQL — WHEN TO USE WHICH Sources: MongoDB documentation, PostgreSQL documentation, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) ch.2-3 Overview: One of the most common system design interview questions is "what database would you use?" There's no universal answer — the right choice depends on your data model, access patterns, consistency requirements, and scale. Understanding the trade-offs is more important than memorizing which is "better." SQL (Relational Databases): Examples: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, Oracle Core Characteristics: - Data organized in tables with fixed schemas (columns defined upfront) - ACID transactions: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability - SQL query language — powerful, joins, aggregations, subqueries - Strong consistency — reads always reflect latest writes - Relations between tables via foreign keys - Vertical scaling primarily (add more CPU/RAM to one server) When to use SQL: - Complex relationships between entities (users → orders → products → inventory) - Need ACID transactions (banking, e-commerce, healthcare) - Data structure is well-defined and unlikely to change frequently - Need complex queries with joins and aggregations - Team knows SQL well (most developers do) - Compliance requirements (many regulations require ACID) NoSQL (Non-Relational Databases): Four types: Document, Key-Value, Column-Family, Graph 1. Document Stores (MongoDB, CouchDB, Firestore): - Data stored as JSON/BSON documents - Flexible schema: different documents can have different fields - Good for: product catalogs, user profiles, content management - Example: MongoDB stores restaurant menus — each restaurant has different menu structure - Query: rich queries on nested fields, but no joins across collections 2. Problem: A 10GB video with a 1KB edit = waste 10GB of bandwidth. Unacceptable. Chunking (Block-Level Sync): 1. File is split into fixed-size blocks (4MB default) 2. Each block is hashed (SHA-256) 3. Metadata (block list with hashes) stored separately from block content Example: Edit 100 lines in a 500MB file - Only the 4MB block containing those lines has a different hash - Upload: 4MB instead of 500MB - 99% bandwidth saving Deduplication: - If block with hash "abc123" already exists in cloud, don't upload it - Many files have common blocks (PDF headers, common library files) - Content-addressed storage: block stored by its hash, not by name - This also means if two users upload the same file, it's only stored once Architecture Overview: Client (Desktop app): - Monitors local file system for changes (OS file watchers: inotify on Linux, FSEvents on Mac, ReadDirectoryChangesW on Windows) - Maintains local SQLite database of: file metadata, block hashes, sync status - On change: compute changed blocks, upload to Block Storage, update Metadata Server Components: 1. text: CDN — CONTENT DELIVERY NETWORK Sources: Cloudflare Learning Center ("What Is a CDN"), AWS CloudFront documentation Overview: A CDN is a geographically distributed network of servers (edge nodes / Points of Presence / PoPs) that cache and serve content closer to users. Instead of every request going to your origin server (e.g., in US-East), a user in India gets content from a CDN node in Mumbai. Result: faster load times, reduced origin load, better global availability. Why CDN Matters: Without CDN: - User in Mumbai requests image hosted in US-East - Round-trip: Mumbai → ocean cables → US-East → back → 200ms+ latency - All users hit your one origin server — must handle all traffic With CDN: - First request: Mumbai CDN node doesn't have it → fetches from origin, caches it - Subsequent requests: served from Mumbai CDN node → 10-20ms latency - Origin handles only cache misses, not all traffic CDN Benefits: 1. Lower latency: content served from nearest edge node 2. Reduced origin load: 80-95% of requests served from cache 3. Absorb DDoS: CDN can absorb massive traffic spikes (Cloudflare handles terabits/second) 4. High availability: if origin is down, CDN serves cached content 5. Global scale: CDN has PoPs in 100+ cities — instant global distribution 6. Bandwidth cost reduction: CDN bandwidth is cheaper than origin bandwidth What CDNs Cache: Static Content (natural fit for CDN): - Images (JPEG, PNG, WebP, SVG) - Videos and audio - JavaScript bundles, CSS stylesheets - HTML files (if static site) - Fonts - Software downloads Dynamic Content (CDN can still help): - API responses with Cache-Control headers - Personalized pages: harder (need user context) — handled with Vary header or edge computing - Edge functions (Cloudflare Workers, Lambda@Edge): run code at CDN edge to personalize CDN Architecture: Hierarchy of servers: 1. Origin returns content → edge caches it → serves to user 5. The core challenge is the news feed — when a user with 50 million followers tweets, 50 million people should see it in their feed almost instantly. This "fanout" problem is one of the hardest in distributed systems. Scale Numbers: - 350+ million monthly active users - 500 million tweets per day (~6000 tweets/second) - 150 million daily active users - Peak: Obama election tweet — 150,000 tweets/second - Average user follows 200 accounts - 1% of users have 1M+ followers (celebrities, news accounts) Core Features to Design: 1. Post a tweet (text, images, videos) 2. Follow/unfollow users 3. Home timeline (feed of people you follow) 4. Search tweets 5. Trending topics 6. Notifications (likes, retweets, replies) The Hard Problem — Timeline/Feed Generation: Two approaches: Fan-out on Write (push) vs Fan-out on Read (pull) Fan-out on Write (Push Model): - When user A tweets, immediately copy tweet ID to every follower's feed cache - Read is fast — just fetch pre-computed feed from Redis - Problem: if A has 50M followers, writing 50M entries takes too long - Called "hot key" problem — celebrity tweets overwhelm the system Fan-out on Read (Pull Model): - When user opens app, fetch tweets from all accounts they follow - Merge and sort by timestamp - Problem: if following 1000 people, need 1000 queries → too slow Twitter's Hybrid Approach: - Regular users (< 1M followers): Fan-out on write — pre-compute their followers' feeds - Celebrities (1M+ followers): Fan-out on read — their tweets are fetched separately when feed is loaded - Feed = pre-computed feed + lazy-loaded celebrity tweets merged at read time Data Storage: Tweets: - MySQL with Vitess (MySQL clustering) for tweets table - Tweet IDs use Snowflake ID generator (timestamp + machine ID + sequence) — guarantees unique, sortable IDs - Old tweets (>7 days) moved to cold storage (Hadoop/S3) User Relationships (Follow Graph): - Separate social graph service - FlockDB (Twitter's own graph database) or Redis sorted sets - Follow relationship: user_id → set of followed_user_ids - Follower relationship: user_id → set of follower_ids - Both directions maintained for fast lookups Timeline Cache: - Redis — each user has a "home timeline" key with list of tweet IDs (not full tweets) - Stores last 800 tweet IDs per user - Full tweet data fetched from Tweet Store via tweet IDs (separate lookup) - This separation reduces memory usage significantly Media Storage: - Images/videos stored in Blob Storage (S3-equivalent) - Served through CDN globally (Fastly) - Videos transcoded to multiple resolutions on upload (FFmpeg pipeline) - Thumbnails generated asynchronously Tweet Posting Flow: 1. User posts tweet → Tweet Service validates (length, content policy) 2. Tweet stored in MySQL, gets Snowflake tweet_id 3. Media processed asynchronously (if any) 4. Fanout Service picks up via Kafka event "tweet_created" 5. Fanout Service queries Social Graph: get all followers of this user

text: Load Balancer System Design Sources: AWS Elastic Load Balancing documentation, NGINX documentation (Load Balancing) What it is: A load balancer distributes incoming network traffic across multiple servers. Prevents any single server from becoming a bottleneck. Essential for high availability and horizontal scaling. Types of Load Balancers: 1. Layer 4 (Transport Layer): Routes based on IP and TCP/UDP port. Fast, no content inspection. Cannot route based on URL path or headers. Example: AWS Network Load Balancer. 2. Layer 7 (Application Layer): Routes based on HTTP content — URL, headers, cookies. Can do path-based routing (/api → API servers, /static → CDN). Example: AWS Application Load Balancer, Nginx. Load Balancing Algorithms: Round Robin: Requests distributed evenly in order. Simple, works well when servers have equal capacity. Weighted Round Robin: Servers get requests proportional to weight. Used when servers have different capacities. Least Connections: New request goes to server with fewest active connections. Better for long-lived connections (WebSockets, streaming). IP Hash: Client IP hashed to always hit same server. Useful for session stickiness (user always hits same server). Problem: uneven distribution if many users share an IP (NAT). Consistent Hashing: Used for distributed cache and storage routing. Minimizes remapping when servers are added or removed. Health Checks: Load balancer pings each server every few seconds. If server fails health check, removed from rotation automatically. When server recovers, added back automatically. This is how zero-downtime deployments work. Session Stickiness (Sticky Sessions): Problem: User login session stored on Server A. Request goes to Server B — user logged out. Solution 1: Sticky sessions — same user always hits same server (IP hash). Solution 2: Externalize sessions to Redis — any server can read any session. Solution 2 is better for true stateless servers. Real-world stack for Swiggy scale: DNS → AWS Route53 (global traffic routing) → AWS CloudFront (CDN + DDoS protection) → AWS ALB (Layer 7, path-based routing) → Auto Scaling Groups (EC2 instances) → Services

query: What are common patterns for large-scale social feed designs?
text: Pinterest System Design (Case Study) Sources: Pinterest Engineering Blog (medium.com/pinterest-engineering) Core challenge: Pinterest's home feed and search need to serve a highly visual, read-heavy product (billions of "pins," each with images) with personalized ranking, at a read:write ratio that's extremely skewed toward reads — most users browse far more pins than they create. Sharded MySQL as the source of truth: Pinterest's engineering blog has documented using sharded MySQL for core data (pins, boards, users) — sharding by a key like user_id so a given user's data mostly lives on one shard, keeping most queries scoped to a single shard rather than fanning out across all of them. This is a common pattern for reaching MySQL-scale-and-beyond throughput without abandoning a relational model the team already knows well. The feed fan-out problem: When a user follows thousands of boards/users, generating their home feed by querying all of those sources at read time (fan-out on read) is expensive per-request. Alternatively, pre-computing each follower's feed at write time (fan-out on write, i.e. when a pin is created, push it into every follower's precomputed feed) is fast to read but expensive for users with huge numbers of followers (a "celebrity" pinner writing once means fanning out to millions of followers' feeds). Pinterest (like Twitter, Instagram) uses a hybrid: fan-out on write for most users, with a separate fan-out on read path merged in at request time for accounts with very large follower counts — avoiding the write amplification blowup for the small number of accounts where fan-out on write would be disproportionately expensive. Image storage and serving: Billions of images at multiple resolutions (thumbnail, feed-size, full-size) are stored in blob storage and served through a CDN — the application database stores only metadata and a reference/URL to the image, never the image bytes themselves, keeping the relational database small and fast while a purpose-built object store and CDN handle the actual (much larger) binary content and its geographic distribution to users. Personalized ranking: Unlike a purely chronological feed, Pinterest's home feed is ranked by a recommendation model considering a user's past engagement — this ranking step is a separate service/pipeline from the raw "fetch candidate pins" step, following the general large-scale feed pattern of candidate generation (get a broad pool of possibly-relevant pins cheaply) followed by ranking (score and reorder a smaller candidate set more expensively) — doing expensive ML ranking over the entire pin corpus per request would not be feasible, so cheap retrieval narrows the set before expensive ranking runs on it. Real-world takeaway for interviews: "Design Pinterest/Instagram feed" questions center on the fan-out on write vs read trade-off (and the hybrid approach for high-follower accounts), plus the candidate-generation-then-ranking split for personalization — both are reusable patterns that show up across most large-scale social feed system designs, not Pinterest-specific tricks.

This is a common pattern for reaching MySQL-scale-and-beyond throughput without abandoning a relational model the team already knows well. The feed fan-out problem: When a user follows thousands of boards/users, generating their home feed by querying all of those sources at read time (fan-out on read) is expensive per-request. Alternatively, pre-computing each follower's feed at write time (fan-out on write, i.e. when a pin is created, push it into every follower's precomputed feed) is fast to read but expensive for users with huge numbers of followers (a "celebrity" pinner writing once means fanning out to millions of followers' feeds). Pinterest (like Twitter, Instagram) uses a hybrid: fan-out on write for most users, with a separate fan-out on read path merged in at request time for accounts with very large follower counts — avoiding the write amplification blowup for the small number of accounts where fan-out on write would be disproportionately expensive. text: Load Balancer System Design Sources: AWS Elastic Load Balancing documentation, NGINX documentation (Load Balancing) What it is: A load balancer distributes incoming network traffic across multiple servers. Prevents any single server from becoming a bottleneck. Essential for high availability and horizontal scaling. Types of Load Balancers: 1. Layer 4 (Transport Layer): Routes based on IP and TCP/UDP port. Fast, no content inspection. Cannot route based on URL path or headers. Example: AWS Network Load Balancer. 2. Layer 7 (Application Layer): Routes based on HTTP content — URL, headers, cookies. Can do path-based routing (/api → API servers, /static → CDN). Example: AWS Application Load Balancer, Nginx. Load Balancing Algorithms: Round Robin: Requests distributed evenly in order. Simple, works well when servers have equal capacity. Weighted Round Robin: Servers get requests proportional to weight. Used when servers have different capacities. Least Connections: New request goes to server with fewest active connections. Better for long-lived connections (WebSockets, streaming). IP Hash: Client IP hashed to always hit same server. Useful for session stickiness (user always hits same server). Problem: uneven distribution if many users share an IP (NAT). Consistent Hashing: Used for distributed cache and storage routing. Minimizes remapping when servers are added or removed. Health Checks: Load balancer pings each server every few seconds. If server fails health check, removed from rotation automatically. When server recovers, added back automatically. This is how zero-downtime deployments work. Session Stickiness (Sticky Sessions): Problem: User login session stored on Server A. Request goes to Server B — user logged out. Solution 1: Sticky sessions — same user always hits same server (IP hash). Solution 2: Externalize sessions to Redis — any server can read any session. Solution 2 is better for true stateless servers. Real-world stack for Swiggy scale: DNS → AWS Route53 (global traffic routing) → AWS CloudFront (CDN + DDoS protection) → AWS ALB (Layer 7, path-based routing) → Auto Scaling Groups (EC2 instances) → Services

text: Rate Limiter System Design Sources: Stripe API documentation (Rate Limiters), Cloudflare Learning Center (Rate Limiting) What it is: A rate limiter controls how many requests a client can make in a given time window. Critical for APIs to prevent abuse, ensure fair usage, and protect backend services. Used by every major API: Twitter, Stripe, Razorpay, GitHub. Algorithms: 1. Token Bucket (most common): Each user gets a bucket with N tokens. Each request consumes one token. Tokens refill at a fixed rate. If bucket empty, request rejected. Allows short bursts (use all tokens at once) but limits sustained rate. Used by: AWS API Gateway, Stripe. 2. Sliding Window Log: Store timestamp of every request in a sorted set (Redis). On each request, remove timestamps older than window, count remaining. If count >= limit, reject. Accurate but memory-intensive. 3. Fixed Window Counter: Simple counter per user per time window (e.g., per minute). Reset counter at window boundary. Fast and memory efficient. Problem: burst at window boundary (double the rate for a brief moment). 4. Leaky Bucket: Requests enter a queue (bucket). Processed at fixed rate. Smooths out bursts. Good for output rate limiting. Implementation with Redis: Redis is ideal for rate limiting because: - Atomic operations (INCR, EXPIRE) prevent race conditions - Sub-millisecond latency - Distributed — works across multiple API server instances Redis token bucket implementation: INCR user:123:requests EXPIRE user:123:requests 60 If value > limit: reject request Where to implement: - API Gateway layer (before hitting your services) - Middleware in FastAPI/Express - Nginx level for simple cases Distributed Rate Limiting Challenge: With multiple servers, each server has its own counter. Solution: Centralized Redis store shared across all servers. Trade-off: Redis becomes a bottleneck — use Redis Cluster for scale. Real example — Razorpay API: 100 requests per minute per API key. Exceeded: HTTP 429 Too Many Requests. Headers returned: X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset.

text: Distributed Locks & Leader Election Sources: Redis documentation (Distributed Locks with Redis / Redlock), Apache ZooKeeper documentation, etcd documentation What it is: A distributed lock lets multiple processes across different machines coordinate so only one of them does a particular piece of work at a time — e.g. only one instance of a cron job runs, or only one node processes a given task. A regular in-process lock (mutex) doesn't work here because the "processes" are on different machines with no shared memory. Why you need one: Running the same scheduled job twice (duplicate emails sent, duplicate charges). Two nodes both thinking they're the "leader" and both writing conflicting data. Preventing two workers from picking up and processing the same queue item. Redis-based locks (simple case): SET a key with a unique value and an expiry (SET lock_key unique_id NX EX 30). NX means "only set if not exists" — this is the actual locking mechanism. Expiry (EX) prevents a deadlock if the holder crashes before releasing. Release by checking the value matches before deleting (via a Lua script, to make compare-and-delete atomic) — otherwise you might delete a lock some other process acquired after your expiry. Limitation: single Redis node is a single point of failure. If it fails over to a replica before the write is replicated, two clients could both believe they hold the lock. Redlock (multi-node Redis locking): Acquire the lock on a majority of independent Redis nodes (e.g. 3 of 5) within a time budget. Considered "acquired" only if majority succeeds before the clock runs out. More resilient to a single node failing, though it has been debated (Martin Kleppmann's critique) as not being fully safe under clock drift/GC pauses — good enough for "efficiency" locks (avoid duplicate work), not for correctness-critical locks (avoid data corruption). ZooKeeper / etcd-based locks (correctness-critical case): Both are consensus-based stores (using ZAB / Raft respectively) — a write is only acknowledged once a majority of nodes agree, which is much stronger than a single Redis node's guarantee. Leader election pattern: each candidate creates an ephemeral sequential node; the candidate with the lowest sequence number is the leader. If the leader's session dies (crash, network partition), its ephemeral node disappears automatically and the next-lowest candidate becomes leader. Use this when correctness matters more than latency — e.g. only one node should ever be allowed to write to a given shard. Fencing tokens: Even with a "correct" lock, a paused process (GC pause, slow disk) can wake up after its lock has expired and still think it holds the lock, then write stale data. Fix: every time a lock is granted, issue a monotonically increasing fencing token. The resource being protected (e.g. storage service) rejects any write that comes with an older token than the last one it saw — this is the actual fix for "lock expired but process is still running" bugs, the lock alone is not sufficient. text: Caching Strategies — System Design Sources: AWS Caching Best Practices documentation, Redis documentation, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) Why cache: Database reads are slow (milliseconds). Cache reads are fast (microseconds). 80% of traffic typically reads 20% of data (Pareto principle). Cache that 20% and handle 80% of load without hitting the database. Cache Types: 1. Application Cache (in-memory, local): Stored in the application's own memory. Fastest possible. Problem: Not shared across servers. Each server has its own cache. Use for: static config, lookup tables that rarely change. 2. Distributed Cache (Redis, Memcached): Shared cache server all application servers connect to. Slightly slower than local cache but consistent across fleet. Redis supports rich data structures: strings, lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes. Use for: session data, rate limiting counters, leaderboards, pub/sub. 3. CDN Cache: Caches static assets (images, JS, CSS) at edge locations globally. Requests served from nearest edge node — dramatically lower latency. Use for: static files, video content, public API responses. Cache Invalidation Strategies (the hard problem): Write-through: Write to cache AND database simultaneously. Pro: Cache always consistent. Con: Write latency increases. Write-behind (Write-back): Write to cache first, async to database. Pro: Low write latency. Con: Data loss risk if cache crashes before DB write. Cache-aside (Lazy loading): Application checks cache first. Miss → read from DB → store in cache → return. Most common pattern. Pro: Only caches what's actually read. Con: First request after cache miss is slow (cache miss penalty). Read-through: Cache sits in front of DB. Cache handles DB reads automatically. Application only talks to cache. TTL (Time to Live): Every cached item should have an expiry time. Without TTL: stale data stays forever (cache poisoning risk). Set TTL based on how often data changes: - User session: 24 hours - Product price: 5 minutes - Static config: 1 hour Cache Eviction Policies (when cache is full): LRU (Least Recently Used): Evict item not accessed for longest time. Most common. LFU (Least Frequently Used): Evict item accessed fewest times. FIFO: Evict oldest item. Simple but often suboptimal. Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd): Problem: Popular cache key expires. 1000 requests all miss → all hit DB simultaneously → DB crashes. Solutions: 1. Mutex lock — only first request fetches from DB, others wait. 2. Background refresh — refresh cache before TTL expires. 3. Jitter — add random offset to TTL so keys don't expire simultaneously. Redis at Scale (Zepto, Swiggy use case): Redis Sentinel: High availability — automatic failover if primary fails. Redis Cluster: Horizontal scaling — data sharded across multiple Redis nodes. Read replicas: Route read-heavy workloads to replicas.

text: Consistent Hashing Sources: Karger et al., "Consistent Hashing and Random Trees" (STOC 1997); DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store" (SOSP 2007) Problem it solves: In a distributed system with N servers, naive hashing (key % N) breaks when servers are added or removed — almost all keys need remapping. Consistent hashing ensures only K/N keys are remapped when a server changes (K = total keys, N = servers). How it works: 1. Place servers on a circular ring using hash(server_id) 2. For each key: hash(key) → find the next server clockwise on the ring 3. Adding a server: only keys between new server and its predecessor move 4. Removing a server: only keys that mapped to it move to next server Virtual Nodes (vnodes): Each physical server gets multiple positions on the ring (e.g., 150 virtual nodes). Benefits: - More even load distribution - When a server fails, its load spreads across multiple servers (not just one) - Accounts for servers of different capacities (powerful server = more vnodes) Real-world usage: - Amazon DynamoDB: partitioning data across nodes - Apache Cassandra: distributing data across cluster - Discord: distributing chat messages - CDNs: routing requests to cache servers - Redis Cluster: slot assignment When to use: Use consistent hashing when you have a distributed cache or storage layer that needs to scale horizontally with minimal data movement on topology changes. Trade-offs: Pro: Minimal remapping when cluster changes Pro: Even distribution with virtual nodes Con: More complex than simple modulo hashing Con: Hot spots possible without virtual nodes

text: Bloom Filters Sources: Burton H. Bloom, "Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding with Allowable Errors" (1970), Redis documentation (Bloom Filter / probabilistic data structures) What it is: A probabilistic data structure that answers "have I possibly seen this item before?" using a fixed, tiny amount of memory — regardless of how many items have been added. Trades perfect accuracy for massive space savings. The guarantee (this is the important part): No false negatives: if the filter says "definitely not present," the item is genuinely not present. Possible false positives: if the filter says "possibly present," it might actually not be — the false positive rate is tunable (smaller filter / more items = higher false positive rate). It never says "definitely present" for something that was never added incorrectly in the wrong direction — the asymmetry only goes one way, which is what makes it usable: you only need a secondary, slower check for the "possibly present" case. How it works: A bit array of m bits, all initially 0, plus k independent hash functions. To add an item: hash it k times, set the k resulting bit positions to 1. To check an item: hash it the same k times, if ALL k bit positions are 1, report "possibly present"; if ANY bit is 0, report "definitely not present" (since adding that item would have set that bit). False positives happen because bits get shared/overwritten by other items' hashes — you can't tell whether a set bit was set by the item you're checking or by pure coincidence from other insertions. Why not just use a hash set: A hash set storing millions of actual keys uses far more memory (must store each key or at least its full hash) than a Bloom filter, which only needs a handful of bits per item regardless of key size. The trade is: a hash set has zero false positives, a Bloom filter accepts a small false-positive rate in exchange for a fraction of the memory. Cannot remove items (in the basic version): Because bits are shared across multiple items' hashes, clearing a bit to "remove" one item could break the correctness for other items that also set that bit. A Counting Bloom Filter (using small counters instead of single bits) supports removal at the cost of more memory — used when deletions are actually needed. Real-world example: A CDN or database wants to avoid an expensive disk/network lookup for keys that definitely don't exist (e.g. checking if a URL is on a known-malicious list, or if a cache key might exist before hitting disk). Check the Bloom filter first: if "definitely not present," skip the expensive lookup entirely. If "possibly present," do the real (slower, authoritative) lookup to confirm — the small false-positive rate just means occasionally doing an unnecessary real lookup, never missing an item that's actually there. This is exactly how Cassandra and HBase use Bloom filters to skip SSTable files that don't contain a given key, avoiding unnecessary disk

text: Caching Strategies — System Design Sources: AWS Caching Best Practices documentation, Redis documentation, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) Why cache: Database reads are slow (milliseconds). Cache reads are fast (microseconds). 80% of traffic typically reads 20% of data (Pareto principle). Cache that 20% and handle 80% of load without hitting the database. Cache Types: 1. Application Cache (in-memory, local): Stored in the application's own memory. Fastest possible. Problem: Not shared across servers. Each server has its own cache. Use for: static config, lookup tables that rarely change. 2. Distributed Cache (Redis, Memcached): Shared cache server all application servers connect to. Slightly slower than local cache but consistent across fleet. Redis supports rich data structures: strings, lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes. Use for: session data, rate limiting counters, leaderboards, pub/sub. 3. CDN Cache: Caches static assets (images, JS, CSS) at edge locations globally. Requests served from nearest edge node — dramatically lower latency. Use for: static files, video content, public API responses. Cache Invalidation Strategies (the hard problem): Write-through: Write to cache AND database simultaneously. Pro: Cache always consistent. Con: Write latency increases. Write-behind (Write-back): Write to cache first, async to database. Pro: Low write latency. Con: Data loss risk if cache crashes before DB write. Cache-aside (Lazy loading): Application checks cache first. Miss → read from DB → store in cache → return. Most common pattern. Pro: Only caches what's actually read. Con: First request after cache miss is slow (cache miss penalty). Read-through: Cache sits in front of DB. Cache handles DB reads automatically. Application only talks to cache. Most common. LFU (Least Frequently Used): Evict item accessed fewest times. FIFO: Evict oldest item. Simple but often suboptimal. Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd): Problem: Popular cache key expires. 1000 requests all miss → all hit DB simultaneously → DB crashes. Solutions: 1. Mutex lock — only first request fetches from DB, others wait. 2. Background refresh — refresh cache before TTL expires. 3. Jitter — add random offset to TTL so keys don't expire simultaneously. Read replicas: Route read-heavy workloads to replicas.

query: What is an inverted index and how does it work?
text: Search & Indexing (Inverted Index) Sources: Elasticsearch documentation ("Inverted index"), Apache Lucene documentation What it is: Searching billions of documents for a keyword by scanning each one would be far too slow. Search engines instead build an inverted index ahead of time — a data structure that maps each word to the list of documents containing it — so a search becomes a fast lookup instead of a full scan. Forward index vs inverted index: Forward index: document → list of words it contains (this is the natural way you'd store a document, but useless for "find all docs containing X"). Inverted index: word → list of documents containing it. Flips the mapping so a query for a term is a single lookup, not a scan of every document. Building the index: 1. Tokenization: split text into individual terms ("The quick fox" → ["the", "quick", "fox"]). 2. Normalization: lowercase, remove punctuation, stemming (running → run) so "run", "runs", "running" all match the same index entry. 3. Stop word removal (optional): common words like "the", "is" are often excluded since they match nearly everything and add little search value. 4. For each remaining term, append the document ID (and often position within the document, for phrase search) to that term's posting list. Querying: A search for "quick fox" looks up the posting list for "quick" and for "fox", then intersects them — documents in both lists contain both words. Ranking (which result appears first) typically uses TF-IDF or BM25: term frequency (how often the word appears in this doc) weighted against inverse document frequency (how rare the word is across all docs) — a rare word matching is a stronger signal than a common word matching. Distributed search (how this scales to billions of documents): The full index doesn't fit on one machine. It's split into shards, each holding a subset of documents and its own local inverted index. A query fans out to every shard in parallel, each returns its top-N matches, and a coordinating node merges and re-ranks the combined results — this is exactly how Elasticsearch/Solr scale search across a cluster. Each shard is also typically replicated for both availability and to spread read (query) load across replicas. Real-time-ish updates: New documents don't need a full index rebuild — an update is added as a small new index segment; a background merge process periodically combines small segments into larger ones for query efficiency. This is why "just indexed" documents often show up in search within seconds, not instantly, and why search indexes trade a small delay for much better write throughput. Real-world example: An e-commerce product search: catalog of 50M products is sharded across many nodes. Searching "wireless headphones" fans out to every shard, each returns its best local matches ranked by BM25, coordinator merges and returns the final top 20 — the same pattern used by product search on any major e-commerce site or by Elasticsearch-backed log search internally at a company.

text: Database Indexing & Query Optimization Sources: PostgreSQL documentation (Indexes), "Use The Index, Luke" (use-the-index-luke.com) What an index is: Without an index, finding a row matching a WHERE clause means scanning every row in the table (a "sequential scan" / "full table scan") — O(n). An index is a separate data structure that lets the database jump straight to matching rows, typically O(log n), at the cost of extra storage and slower writes (the index must be updated on every insert/update/delete too). B-Tree index (the default, general-purpose case): Balanced tree structure, keeps data sorted, supports equality (=) and range (<, >, BETWEEN) queries efficiently, and supports ORDER BY without an extra sort step if the sort matches the index order. This is what you get by default when you index a column in Postgres/MySQL. Hash index: Only supports exact-match equality lookups (=), not ranges. Faster than B-Tree for pure equality lookups in principle, but rarely used in practice because B-Tree covers equality well enough and also handles ranges — using a hash index means giving up range queries for a marginal equality speedup. Composite (multi-column) indexes and column order: An index on (user_id, created_at) can efficiently serve queries filtering on user_id alone, or user_id + created_at together — but NOT an efficient query on created_at alone, because the index is sorted by user_id first. Rule of thumb: put the column used for equality filters first, range/sort columns after — column order in a composite index is not arbitrary. Covering index: An index that includes every column a query needs (in the index itself, via an INCLUDE clause or by being a composite index) lets the database answer the query directly from the index without touching the actual table rows at all ("index-only scan") — this is the fastest possible read path. When an index is NOT used (common surprise): Applying a function to the indexed column in the WHERE clause (WHERE LOWER(email) = 'x') prevents the index from being used unless there's a matching functional index — the database can't know LOWER(email) matches the sorted order of the raw email index. Leading wildcard LIKE ('%foo') can't use a standard B-Tree index either, since the sort order doesn't help when the match could start anywhere. The cost of indexes: Every index must be updated on every write to the table — a table with 10 indexes writes is measurably slower than one with 2, because each insert touches 10 separate structures. This is why indexes aren't added blindly; each one is a real trade-off between read speed and write speed. text: Web Crawler Design Sources: S. Brin & L. Page, "The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine" (1998), standard system design interview treatment (Alex Xu, "System Design Interview") What it does: Starts from a set of seed URLs, downloads each page, extracts new links from it, and adds those links to a queue to be crawled next — recursively discovering and downloading a large portion of the web. Core components: Seed URLs: the starting set of pages to crawl. Frontier (URL queue): the set of URLs discovered but not yet fetched — this is the main piece of shared state the whole system revolves around. Fetcher: downloads the page content for a URL. Parser/Extractor: pulls new links out of the downloaded HTML, plus whatever content the crawler is actually collecting (text for a search index, prices for a shopping comparison site, etc.). Duplicate detector: avoids re-crawling and re-storing content already seen. Storage: the downloaded content and metadata. Avoiding duplicate work: Two different URLs often point to the same content (mobile vs desktop URL, tracking params, http vs https). Hash the normalized content (not just the URL) to detect "we've already stored this page" even if the URL differs. A Bloom filter is commonly used to cheaply check "have we already queued this URL" before adding it to the frontier, without needing to store every full URL in memory to check. Politeness (this is a hard requirement, not an optimization): Crawling a site too fast can look like — or actually be — a denial-of-service attack, and can get the crawler's IP banned. Rules: respect robots.txt (tells the crawler which paths it's not allowed to fetch), and rate-limit per domain (e.g. max 1 request/second to a given host), typically using a separate queue or delay per domain rather than one global rate limit. Priority / freshness: Not all pages are equal — a news homepage changes hourly, a static about-page almost never. Crawlers assign a re-crawl priority per URL based on how often it has historically changed and how important it is (e.g. via inbound link count, an early precursor to PageRank), rather than crawling everything on a fixed schedule. Scaling the frontier: A single machine's queue can't hold "every URL on the web" and a single fetcher can't download fast enough. The frontier is partitioned (e.g. by domain hash) across many worker machines, each responsible for fetching a subset of URLs — this also naturally helps enforce per-domain politeness, since all URLs for one domain land on the same worker's queue. Handling crawler traps and infinite spaces: Some sites generate infinite URLs dynamically (e.g. a calendar with a "next month" link that goes on forever). Crawlers cap max depth per site and max pages per domain to avoid getting stuck indefinitely on a single site's infinite link structure. Real-world example: Building a search engine's crawler: seed with a list of popular domains, fetcher pool downloads pages respecting robots.txt and per-domain rate limits, parser extracts text (for the search index)

text: Database Replication & Failover Sources: PostgreSQL documentation (Replication), MySQL documentation (Replication), "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) ch.5 What it is: Replication keeps copies of the same data on multiple database nodes. Goals: survive a node failure without data loss, serve more read traffic than one machine can handle, and keep data closer to users in different regions. Leader-follower (primary-replica) replication: One node (leader) accepts all writes. Writes are streamed to one or more followers, which apply them and can serve read traffic. Most common setup for relational databases (Postgres, MySQL). Synchronous vs asynchronous replication: Synchronous: leader waits for follower to confirm the write before acknowledging the client. Zero data loss on failover, but write latency includes network round-trip to the follower, and the leader stalls if the follower is slow/down. Asynchronous: leader acknowledges the client immediately, follower catches up in the background. Fast writes, but a leader crash before replication completes means recent writes are lost. Semi-synchronous: at least one follower confirms synchronously, rest are async — common middle ground (used by MySQL semi-sync replication). Replication lag: The delay between a write on the leader and it appearing on a follower. Causes "read-your-own-writes" bugs: user updates their profile, immediately reloads the page, request is routed to a lagging follower, sees stale data. Fixed by: routing a user's own reads to the leader for a short window after they write, or reading from the same replica they just wrote through. Failover: When the leader dies, a follower must be promoted to leader. Manual failover: safer, slower — human confirms the old leader is really dead before promoting, avoiding split-brain. Automatic failover: faster recovery, but risk of split-brain — if the network partition means the old leader is alive but unreachable, promoting a new leader means two leaders may accept writes simultaneously, causing conflicting data. Tools like Patroni (Postgres) or Orchestrator (MySQL) use a consensus store (etcd/ZooKeeper) to agree on the new leader safely. Multi-leader and leaderless replication: Multi-leader: multiple nodes accept writes, used across data centers — but requires conflict resolution when the same record is written in two places. Leaderless (e.g. Cassandra, DynamoDB style): client writes to several replicas directly and reads from several, using quorum (W + R > N) to guarantee it sees the latest write. No single leader means no failover pause, but consistency is weaker and requires read-repair for divergent replicas. Real-world example: A typical production Postgres setup: one primary handles all writes, two read replicas serve read-heavy endpoints (e.g. product catalog browsing). Patroni monitors primary health via etcd; if the primary fails a health check, etcd elects a new leader from the replicas and updates DNS/proxy routing automatically — this is what "high availability" means for a database in practice.

text: Web Crawler Design Sources: S. Brin & L. Page, "The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine" (1998), standard system design interview treatment (Alex Xu, "System Design Interview") What it does: Starts from a set of seed URLs, downloads each page, extracts new links from it, and adds those links to a queue to be crawled next — recursively discovering and downloading a large portion of the web. Core components: Seed URLs: the starting set of pages to crawl. Frontier (URL queue): the set of URLs discovered but not yet fetched — this is the main piece of shared state the whole system revolves around. Fetcher: downloads the page content for a URL. Parser/Extractor: pulls new links out of the downloaded HTML, plus whatever content the crawler is actually collecting (text for a search index, prices for a shopping comparison site, etc.). Duplicate detector: avoids re-crawling and re-storing content already seen. Storage: the downloaded content and metadata. Avoiding duplicate work: Two different URLs often point to the same content (mobile vs desktop URL, tracking params, http vs https). Hash the normalized content (not just the URL) to detect "we've already stored this page" even if the URL differs. A Bloom filter is commonly used to cheaply check "have we already queued this URL" before adding it to the frontier, without needing to store every full URL in memory to check. Politeness (this is a hard requirement, not an optimization): Crawling a site too fast can look like — or actually be — a denial-of-service attack, and can get the crawler's IP banned. Rules: respect robots.txt (tells the crawler which paths it's not allowed to fetch), and rate-limit per domain (e.g. max 1 request/second to a given host), typically using a separate queue or delay per domain rather than one global rate limit. Priority / freshness: Not all pages are equal — a news homepage changes hourly, a static about-page almost never. Crawlers assign a re-crawl priority per URL based on how often it has historically changed and how important it is (e.g. via inbound link count, an early precursor to PageRank), rather than crawling everything on a fixed schedule. Scaling the frontier: A single machine's queue can't hold "every URL on the web" and a single fetcher can't download fast enough. The frontier is partitioned (e.g. by domain hash) across many worker machines, each responsible for fetching a subset of URLs — this also naturally helps enforce per-domain politeness, since all URLs for one domain land on the same worker's queue. Handling crawler traps and infinite spaces: Some sites generate infinite URLs dynamically (e.g. a calendar with a "next month" link that goes on forever). Crawlers cap max depth per site and max pages per domain to avoid getting stuck indefinitely on a single site's infinite link structure. Real-world example: Building a search engine's crawler: seed with a list of popular domains, fetcher pool downloads pages respecting robots.txt and per-domain rate limits, parser extracts text (for the search index)

text: TWITTER (X) SYSTEM DESIGN Sources: Twitter/X Engineering Blog (blog.twitter.com/engineering) Overview: Twitter is a social media platform for short-form posts (tweets, 280 chars). The core challenge is the news feed — when a user with 50 million followers tweets, 50 million people should see it in their feed almost instantly. This "fanout" problem is one of the hardest in distributed systems. Scale Numbers: - 350+ million monthly active users - 500 million tweets per day (~6000 tweets/second) - 150 million daily active users - Peak: Obama election tweet — 150,000 tweets/second - Average user follows 200 accounts - 1% of users have 1M+ followers (celebrities, news accounts) Core Features to Design: 1. Post a tweet (text, images, videos) 2. Follow/unfollow users 3. Home timeline (feed of people you follow) 4. Search tweets 5. Trending topics 6. Notifications (likes, retweets, replies) The Hard Problem — Timeline/Feed Generation: Two approaches: Fan-out on Write (push) vs Fan-out on Read (pull) Fan-out on Write (Push Model): - When user A tweets, immediately copy tweet ID to every follower's feed cache - Read is fast — just fetch pre-computed feed from Redis - Problem: if A has 50M followers, writing 50M entries takes too long - Called "hot key" problem — celebrity tweets overwhelm the system Fan-out on Read (Pull Model): - When user opens app, fetch tweets from all accounts they follow - Merge and sort by timestamp - Problem: if following 1000 people, need 1000 queries → too slow Twitter's Hybrid Approach: - Regular users (< 1M followers): Fan-out on write — pre-compute their followers' feeds - Celebrities (1M+ followers): Fan-out on read — their tweets are fetched separately when feed is loaded - Feed = pre-computed feed + lazy-loaded celebrity tweets merged at read time Data Storage: Tweets: - MySQL with Vitess (MySQL clustering) for tweets table - Tweet IDs use Snowflake ID generator (timestamp + machine ID + sequence) — guarantees unique, sortable IDs - Old tweets (>7 days) moved to cold storage (Hadoop/S3) User Relationships (Follow Graph): - Separate social graph service - FlockDB (Twitter's own graph database) or Redis sorted sets - Follow relationship: user_id → set of followed_user_ids - Follower relationship: user_id → set of follower_ids - Both directions maintained for fast lookups Timeline Cache: - Redis — each user has a "home timeline" key with list of tweet IDs (not full tweets) - Stores last 800 tweet IDs per user - Full tweet data fetched from Tweet Store via tweet IDs (separate lookup) - This separation reduces memory usage significantly Media Storage: - Images/videos stored in Blob Storage (S3-equivalent) - Served through CDN globally (Fastly) - Videos transcoded to multiple resolutions on upload (FFmpeg pipeline) - Thumbnails generated asynchronously Tweet Posting Flow: 1. User posts tweet → Tweet Service validates (length, content policy) 2. Tweet stored in MySQL, gets Snowflake tweet_id 3. Media processed asynchronously (if any) 4. Fanout Service picks up via Kafka event "tweet_created" 5. Fanout Service queries Social Graph: get all followers of this user

text: Search & Indexing (Inverted Index) Sources: Elasticsearch documentation ("Inverted index"), Apache Lucene documentation What it is: Searching billions of documents for a keyword by scanning each one would be far too slow. Search engines instead build an inverted index ahead of time — a data structure that maps each word to the list of documents containing it — so a search becomes a fast lookup instead of a full scan. Forward index vs inverted index: Forward index: document → list of words it contains (this is the natural way you'd store a document, but useless for "find all docs containing X"). Inverted index: word → list of documents containing it. Flips the mapping so a query for a term is a single lookup, not a scan of every document. Building the index: 1. Tokenization: split text into individual terms ("The quick fox" → ["the", "quick", "fox"]). 2. Normalization: lowercase, remove punctuation, stemming (running → run) so "run", "runs", "running" all match the same index entry. 3. Stop word removal (optional): common words like "the", "is" are often excluded since they match nearly everything and add little search value. 4. For each remaining term, append the document ID (and often position within the document, for phrase search) to that term's posting list. Querying: A search for "quick fox" looks up the posting list for "quick" and for "fox", then intersects them — documents in both lists contain both words. Ranking (which result appears first) typically uses TF-IDF or BM25: term frequency (how often the word appears in this doc) weighted against inverse document frequency (how rare the word is across all docs) — a rare word matching is a stronger signal than a common word matching. Distributed search (how this scales to billions of documents): The full index doesn't fit on one machine. It's split into shards, each holding a subset of documents and its own local inverted index. A query fans out to every shard in parallel, each returns its top-N matches, and a coordinating node merges and re-ranks the combined results — this is exactly how Elasticsearch/Solr scale search across a cluster. Each shard is also typically replicated for both availability and to spread read (query) load across replicas. Real-time-ish updates: New documents don't need a full index rebuild — an update is added as a small new index segment; a background merge process periodically combines small segments into larger ones for query efficiency. This is why "just indexed" documents often show up in search within seconds, not instantly, and why search indexes trade a small delay for much better write throughput. Real-world example: An e-commerce product search: catalog of 50M products is sharded across many nodes. Searching "wireless headphones" fans out to every shard, each returns its best local matches ranked by BM25, coordinator merges and returns the final top 20 — the same pattern used by product search on any major e-commerce site or by Elasticsearch-backed log search internally at a company.
