text: UBER SYSTEM DESIGN Sources: Uber Engineering Blog (uber.com/blog/engineering) Overview: Uber connects riders needing a ride with nearby drivers in real-time. The core challenges are: (1) real-time geospatial matching — find the closest driver to a rider in milliseconds, (2) surge pricing — compute dynamic prices based on supply/demand in each zone, (3) trip state machine — manage the full lifecycle from request to payment. Scale Numbers: - 100+ million monthly active users - 5+ million active drivers worldwide - 25 million trips per day - Location updates from every driver every 4 seconds - Operating in 70+ countries, 10,000+ cities Core Features to Design: 1. Rider requests a trip 2. System finds nearest available driver 3. Driver accepts and navigates to rider 4. Trip tracking in real-time 5. Dynamic surge pricing 6. Payment processing after trip The Hardest Problem — Real-Time Location Matching: Naive approach: store (lat, lng) for each driver in a database, query with a radius filter. Problem: 5 million drivers sending location every 4 seconds = 1.25 million writes/second. SQL can't handle this. Uber's solution: Geohashing Geohash converts a (lat, lng) coordinate into a string like "9q8yy8yu" where similar prefixes = nearby locations. A geohash grid divides the world into cells. You can find nearby drivers by searching nearby geohash cells. Location Service: - Redis with GEOADD/GEOSEARCH commands — O(N+log(M)) for radius search - Driver location key: "drivers:{geohash_prefix}" → sorted set of driver IDs with score = timestamp - When rider requests trip: GEOSEARCH for drivers within 5km radius - Returns 10 nearest drivers sorted by distance Alternatively, Uber uses S2 Geometry (Google's library) for more accurate geospatial indexing: - S2 divides the globe into hierarchical cells at multiple precision levels - Level 12 cell ≈ 3.7km x 3.7km — good granularity for city-level matching - Search nearby cells at multiple levels to handle edge cases (rider near cell boundary) Driver Location Update Flow: 1. Driver app sends GPS update every 4 seconds 2. Location Gateway (WebSocket server) receives update 3. Publishes to Kafka topic "driver-location-updates" 4. Location Service consumes, updates Redis geospatial index 5. If driver is on an active trip: publish to "trip-location" topic for rider's app Trip Request Flow: 1. Rider taps "Request Ride" → Trip Service creates trip record (status: SEARCHING) 2. Dispatch Service queries Location Service for nearby drivers (geohash search) 3. Uber's ETA model (ML) calculates pickup time for each candidate driver 4. Dispatch Service sends trip offer to best driver (lowest ETA, highest rating) 5. Driver has 15 seconds to accept 6. If no acceptance: try next best driver 7. query: What is the pattern for distributed search using sharding and ranking?
text: Example: sharding tweets by author_id — Elon Musk's shard gets all the traffic - Solution: split hot shards further, add sub-sharding for popular entities Consistent Hashing (Solves the Resharding Problem): Problem with hash(key) % N: - If you add a shard (N+1): almost all keys need to move to a new shard - Moving data is slow and disruptive Consistent hashing: - Imagine a ring (0 to 2^32) - Both servers and keys are hashed onto this ring - Each key is assigned to the nearest server clockwise - Adding a server: only the keys between the new server and its predecessor move - Removing a server: only its keys move to the next server - On average: only K/N keys need to move (K = total keys, N = number of servers) Virtual nodes (vnodes): - Each physical server owns multiple positions on the ring (virtual nodes) - More even distribution - When a server is added/removed, impact is spread across all remaining servers - Used by: Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak Cross-Shard Queries (The Pain): Query: "find all users who signed up in January" (no shard key filter) - Must query ALL shards - Merge and sort results in application layer - Called "scatter-gather" or "fan-out query" - Expensive — avoid if possible Solution 1: Denormalize and duplicate data for query patterns Solution 2: Maintain a separate query service (Elasticsearch) for cross-shard queries Solution 3: Accept that cross-shard queries are slow, avoid them in hot paths Cross-Shard Joins: - Traditional SQL joins work within a shard - Cross-shard joins must be done in application code - Fetch data from shard A, fetch data from shard B, join in application memory - Very expensive — usually avoided by denormalization Cross-Shard Transactions: - ACID transactions across multiple shards require 2-Phase Commit (2PC) - 2PC is slow and can deadlock - Most distributed systems avoid this: - Use eventual consistency instead of strong consistency - Partition data such that transactions stay within one shard - Use saga pattern for multi-step transactions Resharding: When a shard is too large (data grown) or too hot (traffic grown): 1. Create two new shards 2. Copy half the data from old shard to each new shard 3. Redirect new writes to new shards 4. Let old shard drain (serve reads while migration happens) 5. Decommission old shard This is operationally complex — minimize resharding by: - Choosing shard count 10x what you need today (shards don't need to have equal hardware) - Planning for horizontal expansion within a shard (replication before sharding) Examples of Sharding in Real Systems: Instagram (PostgreSQL Sharding): - Shard key: user_id - Shard ID embedded in all object IDs using Postgres sequence trick - Instagram ran on sharded PostgreSQL for years — proof SQL can scale Discord (Message Sharding): - Shard key: channel_id (all messages in same channel on same Cassandra partition) - This makes "get last N messages in channel" extremely fast — single partition read Twitter (Gizzard): - Custom sharding framework

text: Slack System Design (Case Study) Sources: Slack Engineering Blog (slack.engineering) Core challenge: Real-time message delivery to potentially thousands of connected clients per workspace, while keeping full message history durable and searchable, and keeping every client's view of a channel consistent as new messages, edits, and reactions arrive. Real-time delivery via WebSockets: Each connected client holds a persistent WebSocket connection to a gateway server. When a message is sent, it's written to the durable store first, then fanned out over the open WebSocket connections of every client currently viewing that channel — the WebSocket is for live delivery to already-connected clients, not the system of record; a client reconnecting after being offline fetches missed history from the durable store via a normal API call, not by expecting to replay it from the socket. The "gateway holds connections, backend holds truth" split: Gateway/connection servers are relatively lightweight and mostly hold open sockets and route messages; the actual message data, ordering, and history lives in the backend datastore. This separation lets Slack scale the number of concurrent open connections independently from the storage/query layer — a spike in simultaneous online users stresses connection servers, not necessarily the database. Sharding by workspace/channel: Slack's engineering blog has discussed sharding message storage by team/channel, since most reads and writes for a given message are scoped to one channel — this keeps related data (a channel's message history) together on the same shard, so a typical "load channel history" query hits one shard rather than fanning out across the whole dataset. Historical MySQL scaling (Vitess): Slack has written about outgrowing a single large MySQL setup and adopting Vitess (a MySQL sharding middleware, originally built at YouTube) to shard their relational data horizontally while keeping the MySQL query interface application code already relied on — an example of solving a scaling problem by adding a sharding layer in front of an existing database technology, rather than fully rewriting onto a different database. Presence (online/offline/typing indicators): Presence state changes extremely frequently (far more often than actual messages) and is far less critical to get perfectly right — a "typing..." indicator being a second late or occasionally wrong is a minor UX blemish, not a correctness bug. This makes presence a good candidate for the most relaxed consistency and heaviest batching/throttling in the whole system, illustrating that not every real-time-feeling feature needs the same delivery guarantees as the actual message content. Real-world takeaway for interviews: "Design Slack/a chat app" questions hinge on separating three different problems that are easy to conflate: durable message storage (needs to be correct and never lost), real-time fan-out to online clients (needs to be fast, some staleness on reconnect is fine since history backfills it), and ephemeral presence state (needs to be cheap and fast, correctness is optional) — each deserves a different consistency/durability trade-off.

text: Message Queues & Pub-Sub Sources: AWS SQS Developer Guide, RabbitMQ documentation, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) ch.11 What it is: A message queue decouples producers (services that create work) from consumers (services that process it). Producer pushes a message, queue holds it, consumer pulls and processes it whenever ready. Neither side needs the other to be online at the same instant. Why use one: Smooths traffic spikes — queue absorbs a burst, consumers drain it at their own pace. Decouples services — producer doesn't care if consumer is slow, down, or scaled to zero. Enables retries — failed messages can be redelivered instead of lost. Enables async workflows — user gets a fast response, heavy work happens in background (e.g. "order placed" returns instantly, email/invoice generation happens after). Point-to-point vs Pub/Sub: Point-to-point (queue): one message, one consumer. Used for task distribution — e.g. a pool of workers pulling image-resize jobs off a queue. Pub/Sub (topic): one message, many subscribers. Used for fan-out — e.g. "order placed" event notifies inventory service, billing service, and analytics service simultaneously. Delivery guarantees: At-most-once: message may be lost, never duplicated. Fastest, least safe. At-least-once: message guaranteed delivered, but may be duplicated on retry. Most systems (SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka) default to this — consumers must be idempotent. Exactly-once: hardest to guarantee in a distributed system; usually achieved by combining at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers (dedupe by message ID), not by the queue itself. Visibility timeout / ack: Consumer pulls a message; queue hides it from other consumers for a timeout window. Consumer processes it, then explicitly acknowledges (deletes) the message. If consumer crashes before ack, message becomes visible again and another consumer picks it up — this is why consumers must be idempotent, since a message could be processed twice. Dead-letter queues (DLQ): Messages that fail processing repeatedly (e.g. 5 retries) are moved to a separate DLQ instead of blocking the main queue forever. Lets you inspect and reprocess poison messages without stalling healthy traffic. Queue vs Kafka: Traditional queues (SQS, RabbitMQ) delete a message once consumed — it's gone. Kafka is a log: messages are retained for a configured period and consumers track their own offset, so multiple consumer groups can replay the same stream independently. Use a queue for simple task distribution; use Kafka when you need replay, ordering within a partition, or multiple independent consumers of the same event stream. Real-world example: E-commerce checkout: "order placed" event published to a topic. → Inventory service subscribes, decrements stock. → Billing service subscribes, charges card. → Notification service subscribes, sends confirmation email. Each subscriber processes independently; if the email service is down, the order still completes — the message just waits in that service's queue until it recovers.

text: CAP THEOREM AND DISTRIBUTED SYSTEMS CONSISTENCY Sources: Eric Brewer, "CAP Twelve Years Later: How the 'Rules' Have Changed" (IEEE Computer, 2012); Gilbert & Lynch, "Brewer's Conjecture and the Feasibility of Consistent, Available, Partition-Tolerant Web Services" (2002) Overview: The CAP theorem states that a distributed database system can only guarantee two of three properties simultaneously: Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance. Understanding CAP is fundamental to system design — every database and architectural decision involves these trade-offs. The Three Properties: C — Consistency: Every read returns the most recent write (or an error). If you write a value on node 1 and immediately read it from node 2, you get the updated value. This is "strong consistency." Example: bank account balance — you must see the current balance, not a stale one. A — Availability: Every request receives a response (not an error), though it might not be the most recent data. The system keeps responding even if some nodes are down. Example: Netflix shows you recommendations even if their recommendation engine is partially down. P — Partition Tolerance: The system continues operating even if network messages are lost or delayed between nodes. A "partition" = network split where nodes can't communicate. In reality: you cannot opt out of P. Networks fail. Partitions happen. You MUST handle partitions. The Real Choice — CP or AP: Since P is mandatory, the real choice is: when a partition occurs, do you sacrifice C or A? CP (Consistency + Partition Tolerance): - When partition happens: refuse to answer rather than return stale data - Some requests get errors during partition - But when you respond, you're always correct - Examples: ZooKeeper, HBase, Google Spanner, MongoDB (with journaling), traditional relational databases AP (Availability + Partition Tolerance): - When partition happens: respond with possibly stale data - System always responds, never returns error - Data might be outdated temporarily - Examples: Cassandra, DynamoDB, CouchDB, DNS Neither CP nor AP fully — just P: - Technically, traditional SQL in a single datacenter: gives up P (can't run across partitions) - Rarely applicable in modern distributed systems Consistency Models (Spectrum): Strong Consistency (Linearizability): - Every read sees the most recent write - As if there's only one copy of data - Slowest — requires synchronization - Example: Google Spanner uses atomic clocks to achieve this globally Sequential Consistency: - All nodes see operations in same order, but might lag - Operations appear instantaneous but may not be truly real-time Causal Consistency: - Causally related operations are seen in order - "If you see my reply, you must have seen my original post" - Used by some distributed databases Eventual Consistency: - If no new updates, all nodes will eventually have the same value - Queries may return stale data temporarily - Highest availability, used by: DynamoDB, Cassandra, S3 - Most common choice for high-scale systems Read-Your-Own-Writes: - You always see your own updates (even if others don't yet) - Instagram: after you post a photo, you see it even

Core Concepts: Event/Message: A piece of data — "user_id: 123 placed order_id: 456 at timestamp: 1234567890" Topic: A named log of events. Like a table in a database. E.g., "order-events" topic Producer: Writes events to a topic Consumer: Reads events from a topic Broker: A Kafka server that stores events Cluster: Multiple brokers working together Partition: A topic is split into partitions for parallelism Offset: A sequential ID for each event in a partition (like array index) Consumer Group: Multiple consumers sharing the work of reading a topic Why Kafka? (vs Traditional Message Queues like RabbitMQ): Traditional queue: event consumed → deleted from queue Kafka: events retained for configurable period (default 7 days) → multiple consumers can independently read the same events This is transformative: - Add a new consumer without affecting existing ones - Replay events from past (debugging, backfilling new systems) - Decouple producers from consumers completely Kafka vs RabbitMQ: - RabbitMQ: message broker, push model, messages deleted after consumption, good for task queues - Kafka: event log, pull model, messages retained, good for event streaming and data pipelines - Choose Kafka when: multiple consumers need the same events, need event replay, high throughput - Choose RabbitMQ when: complex routing, guaranteed message ordering per consumer, task-queue pattern Architecture Deep Dive: Topics and Partitions: - Topic "order-events" might have 12 partitions - Each partition is an ordered, immutable log of events - Partitions distributed across brokers (partition 0 on broker 1, partition 1 on broker 2, etc.) - Events within a partition are strictly ordered - Events across partitions have no guaranteed order Partition Key: - Producer specifies a key per event: order.send(key="user_123", value=event) - All events with same key go to same partition - Guarantees ordering for events with same key (e.g., all events for user_123 are ordered) - Without key: round-robin across partitions Replication: - Each partition has a leader and N replicas on different brokers (N = replication factor) - Default replication factor: 3 (1 leader + 2 replicas) - All reads/writes go to leader - Replicas passively sync from leader - If leader fails, a replica is automatically elected as new leader (ZooKeeper or KRaft consensus) - Durability: Kafka can acknowledge write only after all replicas confirm receipt (acks=all) Consumer Groups: - Multiple consumers in a group share partitions - Each partition assigned to exactly one consumer in a group - text: Slack System Design (Case Study) Sources: Slack Engineering Blog (slack.engineering) Core challenge: Real-time message delivery to potentially thousands of connected clients per workspace, while keeping full message history durable and searchable, and keeping every client's view of a channel consistent as new messages, edits, and reactions arrive. Real-time delivery via WebSockets: Each connected client holds a persistent WebSocket connection to a gateway server. When a message is sent, it's written to the durable store first, then fanned out over the open WebSocket connections of every client currently viewing that channel — the WebSocket is for live delivery to already-connected clients, not the system of record; a client reconnecting after being offline fetches missed history from the durable store via a normal API call, not by expecting to replay it from the socket. The "gateway holds connections, backend holds truth" split: Gateway/connection servers are relatively lightweight and mostly hold open sockets and route messages; the actual message data, ordering, and history lives in the backend datastore. This separation lets Slack scale the number of concurrent open connections independently from the storage/query layer — a spike in simultaneous online users stresses connection servers, not necessarily the database. Sharding by workspace/channel: Slack's engineering blog has discussed sharding message storage by team/channel, since most reads and writes for a given message are scoped to one channel — this keeps related data (a channel's message history) together on the same shard, so a typical "load channel history" query hits one shard rather than fanning out across the whole dataset. Historical MySQL scaling (Vitess): Slack has written about outgrowing a single large MySQL setup and adopting Vitess (a MySQL sharding middleware, originally built at YouTube) to shard their relational data horizontally while keeping the MySQL query interface application code already relied on — an example of solving a scaling problem by adding a sharding layer in front of an existing database technology, rather than fully rewriting onto a different database. Presence (online/offline/typing indicators): Presence state changes extremely frequently (far more often than actual messages) and is far less critical to get perfectly right — a "typing..." indicator being a second late or occasionally wrong is a minor UX blemish, not a correctness bug. This makes presence a good candidate for the most relaxed consistency and heaviest batching/throttling in the whole system, illustrating that not every real-time-feeling feature needs the same delivery guarantees as the actual message content. Real-world takeaway for interviews: "Design Slack/a chat app" questions hinge on separating three different problems that are easy to conflate: durable message storage (needs to be correct and never lost), real-time fan-out to online clients (needs to be fast, some staleness on reconnect is fine since history backfills it), and ephemeral presence state (needs to be cheap and fast, correctness is optional) — each deserves a different consistency/durability trade-off.

query: What are the main differences between SQL and NoSQL databases?
text: SQL VS NOSQL — WHEN TO USE WHICH Sources: MongoDB documentation, PostgreSQL documentation, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) ch.2-3 Overview: One of the most common system design interview questions is "what database would you use?" There's no universal answer — the right choice depends on your data model, access patterns, consistency requirements, and scale. Understanding the trade-offs is more important than memorizing which is "better." SQL (Relational Databases): Examples: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, Oracle Core Characteristics: - Data organized in tables with fixed schemas (columns defined upfront) - ACID transactions: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability - SQL query language — powerful, joins, aggregations, subqueries - Strong consistency — reads always reflect latest writes - Relations between tables via foreign keys - Vertical scaling primarily (add more CPU/RAM to one server) When to use SQL: - Complex relationships between entities (users → orders → products → inventory) - Need ACID transactions (banking, e-commerce, healthcare) - Data structure is well-defined and unlikely to change frequently - Need complex queries with joins and aggregations - Team knows SQL well (most developers do) - Compliance requirements (many regulations require ACID) NoSQL (Non-Relational Databases): Four types: Document, Key-Value, Column-Family, Graph 1. Document Stores (MongoDB, CouchDB, Firestore): - Data stored as JSON/BSON documents - Flexible schema: different documents can have different fields - Good for: product catalogs, user profiles, content management - Example: MongoDB stores restaurant menus — each restaurant has different menu structure - Query: rich queries on nested fields, but no joins across collections 2. Key-Value Stores (Redis, DynamoDB, Memcached): - Simplest NoSQL: key → value - Extremely fast (O(1) lookup) - Good for: caching, session storage, rate limiting, leaderboards (Redis sorted sets) - Limited query capability — only lookup by key (or key prefix) - Redis extra: supports list, set, hash, sorted set, stream data structures 3. Wide-Column / Column-Family (Cassandra, HBase, DynamoDB): - Rows with flexible columns, organized by partition key - Data spread across nodes by partition key — horizontally scalable - Good for: time-series data, IoT data, message history, activity logs - Cassandra strengths: write-heavy workloads, no single point of failure - Query: must specify partition key; range queries on sort key; no arbitrary queries 4. Graph Databases (Neo4j, Amazon Neptune, JanusGraph): - Data stored as nodes and edges (relationships) - Optimized for traversing relationships - Good for: social networks (friends-of-friends), recommendation engines, fraud detection - Query: Cypher (Neo4j), Gremlin — traverse graph relationships - Overkill for simple use cases; excellent for complex relationship queries Comparison Table: Property | SQL (PostgreSQL) | Document (MongoDB) | Wide-Column (Cassandra) | Key-Value (Redis) Schema | Fixed | Flexible | Flexible columns | None (any value) Transactions | Full ACID | Multi-doc ACID | Lightweight batch only | Basic (MULTI/EXEC) Query Language | SQL (very powerful) | MQL (moderate) | CQL (limited) | Commands only Horizontal Scale | Hard (sharding) | Built-in sharding | Native (ring) | Cluster mode Consistency | Strong | Tunable | Tunable (eventual) | Strong (single) / Eventual (cluster) Best for

There's no universal answer — the right choice depends on your data model, access patterns, consistency requirements, and scale. Understanding the trade-offs is more important than memorizing which is "better." SQL (Relational Databases): Examples: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, Oracle Core Characteristics: - Data organized in tables with fixed schemas (columns defined upfront) - ACID transactions: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability - SQL query language — powerful, joins, aggregations, subqueries - Strong consistency — reads always reflect latest writes - Relations between tables via foreign keys - Vertical scaling primarily (add more CPU/RAM to one server) When to use SQL: - Complex relationships between entities (users → orders → products → inventory) - Need ACID transactions (banking, e-commerce, healthcare) - Data structure is well-defined and unlikely to change frequently - Need complex queries with joins and aggregations - Team knows SQL well (most developers do) - Compliance requirements (many regulations require ACID) NoSQL (Non-Relational Databases): Four types: Document, Key-Value, Column-Family, Graph 1. Document Stores (MongoDB, CouchDB, Firestore): - Data stored as JSON/BSON documents - Flexible schema: different documents can have different fields - Good for: product catalogs, user profiles, content management - Example: MongoDB stores restaurant menus — each restaurant has different menu structure - Query: rich queries on nested fields, but no joins across collections 2. Key-Value Stores (Redis, DynamoDB, Memcached): - Simplest NoSQL: key → value - Extremely fast (O(1) lookup) - Good for: caching, session storage, rate limiting, leaderboards (Redis sorted sets) - Limited query capability — only lookup by key (or key prefix) - Redis extra: supports list, set, hash, sorted set, stream data structures 3. Wide-Column / Column-Family (Cassandra, HBase, DynamoDB): - Rows with flexible columns, organized by partition key - Data spread across nodes by partition key — horizontally scalable - Good for: time-series data, IoT data, message history, activity logs - Cassandra strengths: write-heavy workloads, no single point of failure - Query: must specify partition key; range queries on sort key; no arbitrary queries 4. Graph Databases (Neo4j, Amazon Neptune, JanusGraph): - Data stored as nodes and edges (relationships) - Optimized for traversing relationships - Good for: social networks (friends-of-friends), recommendation engines, fraud detection - Query: Cypher (Neo4j), Gremlin — traverse graph relationships - Overkill for simple use cases; excellent for complex relationship queries Comparison Table: Property | SQL (PostgreSQL) | Document (MongoDB) | Wide-Column (Cassandra) | Key-Value (Redis) Schema | Fixed | Flexible | Flexible columns | None (any value) Transactions | Full ACID | Multi-doc ACID | Lightweight batch only | Basic (MULTI/EXEC) Query Language | SQL (very powerful) | MQL (moderate) | CQL (limited) | Commands only Horizontal Scale | Hard (sharding) | Built-in sharding | Native (ring) | Cluster mode Consistency | Strong | Tunable | Tunable (eventual) | Strong (single) / Eventual (cluster) Best for

text: Consistent Hashing Sources: Karger et al., "Consistent Hashing and Random Trees" (STOC 1997); DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store" (SOSP 2007) Problem it solves: In a distributed system with N servers, naive hashing (key % N) breaks when servers are added or removed — almost all keys need remapping. Consistent hashing ensures only K/N keys are remapped when a server changes (K = total keys, N = servers). How it works: 1. Place servers on a circular ring using hash(server_id) 2. For each key: hash(key) → find the next server clockwise on the ring 3. Adding a server: only keys between new server and its predecessor move 4. Removing a server: only keys that mapped to it move to next server Virtual Nodes (vnodes): Each physical server gets multiple positions on the ring (e.g., 150 virtual nodes). Benefits: - More even load distribution - When a server fails, its load spreads across multiple servers (not just one) - Accounts for servers of different capacities (powerful server = more vnodes) Real-world usage: - Amazon DynamoDB: partitioning data across nodes - Apache Cassandra: distributing data across cluster - Discord: distributing chat messages - CDNs: routing requests to cache servers - Redis Cluster: slot assignment When to use: Use consistent hashing when you have a distributed cache or storage layer that needs to scale horizontally with minimal data movement on topology changes. Trade-offs: Pro: Minimal remapping when cluster changes Pro: Even distribution with virtual nodes Con: More complex than simple modulo hashing Con: Hot spots possible without virtual nodes

This is called sharding (horizontal partitioning). Understanding sharding is critical for system design interviews — almost every large-scale system uses it. Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling: - Vertical (scale up): add more CPU/RAM/disk to existing server. Simple but has limits. - Horizontal (scale out): add more servers. Complex but theoretically unlimited scale. - Sharding is horizontal scaling for databases. Types of Partitioning: 1. Horizontal Partitioning (Sharding): - Split rows across multiple tables/servers - Different rows in different places - Example: users 1-1M on server 1, users 1M-2M on server 2 - Most common type when people say "sharding" 2. Vertical Partitioning: - Split columns across multiple tables/servers - User profile (name, email) on one server, user media (photos, videos) on another - Good for separating hot (frequently accessed) from cold data Sharding Strategies: 1. Range-Based Sharding: - Partition by value range: users A-M on shard 1, N-Z on shard 2 - Or by ID range: IDs 0-1M on shard 1, 1M-2M on shard 2 - Pros: simple to implement, range queries easy - Cons: uneven distribution (many users start with common letters), hot shards 2. Hash-Based Sharding: - shard_id = hash(shard_key) % num_shards - Example: user_id=123 → hash(123) % 4 → shard 2 - Pros: even distribution, simple routing - Cons: range queries hard, adding/removing shards requires resharding 3. Directory-Based Sharding: - Lookup table: shard_key → shard_id - Example: user_id=123 → shard_id=3 (looked up from directory) - Pros: flexible, can move data between shards easily - Cons: lookup table is a bottleneck/single point of failure 4. text: Example: sharding tweets by author_id — Elon Musk's shard gets all the traffic - Solution: split hot shards further, add sub-sharding for popular entities Consistent Hashing (Solves the Resharding Problem): Problem with hash(key) % N: - If you add a shard (N+1): almost all keys need to move to a new shard - Moving data is slow and disruptive Consistent hashing: - Imagine a ring (0 to 2^32) - Both servers and keys are hashed onto this ring - Each key is assigned to the nearest server clockwise - Adding a server: only the keys between the new server and its predecessor move - Removing a server: only its keys move to the next server - On average: only K/N keys need to move (K = total keys, N = number of servers) Virtual nodes (vnodes): - Each physical server owns multiple positions on the ring (virtual nodes) - More even distribution - When a server is added/removed, impact is spread across all remaining servers - Used by: Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak Cross-Shard Queries (The Pain): Query: "find all users who signed up in January" (no shard key filter) - Must query ALL shards - Merge and sort results in application layer - Called "scatter-gather" or "fan-out query" - Expensive — avoid if possible Solution 1: Denormalize and duplicate data for query patterns Solution 2: Maintain a separate query service (Elasticsearch) for cross-shard queries Solution 3: Accept that cross-shard queries are slow, avoid them in hot paths Cross-Shard Joins: - Traditional SQL joins work within a shard - Cross-shard joins must be done in application code - Fetch data from shard A, fetch data from shard B, join in application memory - Very expensive — usually avoided by denormalization Cross-Shard Transactions: - ACID transactions across multiple shards require 2-Phase Commit (2PC) - 2PC is slow and can deadlock - Most distributed systems avoid this: - Use eventual consistency instead of strong consistency - Partition data such that transactions stay within one shard - Use saga pattern for multi-step transactions Resharding: When a shard is too large (data grown) or too hot (traffic grown): 1. Create two new shards 2. Copy half the data from old shard to each new shard 3. Redirect new writes to new shards 4. Let old shard drain (serve reads while migration happens) 5. Decommission old shard This is operationally complex — minimize resharding by: - Choosing shard count 10x what you need today (shards don't need to have equal hardware) - Planning for horizontal expansion within a shard (replication before sharding) Examples of Sharding in Real Systems: Instagram (PostgreSQL Sharding): - Shard key: user_id - Shard ID embedded in all object IDs using Postgres sequence trick - Instagram ran on sharded PostgreSQL for years — proof SQL can scale Discord (Message Sharding): - Shard key: channel_id (all messages in same channel on same Cassandra partition) - This makes "get last N messages in channel" extremely fast — single partition read Twitter (Gizzard): - Custom sharding framework

Metadata (block list with hashes) stored separately from block content Example: Edit 100 lines in a 500MB file - Only the 4MB block containing those lines has a different hash - Upload: 4MB instead of 500MB - 99% bandwidth saving Deduplication: - If block with hash "abc123" already exists in cloud, don't upload it - Many files have common blocks (PDF headers, common library files) - Content-addressed storage: block stored by its hash, not by name - This also means if two users upload the same file, it's only stored once Architecture Overview: Client (Desktop app): - Monitors local file system for changes (OS file watchers: inotify on Linux, FSEvents on Mac, ReadDirectoryChangesW on Windows) - Maintains local SQLite database of: file metadata, block hashes, sync status - On change: compute changed blocks, upload to Block Storage, update Metadata Server Components: 1. query: When should Redis or Elasticsearch be added to a database architecture?
text: Caching Strategies — System Design Sources: AWS Caching Best Practices documentation, Redis documentation, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) Why cache: Database reads are slow (milliseconds). Cache reads are fast (microseconds). 80% of traffic typically reads 20% of data (Pareto principle). Cache that 20% and handle 80% of load without hitting the database. Cache Types: 1. Application Cache (in-memory, local): Stored in the application's own memory. Fastest possible. Problem: Not shared across servers. Each server has its own cache. Use for: static config, lookup tables that rarely change. 2. Distributed Cache (Redis, Memcached): Shared cache server all application servers connect to. Slightly slower than local cache but consistent across fleet. Redis supports rich data structures: strings, lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes. Use for: session data, rate limiting counters, leaderboards, pub/sub. 3. CDN Cache: Caches static assets (images, JS, CSS) at edge locations globally. Requests served from nearest edge node — dramatically lower latency. Use for: static files, video content, public API responses. Cache Invalidation Strategies (the hard problem): Write-through: Write to cache AND database simultaneously. Pro: Cache always consistent. Con: Write latency increases. Write-behind (Write-back): Write to cache first, async to database. Pro: Low write latency. Con: Data loss risk if cache crashes before DB write. Cache-aside (Lazy loading): Application checks cache first. Miss → read from DB → store in cache → return. Most common pattern. Pro: Only caches what's actually read. Con: First request after cache miss is slow (cache miss penalty). Read-through: Cache sits in front of DB. Cache handles DB reads automatically. Application only talks to cache. TTL (Time to Live): Every cached item should have an expiry time. Without TTL: stale data stays forever (cache poisoning risk). Set TTL based on how often data changes: - User session: 24 hours - Product price: 5 minutes - Static config: 1 hour Cache Eviction Policies (when cache is full): LRU (Least Recently Used): Evict item not accessed for longest time. Most common. LFU (Least Frequently Used): Evict item accessed fewest times. FIFO: Evict oldest item. Simple but often suboptimal. Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd): Problem: Popular cache key expires. 1000 requests all miss → all hit DB simultaneously → DB crashes. Solutions: 1. Mutex lock — only first request fetches from DB, others wait. 2. Background refresh — refresh cache before TTL expires. 3. Jitter — add random offset to TTL so keys don't expire simultaneously. Redis at Scale (Zepto, Swiggy use case): Redis Sentinel: High availability — automatic failover if primary fails. Redis Cluster: Horizontal scaling — data sharded across multiple Redis nodes. Read replicas: Route read-heavy workloads to replicas.

text: UBER SYSTEM DESIGN Sources: Uber Engineering Blog (uber.com/blog/engineering) Overview: Uber connects riders needing a ride with nearby drivers in real-time. The core challenges are: (1) real-time geospatial matching — find the closest driver to a rider in milliseconds, (2) surge pricing — compute dynamic prices based on supply/demand in each zone, (3) trip state machine — manage the full lifecycle from request to payment. Scale Numbers: - 100+ million monthly active users - 5+ million active drivers worldwide - 25 million trips per day - Location updates from every driver every 4 seconds - Operating in 70+ countries, 10,000+ cities Core Features to Design: 1. Rider requests a trip 2. System finds nearest available driver 3. Driver accepts and navigates to rider 4. Trip tracking in real-time 5. Dynamic surge pricing 6. Payment processing after trip The Hardest Problem — Real-Time Location Matching: Naive approach: store (lat, lng) for each driver in a database, query with a radius filter. text: API Gateway Sources: AWS API Gateway Developer Guide, Kong Gateway documentation What it is: A single entry point that sits in front of a collection of backend services (especially in a microservices architecture) and routes each incoming request to the right service. Clients talk to one gateway instead of knowing about every individual service's address. What it handles (so individual services don't have to): Routing: maps a path/method to the right backend service (/users → user-service, /orders → order-service). Authentication: validates JWT/API keys once at the edge, so downstream services trust the gateway instead of each re-implementing auth. Rate limiting: throttles per-client request rate before it ever reaches backend services, protecting them from being overwhelmed. Request/response transformation: e.g. converting a legacy SOAP backend response to JSON for modern clients, without changing the backend. Aggregation: combining calls to multiple services into a single client-facing response (sometimes called the "backend for frontend" pattern) — a mobile app screen might need data from 3 services, gateway can fan out and merge. Observability: single place to log, trace, and monitor all API traffic instead of instrumenting every service separately. TLS termination: gateway handles HTTPS, internal traffic between gateway and services can be plain HTTP within a trusted network. Gateway vs Load Balancer: A load balancer (L4/L7) distributes traffic across replicas of the *same* service based on IP/path. An API gateway routes across *different* services and adds application-level concerns (auth, rate limiting, transformation) on top — they're often used together: gateway routes to a service name, load balancer distributes across that service's replicas. Failure mode to watch for: Single point of failure — if the gateway goes down, every service behind it is unreachable even if they're all healthy. Mitigated by running multiple gateway instances behind their own load balancer, and keeping the gateway itself stateless so any instance can handle any request. Backend for Frontend (BFF) pattern: Instead of one generic gateway for all clients, run a dedicated gateway per client type (mobile-BFF, web-BFF) — each shaped to that client's specific data needs, avoiding a single gateway trying to please every consumer with one generic contract. Real-world example: A ride-sharing app's mobile client hits a single gateway endpoint. Gateway validates the JWT, then calls trip-service, pricing-service, and driver-location-service in parallel, merges their responses into one JSON payload the app expects — the mobile client never needs to know these are three separate backend services, or that pricing-service might be redeployed independently tomorrow.

Scale Numbers: - 350+ million monthly active users - 500 million tweets per day (~6000 tweets/second) - 150 million daily active users - Peak: Obama election tweet — 150,000 tweets/second - Average user follows 200 accounts - 1% of users have 1M+ followers (celebrities, news accounts) Core Features to Design: 1. Notifications (likes, retweets, replies) The Hard Problem — Timeline/Feed Generation: Two approaches: Fan-out on Write (push) vs Fan-out on Read (pull) Fan-out on Write (Push Model): - When user A tweets, immediately copy tweet ID to every follower's feed cache - Read is fast — just fetch pre-computed feed from Redis - Problem: if A has 50M followers, writing 50M entries takes too long - Called "hot key" problem — celebrity tweets overwhelm the system Fan-out on Read (Pull Model): - When user opens app, fetch tweets from all accounts they follow - Merge and sort by timestamp - Problem: if following 1000 people, need 1000 queries → too slow Twitter's Hybrid Approach: - Regular users (< 1M followers): Fan-out on write — pre-compute their followers' feeds - Celebrities (1M+ followers): Fan-out on read — their tweets are fetched separately when feed is loaded - Feed = pre-computed feed + lazy-loaded celebrity tweets merged at read time Data Storage: Tweets: - MySQL with Vitess (MySQL clustering) for tweets table - Tweet IDs use Snowflake ID generator (timestamp + machine ID + sequence) — guarantees unique, sortable IDs - Old tweets (>7 days) moved to cold storage (Hadoop/S3) User Relationships (Follow Graph): - Separate social graph service - FlockDB (Twitter's own graph database) or Redis sorted sets - Follow relationship: user_id → set of followed_user_ids - Follower relationship: user_id → set of follower_ids - Both directions maintained for fast lookups Timeline Cache: - Redis — each user has a "home timeline" key with list of tweet IDs (not full tweets) - Stores last 800 tweet IDs per user - Full tweet data fetched from Tweet Store via tweet IDs (separate lookup) - This separation reduces memory usage significantly Media Storage: - Images/videos stored in Blob Storage (S3-equivalent) - Served through CDN globally (Fastly) - Videos transcoded to multiple resolutions on upload (FFmpeg pipeline) - Thumbnails generated asynchronously Tweet Posting Flow: 1. text: Pinterest System Design (Case Study) Sources: Pinterest Engineering Blog (medium.com/pinterest-engineering) Core challenge: Pinterest's home feed and search need to serve a highly visual, read-heavy product (billions of "pins," each with images) with personalized ranking, at a read:write ratio that's extremely skewed toward reads — most users browse far more pins than they create. Sharded MySQL as the source of truth: Pinterest's engineering blog has documented using sharded MySQL for core data (pins, boards, users) — sharding by a key like user_id so a given user's data mostly lives on one shard, keeping most queries scoped to a single shard rather than fanning out across all of them. This is a common pattern for reaching MySQL-scale-and-beyond throughput without abandoning a relational model the team already knows well. The feed fan-out problem: When a user follows thousands of boards/users, generating their home feed by querying all of those sources at read time (fan-out on read) is expensive per-request. Alternatively, pre-computing each follower's feed at write time (fan-out on write, i.e. when a pin is created, push it into every follower's precomputed feed) is fast to read but expensive for users with huge numbers of followers (a "celebrity" pinner writing once means fanning out to millions of followers' feeds). Pinterest (like Twitter, Instagram) uses a hybrid: fan-out on write for most users, with a separate fan-out on read path merged in at request time for accounts with very large follower counts — avoiding the write amplification blowup for the small number of accounts where fan-out on write would be disproportionately expensive. Image storage and serving: Billions of images at multiple resolutions (thumbnail, feed-size, full-size) are stored in blob storage and served through a CDN — the application database stores only metadata and a reference/URL to the image, never the image bytes themselves, keeping the relational database small and fast while a purpose-built object store and CDN handle the actual (much larger) binary content and its geographic distribution to users. Personalized ranking: Unlike a purely chronological feed, Pinterest's home feed is ranked by a recommendation model considering a user's past engagement — this ranking step is a separate service/pipeline from the raw "fetch candidate pins" step, following the general large-scale feed pattern of candidate generation (get a broad pool of possibly-relevant pins cheaply) followed by ranking (score and reorder a smaller candidate set more expensively) — doing expensive ML ranking over the entire pin corpus per request would not be feasible, so cheap retrieval narrows the set before expensive ranking runs on it. text: Facebook TAO & Memcache at Scale (Case Study) Sources: Bronson et al., "TAO: Facebook's Distributed Data Store for the Social Graph" (USENIX ATC 2013), Nishtala et al., "Scaling Memcache at Facebook" (NSDI 2013) The problem: Facebook's social graph (users, friendships, likes, comments — modeled as nodes and edges) is read far more often than it's written, at massive scale, and the underlying data lived in sharded MySQL. Serving graph reads directly from MySQL at that read volume was not feasible — the read/write ratio was extremely skewed toward reads. Scaling Memcache at Facebook (the caching layer): Facebook ran one of the largest memcached deployments in the world — trillions of items across many clusters. Key lessons from that paper: Look-aside cache pattern: application code checks memcache first, on a miss reads from MySQL and populates the cache — memcache itself has no knowledge of the database, it's purely a fast key-value layer in front of it. Thundering herd / cache stampede problem: if a popular key expires, many requests can miss simultaneously and all hit the database at once for the same key. Mitigated with a "lease" mechanism — only one request is allowed to go fetch from the database and repopulate the cache; other concurrent requests for the same key wait briefly rather than all hitting the DB. Invalidation across regions: when data changes, the region owning the write broadcasts invalidations to caches in other regions — because Facebook serves from multiple geographic regions, simply relying on TTL expiry alone would leave far-flung caches stale for too long. TAO (the graph-aware layer built on top of that caching experience): Rather than have every service reimplement "cache the graph efficiently," Facebook built TAO as a dedicated read-through cache purpose-built for the social graph's actual access patterns — objects (nodes: a post, a user) and associations (edges: "likes," "friends") — instead of a generic key-value cache that every team had to hand-tune for graph queries. Read-heavy optimization: TAO explicitly favors availability and low latency for reads over strict consistency — a "like" count might be very briefly stale across regions, an acceptable trade for the massive read volume TAO serves. Write-through with async replication: writes go to the region's master database, and are asynchronously replicated to other regions' caches — again prioritizing not blocking the write path on cross-region consistency. The general lesson (useful beyond Facebook specifically): Both papers describe the same underlying pattern: a very read-heavy workload at extreme scale is served by pushing reads into a cache layer tuned for the specific access pattern (generic key-value for Memcache, graph-specific for TAO), while accepting eventual/relaxed consistency as a deliberate trade-off for availability and latency — and building explicit mechanisms (leases, cross-region invalidation) to control exactly how stale the cache is allowed to get, rather than leaving it unbounded.

text: Search & Indexing (Inverted Index) Sources: Elasticsearch documentation ("Inverted index"), Apache Lucene documentation What it is: Searching billions of documents for a keyword by scanning each one would be far too slow. Search engines instead build an inverted index ahead of time — a data structure that maps each word to the list of documents containing it — so a search becomes a fast lookup instead of a full scan. Forward index vs inverted index: Forward index: document → list of words it contains (this is the natural way you'd store a document, but useless for "find all docs containing X"). Inverted index: word → list of documents containing it. Flips the mapping so a query for a term is a single lookup, not a scan of every document. Building the index: 1. Tokenization: split text into individual terms ("The quick fox" → ["the", "quick", "fox"]). 2. Normalization: lowercase, remove punctuation, stemming (running → run) so "run", "runs", "running" all match the same index entry. 3. Stop word removal (optional): common words like "the", "is" are often excluded since they match nearly everything and add little search value. 4. For each remaining term, append the document ID (and often position within the document, for phrase search) to that term's posting list. Querying: A search for "quick fox" looks up the posting list for "quick" and for "fox", then intersects them — documents in both lists contain both words. Ranking (which result appears first) typically uses TF-IDF or BM25: term frequency (how often the word appears in this doc) weighted against inverse document frequency (how rare the word is across all docs) — a rare word matching is a stronger signal than a common word matching. Distributed search (how this scales to billions of documents): The full index doesn't fit on one machine. It's split into shards, each holding a subset of documents and its own local inverted index. A query fans out to every shard in parallel, each returns its top-N matches, and a coordinating node merges and re-ranks the combined results — this is exactly how Elasticsearch/Solr scale search across a cluster. Each shard is also typically replicated for both availability and to spread read (query) load across replicas. Real-time-ish updates: New documents don't need a full index rebuild — an update is added as a small new index segment; a background merge process periodically combines small segments into larger ones for query efficiency. This is why "just indexed" documents often show up in search within seconds, not instantly, and why search indexes trade a small delay for much better write throughput. Real-world example: An e-commerce product search: catalog of 50M products is sharded across many nodes. Searching "wireless headphones" fans out to every shard, each returns its best local matches ranked by BM25, coordinator merges and returns the final top 20 — the same pattern used by product search on any major e-commerce site or by Elasticsearch-backed log search internally at a company.

text: Pinterest System Design (Case Study) Sources: Pinterest Engineering Blog (medium.com/pinterest-engineering) Core challenge: Pinterest's home feed and search need to serve a highly visual, read-heavy product (billions of "pins," each with images) with personalized ranking, at a read:write ratio that's extremely skewed toward reads — most users browse far more pins than they create. Sharded MySQL as the source of truth: Pinterest's engineering blog has documented using sharded MySQL for core data (pins, boards, users) — sharding by a key like user_id so a given user's data mostly lives on one shard, keeping most queries scoped to a single shard rather than fanning out across all of them. This is a common pattern for reaching MySQL-scale-and-beyond throughput without abandoning a relational model the team already knows well. The feed fan-out problem: When a user follows thousands of boards/users, generating their home feed by querying all of those sources at read time (fan-out on read) is expensive per-request. Alternatively, pre-computing each follower's feed at write time (fan-out on write, i.e. when a pin is created, push it into every follower's precomputed feed) is fast to read but expensive for users with huge numbers of followers (a "celebrity" pinner writing once means fanning out to millions of followers' feeds). Pinterest (like Twitter, Instagram) uses a hybrid: fan-out on write for most users, with a separate fan-out on read path merged in at request time for accounts with very large follower counts — avoiding the write amplification blowup for the small number of accounts where fan-out on write would be disproportionately expensive. Image storage and serving: Billions of images at multiple resolutions (thumbnail, feed-size, full-size) are stored in blob storage and served through a CDN — the application database stores only metadata and a reference/URL to the image, never the image bytes themselves, keeping the relational database small and fast while a purpose-built object store and CDN handle the actual (much larger) binary content and its geographic distribution to users. Personalized ranking: Unlike a purely chronological feed, Pinterest's home feed is ranked by a recommendation model considering a user's past engagement — this ranking step is a separate service/pipeline from the raw "fetch candidate pins" step, following the general large-scale feed pattern of candidate generation (get a broad pool of possibly-relevant pins cheaply) followed by ranking (score and reorder a smaller candidate set more expensively) — doing expensive ML ranking over the entire pin corpus per request would not be feasible, so cheap retrieval narrows the set before expensive ranking runs on it. Real-world takeaway for interviews: "Design Pinterest/Instagram feed" questions center on the fan-out on write vs read trade-off (and the hybrid approach for high-follower accounts), plus the candidate-generation-then-ranking split for personalization — both are reusable patterns that show up across most large-scale social feed system designs, not Pinterest-specific tricks.

text: Facebook TAO & Memcache at Scale (Case Study) Sources: Bronson et al., "TAO: Facebook's Distributed Data Store for the Social Graph" (USENIX ATC 2013), Nishtala et al., "Scaling Memcache at Facebook" (NSDI 2013) The problem: Facebook's social graph (users, friendships, likes, comments — modeled as nodes and edges) is read far more often than it's written, at massive scale, and the underlying data lived in sharded MySQL. Serving graph reads directly from MySQL at that read volume was not feasible — the read/write ratio was extremely skewed toward reads. Scaling Memcache at Facebook (the caching layer): Facebook ran one of the largest memcached deployments in the world — trillions of items across many clusters. Key lessons from that paper: Look-aside cache pattern: application code checks memcache first, on a miss reads from MySQL and populates the cache — memcache itself has no knowledge of the database, it's purely a fast key-value layer in front of it. Thundering herd / cache stampede problem: if a popular key expires, many requests can miss simultaneously and all hit the database at once for the same key. Mitigated with a "lease" mechanism — only one request is allowed to go fetch from the database and repopulate the cache; other concurrent requests for the same key wait briefly rather than all hitting the DB. Invalidation across regions: when data changes, the region owning the write broadcasts invalidations to caches in other regions — because Facebook serves from multiple geographic regions, simply relying on TTL expiry alone would leave far-flung caches stale for too long. TAO (the graph-aware layer built on top of that caching experience): Rather than have every service reimplement "cache the graph efficiently," Facebook built TAO as a dedicated read-through cache purpose-built for the social graph's actual access patterns — objects (nodes: a post, a user) and associations (edges: "likes," "friends") — instead of a generic key-value cache that every team had to hand-tune for graph queries. Read-heavy optimization: TAO explicitly favors availability and low latency for reads over strict consistency — a "like" count might be very briefly stale across regions, an acceptable trade for the massive read volume TAO serves. Write-through with async replication: writes go to the region's master database, and are asynchronously replicated to other regions' caches — again prioritizing not blocking the write path on cross-region consistency. The general lesson (useful beyond Facebook specifically): Both papers describe the same underlying pattern: a very read-heavy workload at extreme scale is served by pushing reads into a cache layer tuned for the specific access pattern (generic key-value for Memcache, graph-specific for TAO), while accepting eventual/relaxed consistency as a deliberate trade-off for availability and latency — and building explicit mechanisms (leases, cross-region invalidation) to control exactly how stale the cache is allowed to get, rather than leaving it unbounded.

text: Web Crawler Design Sources: S. Brin & L. Page, "The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine" (1998), standard system design interview treatment (Alex Xu, "System Design Interview") What it does: Starts from a set of seed URLs, downloads each page, extracts new links from it, and adds those links to a queue to be crawled next — recursively discovering and downloading a large portion of the web. Core components: Seed URLs: the starting set of pages to crawl. Frontier (URL queue): the set of URLs discovered but not yet fetched — this is the main piece of shared state the whole system revolves around. Fetcher: downloads the page content for a URL. Parser/Extractor: pulls new links out of the downloaded HTML, plus whatever content the crawler is actually collecting (text for a search index, prices for a shopping comparison site, etc.). Duplicate detector: avoids re-crawling and re-storing content already seen. Storage: the downloaded content and metadata. Avoiding duplicate work: Two different URLs often point to the same content (mobile vs desktop URL, tracking params, http vs https). Hash the normalized content (not just the URL) to detect "we've already stored this page" even if the URL differs. A Bloom filter is commonly used to cheaply check "have we already queued this URL" before adding it to the frontier, without needing to store every full URL in memory to check. Politeness (this is a hard requirement, not an optimization): Crawling a site too fast can look like — or actually be — a denial-of-service attack, and can get the crawler's IP banned. Rules: respect robots.txt (tells the crawler which paths it's not allowed to fetch), and rate-limit per domain (e.g. max 1 request/second to a given host), typically using a separate queue or delay per domain rather than one global rate limit. Priority / freshness: Not all pages are equal — a news homepage changes hourly, a static about-page almost never. Crawlers assign a re-crawl priority per URL based on how often it has historically changed and how important it is (e.g. via inbound link count, an early precursor to PageRank), rather than crawling everything on a fixed schedule. Scaling the frontier: A single machine's queue can't hold "every URL on the web" and a single fetcher can't download fast enough. The frontier is partitioned (e.g. by domain hash) across many worker machines, each responsible for fetching a subset of URLs — this also naturally helps enforce per-domain politeness, since all URLs for one domain land on the same worker's queue. Handling crawler traps and infinite spaces: Some sites generate infinite URLs dynamically (e.g. a calendar with a "next month" link that goes on forever). Crawlers cap max depth per site and max pages per domain to avoid getting stuck indefinitely on a single site's infinite link structure. Real-world example: Building a search engine's crawler: seed with a list of popular domains, fetcher pool downloads pages respecting robots.txt and per-domain rate limits, parser extracts text (for the search index)

text: Event-Driven Architecture & CQRS Sources: Martin Fowler's blog (martinfowler.com — "CQRS", "Event Sourcing"), Microsoft Azure Architecture Center (CQRS pattern, Event-driven architecture style) What event-driven architecture is: Services communicate by emitting events ("OrderPlaced", "PaymentFailed") to a broker (Kafka, SNS, RabbitMQ) rather than calling each other's APIs directly. Interested services subscribe to the events they care about and react independently. Producer doesn't know or care who's listening. Why use it over direct service-to-service calls: Loose coupling — order-service doesn't need to know inventory-service, billing-service, and analytics-service exist; it just publishes "OrderPlaced". Adding a new consumer (e.g. a new fraud-detection service) requires zero changes to the producer. Resilience — if notification-service is down, the event waits in its queue; order-service isn't blocked waiting on a slow downstream call. CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation): Split the model used for writes (commands) from the model used for reads (queries) — instead of one model trying to serve both efficiently. Write side: optimized for validating and persisting a change (e.g. normalized relational tables, enforcing invariants). Read side: optimized for how the data is actually queried (e.g. a denormalized, pre-joined view tailored to a specific screen). The two are kept in sync via events — write side publishes an event on every change, read side subscribes and updates its own denormalized copy. Why CQRS pairs with event-driven design: The event stream that keeps read models in sync *is* the event-driven mechanism — a write triggers an event, one or more read models rebuild themselves from it, independently and asynchronously. Trade-off: eventual consistency. Because the read model updates asynchronously after the write event, there's a window where a query might return stale data (read model hasn't caught up yet). This is fine for a lot of use cases (a "likes count" being one event behind is not a problem) but wrong for anything requiring strict consistency (reading your own bank balance right after a transfer). Event Sourcing (often paired with CQRS, but a separate concept): Instead of storing current state and overwriting it, store the full sequence of events that led to the current state ("AccountOpened", "Deposited $100", "Withdrew $30"). Current state is derived by replaying events. Benefit: full audit trail for free, and you can rebuild any past state or fix a bug in projection logic by replaying history with corrected logic. Cost: replaying a long event history to get current state is slow without periodic snapshots; more operational complexity than just storing current state. text: SQL VS NOSQL — WHEN TO USE WHICH Sources: MongoDB documentation, PostgreSQL documentation, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) ch.2-3 Overview: One of the most common system design interview questions is "what database would you use?" There's no universal answer — the right choice depends on your data model, access patterns, consistency requirements, and scale. Understanding the trade-offs is more important than memorizing which is "better." SQL (Relational Databases): Examples: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, Oracle Core Characteristics: - Data organized in tables with fixed schemas (columns defined upfront) - ACID transactions: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability - SQL query language — powerful, joins, aggregations, subqueries - Strong consistency — reads always reflect latest writes - Relations between tables via foreign keys - Vertical scaling primarily (add more CPU/RAM to one server) When to use SQL: - Complex relationships between entities (users → orders → products → inventory) - Need ACID transactions (banking, e-commerce, healthcare) - Data structure is well-defined and unlikely to change frequently - Need complex queries with joins and aggregations - Team knows SQL well (most developers do) - Compliance requirements (many regulations require ACID) NoSQL (Non-Relational Databases): Four types: Document, Key-Value, Column-Family, Graph 1. Document Stores (MongoDB, CouchDB, Firestore): - Data stored as JSON/BSON documents - Flexible schema: different documents can have different fields - Good for: product catalogs, user profiles, content management - Example: MongoDB stores restaurant menus — each restaurant has different menu structure - Query: rich queries on nested fields, but no joins across collections 2. Key-Value Stores (Redis, DynamoDB, Memcached): - Simplest NoSQL: key → value - Extremely fast (O(1) lookup) - Good for: caching, session storage, rate limiting, leaderboards (Redis sorted sets) - Limited query capability — only lookup by key (or key prefix) - Redis extra: supports list, set, hash, sorted set, stream data structures 3. Wide-Column / Column-Family (Cassandra, HBase, DynamoDB): - Rows with flexible columns, organized by partition key - Data spread across nodes by partition key — horizontally scalable - Good for: time-series data, IoT data, message history, activity logs - Cassandra strengths: write-heavy workloads, no single point of failure - Query: must specify partition key; range queries on sort key; no arbitrary queries 4. Graph Databases (Neo4j, Amazon Neptune, JanusGraph): - Data stored as nodes and edges (relationships) - Optimized for traversing relationships - Good for: social networks (friends-of-friends), recommendation engines, fraud detection - Query: Cypher (Neo4j), Gremlin — traverse graph relationships - Overkill for simple use cases; excellent for complex relationship queries Comparison Table: Property | SQL (PostgreSQL) | Document (MongoDB) | Wide-Column (Cassandra) | Key-Value (Redis) Schema | Fixed | Flexible | Flexible columns | None (any value) Transactions | Full ACID | Multi-doc ACID | Lightweight batch only | Basic (MULTI/EXEC) Query Language | SQL (very powerful) | MQL (moderate) | CQL (limited) | Commands only Horizontal Scale | Hard (sharding) | Built-in sharding | Native (ring) | Cluster mode Consistency | Strong | Tunable | Tunable (eventual) | Strong (single) / Eventual (cluster) Best for

text: Search & Indexing (Inverted Index) Sources: Elasticsearch documentation ("Inverted index"), Apache Lucene documentation What it is: Searching billions of documents for a keyword by scanning each one would be far too slow. Search engines instead build an inverted index ahead of time — a data structure that maps each word to the list of documents containing it — so a search becomes a fast lookup instead of a full scan. Forward index vs inverted index: Forward index: document → list of words it contains (this is the natural way you'd store a document, but useless for "find all docs containing X"). Inverted index: word → list of documents containing it. Flips the mapping so a query for a term is a single lookup, not a scan of every document. Building the index: 1. Tokenization: split text into individual terms ("The quick fox" → ["the", "quick", "fox"]). 2. Normalization: lowercase, remove punctuation, stemming (running → run) so "run", "runs", "running" all match the same index entry. 3. Stop word removal (optional): common words like "the", "is" are often excluded since they match nearly everything and add little search value. 4. For each remaining term, append the document ID (and often position within the document, for phrase search) to that term's posting list. Querying: A search for "quick fox" looks up the posting list for "quick" and for "fox", then intersects them — documents in both lists contain both words. Ranking (which result appears first) typically uses TF-IDF or BM25: term frequency (how often the word appears in this doc) weighted against inverse document frequency (how rare the word is across all docs) — a rare word matching is a stronger signal than a common word matching. Distributed search (how this scales to billions of documents): The full index doesn't fit on one machine. It's split into shards, each holding a subset of documents and its own local inverted index. A query fans out to every shard in parallel, each returns its top-N matches, and a coordinating node merges and re-ranks the combined results — this is exactly how Elasticsearch/Solr scale search across a cluster. Each shard is also typically replicated for both availability and to spread read (query) load across replicas. Real-time-ish updates: New documents don't need a full index rebuild — an update is added as a small new index segment; a background merge process periodically combines small segments into larger ones for query efficiency. This is why "just indexed" documents often show up in search within seconds, not instantly, and why search indexes trade a small delay for much better write throughput. Real-world example: An e-commerce product search: catalog of 50M products is sharded across many nodes. Searching "wireless headphones" fans out to every shard, each returns its best local matches ranked by BM25, coordinator merges and returns the final top 20 — the same pattern used by product search on any major e-commerce site or by Elasticsearch-backed log search internally at a company.

text: Web Crawler Design Sources: S. Brin & L. Page, "The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine" (1998), standard system design interview treatment (Alex Xu, "System Design Interview") What it does: Starts from a set of seed URLs, downloads each page, extracts new links from it, and adds those links to a queue to be crawled next — recursively discovering and downloading a large portion of the web. Core components: Seed URLs: the starting set of pages to crawl. Frontier (URL queue): the set of URLs discovered but not yet fetched — this is the main piece of shared state the whole system revolves around. Fetcher: downloads the page content for a URL. Parser/Extractor: pulls new links out of the downloaded HTML, plus whatever content the crawler is actually collecting (text for a search index, prices for a shopping comparison site, etc.). Duplicate detector: avoids re-crawling and re-storing content already seen. Storage: the downloaded content and metadata. Avoiding duplicate work: Two different URLs often point to the same content (mobile vs desktop URL, tracking params, http vs https). Hash the normalized content (not just the URL) to detect "we've already stored this page" even if the URL differs. A Bloom filter is commonly used to cheaply check "have we already queued this URL" before adding it to the frontier, without needing to store every full URL in memory to check. Politeness (this is a hard requirement, not an optimization): Crawling a site too fast can look like — or actually be — a denial-of-service attack, and can get the crawler's IP banned. Rules: respect robots.txt (tells the crawler which paths it's not allowed to fetch), and rate-limit per domain (e.g. max 1 request/second to a given host), typically using a separate queue or delay per domain rather than one global rate limit. Priority / freshness: Not all pages are equal — a news homepage changes hourly, a static about-page almost never. Crawlers assign a re-crawl priority per URL based on how often it has historically changed and how important it is (e.g. via inbound link count, an early precursor to PageRank), rather than crawling everything on a fixed schedule. Scaling the frontier: A single machine's queue can't hold "every URL on the web" and a single fetcher can't download fast enough. The frontier is partitioned (e.g. by domain hash) across many worker machines, each responsible for fetching a subset of URLs — this also naturally helps enforce per-domain politeness, since all URLs for one domain land on the same worker's queue. Handling crawler traps and infinite spaces: Some sites generate infinite URLs dynamically (e.g. a calendar with a "next month" link that goes on forever). Crawlers cap max depth per site and max pages per domain to avoid getting stuck indefinitely on a single site's infinite link structure. Real-world example: Building a search engine's crawler: seed with a list of popular domains, fetcher pool downloads pages respecting robots.txt and per-domain rate limits, parser extracts text (for the search index)

text: Search & Indexing (Inverted Index) Sources: Elasticsearch documentation ("Inverted index"), Apache Lucene documentation What it is: Searching billions of documents for a keyword by scanning each one would be far too slow. Search engines instead build an inverted index ahead of time — a data structure that maps each word to the list of documents containing it — so a search becomes a fast lookup instead of a full scan. Forward index vs inverted index: Forward index: document → list of words it contains (this is the natural way you'd store a document, but useless for "find all docs containing X"). Inverted index: word → list of documents containing it. Flips the mapping so a query for a term is a single lookup, not a scan of every document. Building the index: 1. Tokenization: split text into individual terms ("The quick fox" → ["the", "quick", "fox"]). 2. Normalization: lowercase, remove punctuation, stemming (running → run) so "run", "runs", "running" all match the same index entry. 3. Stop word removal (optional): common words like "the", "is" are often excluded since they match nearly everything and add little search value. 4. For each remaining term, append the document ID (and often position within the document, for phrase search) to that term's posting list. Querying: A search for "quick fox" looks up the posting list for "quick" and for "fox", then intersects them — documents in both lists contain both words. Ranking (which result appears first) typically uses TF-IDF or BM25: term frequency (how often the word appears in this doc) weighted against inverse document frequency (how rare the word is across all docs) — a rare word matching is a stronger signal than a common word matching. Distributed search (how this scales to billions of documents): The full index doesn't fit on one machine. It's split into shards, each holding a subset of documents and its own local inverted index. A query fans out to every shard in parallel, each returns its top-N matches, and a coordinating node merges and re-ranks the combined results — this is exactly how Elasticsearch/Solr scale search across a cluster. Each shard is also typically replicated for both availability and to spread read (query) load across replicas. Real-time-ish updates: New documents don't need a full index rebuild — an update is added as a small new index segment; a background merge process periodically combines small segments into larger ones for query efficiency. This is why "just indexed" documents often show up in search within seconds, not instantly, and why search indexes trade a small delay for much better write throughput. Real-world example: An e-commerce product search: catalog of 50M products is sharded across many nodes. Searching "wireless headphones" fans out to every shard, each returns its best local matches ranked by BM25, coordinator merges and returns the final top 20 — the same pattern used by product search on any major e-commerce site or by Elasticsearch-backed log search internally at a company.
