text: Bloom Filters Sources: Burton H. Bloom, "Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding with Allowable Errors" (1970), Redis documentation (Bloom Filter / probabilistic data structures) What it is: A probabilistic data structure that answers "have I possibly seen this item before?" using a fixed, tiny amount of memory — regardless of how many items have been added. Trades perfect accuracy for massive space savings. The guarantee (this is the important part): No false negatives: if the filter says "definitely not present," the item is genuinely not present. Possible false positives: if the filter says "possibly present," it might actually not be — the false positive rate is tunable (smaller filter / more items = higher false positive rate). It never says "definitely present" for something that was never added incorrectly in the wrong direction — the asymmetry only goes one way, which is what makes it usable: you only need a secondary, slower check for the "possibly present" case. How it works: A bit array of m bits, all initially 0, plus k independent hash functions. To add an item: hash it k times, set the k resulting bit positions to 1. To check an item: hash it the same k times, if ALL k bit positions are 1, report "possibly present"; if ANY bit is 0, report "definitely not present" (since adding that item would have set that bit). False positives happen because bits get shared/overwritten by other items' hashes — you can't tell whether a set bit was set by the item you're checking or by pure coincidence from other insertions. Why not just use a hash set: A hash set storing millions of actual keys uses far more memory (must store each key or at least its full hash) than a Bloom filter, which only needs a handful of bits per item regardless of key size. The trade is: a hash set has zero false positives, a Bloom filter accepts a small false-positive rate in exchange for a fraction of the memory. Cannot remove items (in the basic version): Because bits are shared across multiple items' hashes, clearing a bit to "remove" one item could break the correctness for other items that also set that bit. A Counting Bloom Filter (using small counters instead of single bits) supports removal at the cost of more memory — used when deletions are actually needed. Real-world example: A CDN or database wants to avoid an expensive disk/network lookup for keys that definitely don't exist (e.g. checking if a URL is on a known-malicious list, or if a cache key might exist before hitting disk). Check the Bloom filter first: if "definitely not present," skip the expensive lookup entirely. If "possibly present," do the real (slower, authoritative) lookup to confirm — the small false-positive rate just means occasionally doing an unnecessary real lookup, never missing an item that's actually there. This is exactly how Cassandra and HBase use Bloom filters to skip SSTable files that don't contain a given key, avoiding unnecessary disk

text: Slack System Design (Case Study) Sources: Slack Engineering Blog (slack.engineering) Core challenge: Real-time message delivery to potentially thousands of connected clients per workspace, while keeping full message history durable and searchable, and keeping every client's view of a channel consistent as new messages, edits, and reactions arrive. Real-time delivery via WebSockets: Each connected client holds a persistent WebSocket connection to a gateway server. When a message is sent, it's written to the durable store first, then fanned out over the open WebSocket connections of every client currently viewing that channel — the WebSocket is for live delivery to already-connected clients, not the system of record; a client reconnecting after being offline fetches missed history from the durable store via a normal API call, not by expecting to replay it from the socket. The "gateway holds connections, backend holds truth" split: Gateway/connection servers are relatively lightweight and mostly hold open sockets and route messages; the actual message data, ordering, and history lives in the backend datastore. This separation lets Slack scale the number of concurrent open connections independently from the storage/query layer — a spike in simultaneous online users stresses connection servers, not necessarily the database. Sharding by workspace/channel: Slack's engineering blog has discussed sharding message storage by team/channel, since most reads and writes for a given message are scoped to one channel — this keeps related data (a channel's message history) together on the same shard, so a typical "load channel history" query hits one shard rather than fanning out across the whole dataset. Historical MySQL scaling (Vitess): Slack has written about outgrowing a single large MySQL setup and adopting Vitess (a MySQL sharding middleware, originally built at YouTube) to shard their relational data horizontally while keeping the MySQL query interface application code already relied on — an example of solving a scaling problem by adding a sharding layer in front of an existing database technology, rather than fully rewriting onto a different database. Presence (online/offline/typing indicators): Presence state changes extremely frequently (far more often than actual messages) and is far less critical to get perfectly right — a "typing..." indicator being a second late or occasionally wrong is a minor UX blemish, not a correctness bug. This makes presence a good candidate for the most relaxed consistency and heaviest batching/throttling in the whole system, illustrating that not every real-time-feeling feature needs the same delivery guarantees as the actual message content. Real-world takeaway for interviews: "Design Slack/a chat app" questions hinge on separating three different problems that are easy to conflate: durable message storage (needs to be correct and never lost), real-time fan-out to online clients (needs to be fast, some staleness on reconnect is fine since history backfills it), and ephemeral presence state (needs to be cheap and fast, correctness is optional) — each deserves a different consistency/durability trade-off.

Users can store files in the cloud and access them from multiple devices, with changes synced automatically. Core challenges: (1) efficient sync — only send what changed, not the entire file, (2) handle concurrent edits from multiple devices, (3) store and retrieve petabytes of files reliably. Scale Numbers (Dropbox): - 700+ million registered users - 600,000+ business customers - 500 petabytes of data stored - 1 billion files uploaded per day - 10 million concurrent connected devices Core Features: 1. Upload files to cloud storage 2. Sync files across multiple devices 3. Share files and folders with others 4. Version history (restore deleted/older files) 5. Offline access (local cache) 6. Real-time collaboration (Google Docs style, for Google Drive) The Sync Problem — This is Everything: Naive approach: When file changes, upload entire file. Problem: A 10GB video with a 1KB edit = waste 10GB of bandwidth. Unacceptable. Chunking (Block-Level Sync): 1. File is split into fixed-size blocks (4MB default) 2. Each block is hashed (SHA-256) 3. When file changes, only the changed blocks are identified by comparing hashes 4. Only changed blocks are uploaded 5. Metadata (block list with hashes) stored separately from block content Example: Edit 100 lines in a 500MB file - Only the 4MB block containing those lines has a different hash - Upload: 4MB instead of 500MB - 99% bandwidth saving Deduplication: - If block with hash "abc123" already exists in cloud, don't upload it - Many files have common blocks (PDF headers, common library files) - Content-addressed storage: block stored by its hash, not by name - This also means if two users upload the same file, it's only stored once Architecture Overview: Client (Desktop app): - Monitors local file system for changes (OS file watchers: inotify on Linux, FSEvents on Mac, ReadDirectoryChangesW on Windows) - Maintains local SQLite database of: file metadata, block hashes, sync status - On change: compute changed blocks, upload to Block Storage, update Metadata Server Components: 1. Client apps (desktop, mobile, web) 2. Block Storage Service — stores actual file content (blocks) 3. Metadata Service — stores file/folder structure, block lists, versions 4. Notification Service — notifies all connected devices when remote change happens 5. text: Load Balancer System Design Sources: AWS Elastic Load Balancing documentation, NGINX documentation (Load Balancing) What it is: A load balancer distributes incoming network traffic across multiple servers. Prevents any single server from becoming a bottleneck. Essential for high availability and horizontal scaling. Types of Load Balancers: 1. Layer 4 (Transport Layer): Routes based on IP and TCP/UDP port. Fast, no content inspection. Cannot route based on URL path or headers. Example: AWS Network Load Balancer. 2. Layer 7 (Application Layer): Routes based on HTTP content — URL, headers, cookies. Can do path-based routing (/api → API servers, /static → CDN). Example: AWS Application Load Balancer, Nginx. Load Balancing Algorithms: Round Robin: Requests distributed evenly in order. Simple, works well when servers have equal capacity. Weighted Round Robin: Servers get requests proportional to weight. Used when servers have different capacities. Least Connections: New request goes to server with fewest active connections. Better for long-lived connections (WebSockets, streaming). IP Hash: Client IP hashed to always hit same server. Useful for session stickiness (user always hits same server). Problem: uneven distribution if many users share an IP (NAT). Consistent Hashing: Used for distributed cache and storage routing. Minimizes remapping when servers are added or removed. Health Checks: Load balancer pings each server every few seconds. If server fails health check, removed from rotation automatically. When server recovers, added back automatically. This is how zero-downtime deployments work. Session Stickiness (Sticky Sessions): Problem: User login session stored on Server A. Request goes to Server B — user logged out. Solution 1: Sticky sessions — same user always hits same server (IP hash). Solution 2: Externalize sessions to Redis — any server can read any session. Solution 2 is better for true stateless servers. Real-world stack for Swiggy scale: DNS → AWS Route53 (global traffic routing) → AWS CloudFront (CDN + DDoS protection) → AWS ALB (Layer 7, path-based routing) → Auto Scaling Groups (EC2 instances) → Services

text: LinkedIn & the Origin of Kafka (Case Study) Sources: LinkedIn Engineering Blog, Kreps, Narkhede, Rao — "Kafka: a Distributed Messaging System for Log Processing" (NetDB 2011) The problem LinkedIn had: By the early 2010s, LinkedIn had many separate systems that needed the same underlying activity data — the news feed, search indexing, relevance/ML pipelines, monitoring, and analytics all needed a feed of user activity events (page views, connections made, likes). Each consumer had built its own point-to-point pipeline to get this data, resulting in an N×M mess of custom, fragile integrations between every producer and every consumer. Why existing message queues weren't a fit: Traditional queues (JMS-style brokers) were built for low-throughput, transactional messaging, not the sustained high-throughput firehose of activity events LinkedIn needed to move (hundreds of billions of events/day at LinkedIn's later scale). They also typically delete a message once consumed, so a second, independent consumer couldn't replay the same stream. Kafka's core design choices (as a direct response to that problem): Log-based storage: instead of deleting messages after delivery, Kafka retains them for a configured period (or forever) as an append-only log. Multiple independent consumer groups can each read the same stream at their own pace, tracking their own offset — this single change is what let LinkedIn support many different downstream consumers off one shared pipeline instead of N separate point-to-point integrations. Partitioning: each topic is split into partitions, each handled independently and in order, allowing horizontal scaling of both writes and reads by adding more partitions and consumers. Sequential disk I/O: Kafka relies on sequential reads/writes to disk (fast, even on spinning disks) plus OS page cache, rather than random access — this is why Kafka achieves very high throughput despite persisting everything. Pull-based consumption: consumers pull at their own pace and track their own offset, rather than the broker pushing and needing to track per-consumer state — simplifies the broker and lets slow consumers fall behind without overwhelming themselves, catching up later from their last offset. Outcome: LinkedIn open-sourced Kafka in 2011 and it became an Apache project; it's now the de facto standard for high-throughput event streaming across the industry (adopted by Netflix, Uber, and most large-scale systems that need a durable, replayable, multi-consumer event backbone) — a direct example of solving an internal integration problem generally enough that it became foundational infrastructure well beyond its original use case. Relevance to system design interviews: "Why Kafka over a traditional queue" is a common follow-up question — the answer is precisely this history: replayability (log retention, multiple independent consumer groups) and throughput (partitioning + sequential I/O), not just "it's a queue but faster."

text: APACHE KAFKA — SYSTEM DESIGN DEEP DIVE Sources: Apache Kafka documentation, Kreps, Narkhede, Rao — "Kafka: a Distributed Messaging System for Log Processing" (NetDB 2011) Overview: Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform. Think of it as a highly durable, infinitely scalable message queue where producers write events and consumers read them. It's used in almost every large-scale system: Uber uses it for location updates, LinkedIn (who built Kafka) uses it for activity feeds, Netflix uses it for analytics pipeline. Core Concepts: Event/Message: A piece of data — "user_id: 123 placed order_id: 456 at timestamp: 1234567890" Topic: A named log of events. Like a table in a database. E.g., "order-events" topic Producer: Writes events to a topic Consumer: Reads events from a topic Broker: A Kafka server that stores events Cluster: Multiple brokers working together Partition: A topic is split into partitions for parallelism Offset: A sequential ID for each event in a partition (like array index) Consumer Group: Multiple consumers sharing the work of reading a topic Why Kafka? (vs Traditional Message Queues like RabbitMQ): Traditional queue: event consumed → deleted from queue Kafka: events retained for configurable period (default 7 days) → multiple consumers can independently read the same events This is transformative: - Add a new consumer without affecting existing ones - Replay events from past (debugging, backfilling new systems) - Decouple producers from consumers completely Kafka vs RabbitMQ: - RabbitMQ: message broker, push model, messages deleted after consumption, good for task queues - Kafka: event log, pull model, messages retained, good for event streaming and data pipelines - Choose Kafka when: multiple consumers need the same events, need event replay, high throughput - Choose RabbitMQ when: complex routing, guaranteed message ordering per consumer, task-queue pattern Architecture Deep Dive: Topics and Partitions: - Topic "order-events" might have 12 partitions - Each partition is an ordered, immutable log of events - Partitions distributed across brokers (partition 0 on broker 1, partition 1 on broker 2, etc.) - Events within a partition are strictly ordered - Events across partitions have no guaranteed order Partition Key: - Producer specifies a key per event: order.send(key="user_123", value=event) - All events with same key go to same partition - Guarantees ordering for events with same key (e.g., all events for user_123 are ordered) - Without key: round-robin across partitions Replication: - Each partition has a leader and N replicas on different brokers (N = replication factor) - Default replication factor: 3 (1 leader + 2 replicas) - All reads/writes go to leader - Replicas passively sync from leader - If leader fails, a replica is automatically elected as new leader (ZooKeeper or KRaft consensus) - Durability: Kafka can acknowledge write only after all replicas confirm receipt (acks=all) Consumer Groups: - Multiple consumers in a group share partitions - Each partition assigned to exactly one consumer in a group - 12 partitions + 6 consumers = 2 partitions per consumer (parallelism) - 12 partitions + 12 consumers = 1 partition per consumer (max parallelism)

text: CAP THEOREM AND DISTRIBUTED SYSTEMS CONSISTENCY Sources: Eric Brewer, "CAP Twelve Years Later: How the 'Rules' Have Changed" (IEEE Computer, 2012); Gilbert & Lynch, "Brewer's Conjecture and the Feasibility of Consistent, Available, Partition-Tolerant Web Services" (2002) Overview: The CAP theorem states that a distributed database system can only guarantee two of three properties simultaneously: Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance. Understanding CAP is fundamental to system design — every database and architectural decision involves these trade-offs. The Three Properties: C — Consistency: Every read returns the most recent write (or an error). If you write a value on node 1 and immediately read it from node 2, you get the updated value. This is "strong consistency." Example: bank account balance — you must see the current balance, not a stale one. A — Availability: Every request receives a response (not an error), though it might not be the most recent data. The system keeps responding even if some nodes are down. Example: Netflix shows you recommendations even if their recommendation engine is partially down. P — Partition Tolerance: The system continues operating even if network messages are lost or delayed between nodes. A "partition" = network split where nodes can't communicate. In reality: you cannot opt out of P. Networks fail. Partitions happen. You MUST handle partitions. The Real Choice — CP or AP: Since P is mandatory, the real choice is: when a partition occurs, do you sacrifice C or A? CP (Consistency + Partition Tolerance): - When partition happens: refuse to answer rather than return stale data - Some requests get errors during partition - But when you respond, you're always correct - Examples: ZooKeeper, HBase, Google Spanner, MongoDB (with journaling), traditional relational databases AP (Availability + Partition Tolerance): - When partition happens: respond with possibly stale data - System always responds, never returns error - Data might be outdated temporarily - Examples: Cassandra, DynamoDB, CouchDB, DNS Neither CP nor AP fully — just P: - Technically, traditional SQL in a single datacenter: gives up P (can't run across partitions) - Rarely applicable in modern distributed systems Consistency Models (Spectrum): Strong Consistency (Linearizability): - Every read sees the most recent write - As if there's only one copy of data - Slowest — requires synchronization - Example: Google Spanner uses atomic clocks to achieve this globally Sequential Consistency: - All nodes see operations in same order, but might lag - Operations appear instantaneous but may not be truly real-time Causal Consistency: - Causally related operations are seen in order - "If you see my reply, you must have seen my original post" - Used by some distributed databases Eventual Consistency: - If no new updates, all nodes will eventually have the same value - Queries may return stale data temporarily - Highest availability, used by: DynamoDB, Cassandra, S3 - Most common choice for high-scale systems Read-Your-Own-Writes: - You always see your own updates (even if others don't yet) - Instagram: after you post a photo, you see it even

text: API Gateway Sources: AWS API Gateway Developer Guide, Kong Gateway documentation What it is: A single entry point that sits in front of a collection of backend services (especially in a microservices architecture) and routes each incoming request to the right service. Clients talk to one gateway instead of knowing about every individual service's address. What it handles (so individual services don't have to): Routing: maps a path/method to the right backend service (/users → user-service, /orders → order-service). Authentication: validates JWT/API keys once at the edge, so downstream services trust the gateway instead of each re-implementing auth. Rate limiting: throttles per-client request rate before it ever reaches backend services, protecting them from being overwhelmed. Request/response transformation: e.g. converting a legacy SOAP backend response to JSON for modern clients, without changing the backend. Aggregation: combining calls to multiple services into a single client-facing response (sometimes called the "backend for frontend" pattern) — a mobile app screen might need data from 3 services, gateway can fan out and merge. Observability: single place to log, trace, and monitor all API traffic instead of instrumenting every service separately. TLS termination: gateway handles HTTPS, internal traffic between gateway and services can be plain HTTP within a trusted network. Gateway vs Load Balancer: A load balancer (L4/L7) distributes traffic across replicas of the *same* service based on IP/path. An API gateway routes across *different* services and adds application-level concerns (auth, rate limiting, transformation) on top — they're often used together: gateway routes to a service name, load balancer distributes across that service's replicas. Failure mode to watch for: Single point of failure — if the gateway goes down, every service behind it is unreachable even if they're all healthy. Mitigated by running multiple gateway instances behind their own load balancer, and keeping the gateway itself stateless so any instance can handle any request. Backend for Frontend (BFF) pattern: Instead of one generic gateway for all clients, run a dedicated gateway per client type (mobile-BFF, web-BFF) — each shaped to that client's specific data needs, avoiding a single gateway trying to please every consumer with one generic contract. Real-world example: A ride-sharing app's mobile client hits a single gateway endpoint. Gateway validates the JWT, then calls trip-service, pricing-service, and driver-location-service in parallel, merges their responses into one JSON payload the app expects — the mobile client never needs to know these are three separate backend services, or that pricing-service might be redeployed independently tomorrow.
